lessons.title: Before changing the IR
lessons.summary: Recall SSA and dominance, learn the memory operations we will introduce, and locate the exact boundary between inspection and transformation.
lessons.takeaway: Changing IR means taking responsibility for both its structure and behavior.

blocks.text: Why changing a branch can break a value

We work with LLVM intermediate representation (IR), the instructions between source code and machine code. A function body is divided into basic blocks: straight-line instruction sequences ending in a terminator such as a branch or return. Branches connect blocks into a control-flow graph (CFG). A predecessor is a block with an incoming edge to the block we are discussing; a successor is a destination of an outgoing edge. An instruction defines a result when it produces a value, and another instruction uses that result when it consumes it.

Day 1 described programs. Day 2 changes how they execute. Our goal is to route decisions through one dispatcher while preserving the answers, effects, and termination of every execution covered by our support contract. This is why we cannot start by replacing all the branches: a program carries both control flow (which block runs next) and data flow (which computed values later instructions use).

Why route decisions through a dispatcher at all? Ordinary branches expose familiar shapes such as a diamond for an if/else and a back edge for a loop. Control-flow flattening aims to obscure that direct structure by making many transitions use one shared routing mechanism. We still owe the caller the same computation. This project lets us study that representation change and its costs; whether it remains difficult to analyze after optimization is a separate question.

Imagine one block computes a subtotal and another returns it. The old route guarantees that calculation happens before the return. New dispatcher edges change the routes LLVM sees. Even if our state numbers are intended to choose the right order at runtime, the rewritten IR must still obey LLVM’s rules for where each value can be used.

rows: What you should understand before coding
Existing value dependencies were designed for the old graph.
Where each value comes from and how a later use receives it.
The next block must be selected through the dispatcher.
How each old decision becomes a next-state choice.
A valid-looking graph may still compute the wrong answer.
Which structural rules and observable results must remain true.

blocks.text: The first lessons therefore concentrate on values, especially PHIs. These are preparation steps for flattening, not unrelated instruction-counting exercises. Each later lesson explains which part of the same control-and-data problem it addresses.
Task: Read this context before editing FlatteningPass. Day 1 built the plugin, statistics, CFG analysis, and eligibility checker. Day 2 starts changing eligible functions.
What are we trying to build?

A dispatcher is a block that reads a state number and uses a switch to choose the next program block. Eventually, an original branch will become “store the destination state, then branch to the dispatcher.” We have not implemented that complete transformation yet.

original entry/setup → dispatcher → selected original block
                           ↑                  |
                           └──────────────────┘
The original entry stays a one-time setup block. Its stack slots must not be allocated repeatedly in the dispatcher. Return and unreachable blocks finish their path instead of looping back.
Recall SSA and dominance

An SSA value has one definition. That definition must dominate its uses: every reachable path from entry to a use passes through the definition. Adding dispatcher edges can create new paths that violate that relationship, even if the original program never had a problem.
The memory operations you will see

rows: Allocate space for one i32 in the current function’s stack frame; the result is a pointer.
Write %x into the storage addressed by %slot; the instruction produces no result.
Read an i32 from that address; the result is a new SSA value.
Select an incoming value according to the predecessor edge used to enter the block.

blocks.text: Demotion replaces selected SSA dependencies with stores and loads. “Register” here means an LLVM SSA, register-like value—not a guaranteed physical CPU register. The original arithmetic remains; the way its result reaches users changes.
Your starting template
Edit the existing lib/FlatteningPass.cpp. Do not create a second run() definition. The eligibility guard from Day 1 stays at the top; every new mutation belongs after it.
How to use the lessons

items: Start with the template. Fill in each numbered step yourself.
Use the full implementation to compare only after trying the exercise. Snippets state where to insert them.
Run verify after each complete structural change. It checks valid IR, not equivalent program behavior.
A template containing TODOs is an exercise scaffold, not a claim that the transformation is finished.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: Why must eligibility run before mutation? Why is a successful verifier run weaker than proving that a transformation preserves behavior?

items: The pass's contract is that rejected input comes back untouched: the eligibility guard sits at the top of `run()` (before the TODO mutation site in the template), so if we demoted instructions first and then discovered an unsupported feature, the function would be left half-transformed and could no longer be returned unchanged. The support decision must therefore complete before the first edit.

The verifier checks structural IR rules — well-formed instructions, valid terminators, SSA dominance — and says nothing about whether the transformed function computes what the original did: a swapped branch destination would verify cleanly and return the wrong answer, which is why Day 2 adds a differential comparison on a defined domain as separate evidence of behavior.

blocks.text: Study-session walkthrough — make one representation change at a time

Move from inspection to transformation through small checkpoints. Printing diagnostics does not intentionally change the graph, while inserting instructions or edges can break its rules. Decide the expected difference for one stage before adding the next.
Before writing, answer: What should I change first, and how can I tell whether that change—not a later stage—caused a failure?

inspect original → collect PHIs → demote PHIs → prepare other values
                 → map states → construct dispatch → connect transitions

This is an implementation sequence, not a promise to execute those stages as target-program instructions. Each arrow establishes assumptions for the next step. Keep the existing declaration/eligibility exits before all mutation, and keep generated outputs under build/. A PHI-only checkpoint may legitimately leave the old branch structure intact.
Task: Small writing step: Mark the current checkpoint in your own notes before editing. Identify which existing run() will contain the change; do not add a second definition.

Checkpoint: After the next small edit, can you name the expected IR difference and the relevant input fixture before running opt? The complete before/after section shows reference endpoints, not evidence that your working pass already implements them.

items: Yes — before running, name the fixture the edit affects (for example `merge.ll` for a demotion step, `loop.ll` for an entry-branch step) and the exact expected difference: which instruction appears (a store/load pair, a new `ms.dispatch` block, a rewritten terminator) and which fixtures must remain byte-identical at that stage.

The book's complete before/after module is the reference endpoint — what the finished pipeline emits — so matching it mid-build is accidental and mismatching it is expected; at this step your pass should be compared against the input fixture and the one difference you predicted, not against the final reference.

blocks.text: LLVM program before and after this checkpoint
Preview of the complete Day 2 pipeline, not an edit to make in the background lesson. Later checkpoints reach this shape in smaller steps.
What changes: The PHI becomes path-specific stores plus a load; state storage and a switch route original transitions through dispatch.
Reading this LLVM program from zero

Do not read every displayed block as one straight-line script. A call supplies the function inputs and starts its first block. Within the selected block, follow the written instructions until a terminator chooses another block or returns to the caller. A label names a block; it does not execute an operation by itself.

rows: `define` starts a function body. `@merge` is the module-level function name; `i32` immediately before it is the return type. Parentheses contain typed inputs supplied by the caller; braces contain its blocks.

i1 means one bit: 0 is false and 1 is true for a condition; i32 means a 32-bit integer bit pattern; signed interpretation comes from operations such as slt or sdiv, not from a separate signed i32 type.

An opaque pointer value: it can represent an address or the special handle returned in the coroutine example. It does not contain an i32 integer or encode a pointee type. A load/store spells out the type of value accessed separately from the pointer.

The left side names the result of this instruction. Each SSA result has one static defining instruction; input arguments are values supplied at function entry. A name is a handle for a value, not a mutable source variable or a guaranteed CPU register.

The colon defines a block label; the label operand names a jump destination. `%` is also used for local result/argument names, so use the type/context to distinguish a value from a block target. `@` instead identifies a module-level symbol.

This is a typed literal: the i-prefixed part specifies the bit width, and the decimal part is the constant value. For example, a case number or stored state ID is an integer value, unlike a `%name` or `name:` label.

Everything after a semicolon on that line is a comment for the reader. The printer lists incoming blocks after preds; it is not an instruction, an execution order, or a separate edge definition. Branch/switch operands actually define the edges.

Alignment is in bytes, not elements, bits, or a value to store. An aligned alloca provides suitably aligned storage; an aligned load/store promises that its pointer meets that alignment. It does not initialize memory or change the integer read/written.

blocks.text: Every instruction used in this pair

rows: Meaning and operand order in these listings

Reserve storage for the shown element type in this function invocation and produce its address, not the stored integer. `alloca i32` reserves one i32 slot. The allocation does not initialize its contents; a store must supply a value before an intended read.

`br label %B` always transfers control to block B. `br i1 %C, label %A, label %B` goes to A for true and B for false; their order matters. A branch is the block’s final instruction and produces no result. It does not execute both destinations.

Read a value from memory: in `load i32, ptr %slot`, i32 is the loaded value’s type and %slot is its address. The left-hand result gets the current contents, not another copy of the address. Each load defines a new SSA value; it does not compute the value that a missing earlier store should have supplied.

Define one value by the edge just used to enter this block. Each `[ VALUE, %PREDECESSOR ]` pairs an incoming value with its source block; it is not an array access. The PHI’s i32 type applies to every incoming value, so a literal inside a bracket does not repeat the type. PHIs go at the start of a block. On a loop’s first entry choose its entry value, and on a back edge choose its carried value. Multiple PHIs select incoming values together, rather than sequentially overwriting each other.

End this function invocation and return the typed operand to its caller. `ret i32 %v` returns the integer value, while `ret ptr ...` returns a pointer. A return does not proceed to the next printed block or automatically go back to dispatch.

Produce a value from `select i1 CONDITION, TYPE TRUE_VALUE, TYPE FALSE_VALUE`. A true condition chooses the first alternative, false the second; alternatives have the same type. This does not branch or conditionally execute the instructions that computed the operands. Here the chosen result is either a destination’s state number or the final return value.

Write memory: in `store i32 VALUE, ptr ADDRESS`, the first operand is the value and the second is the destination address. A store has an effect but no result name. Writing a state slot changes the next routing choice; writing a demotion slot transports an original program value.

Transfer control according to one integer value. The destination immediately after the condition is the default for no matching case. Each line inside `[...]` pairs a typed case constant with `label %DESTINATION`; only one destination is taken. An original switch chooses a program outcome; a dispatcher switch decodes the stored state ID. The brackets are a case list, not a runtime array.

End the block by asserting that execution never reaches this point on a defined run. Actually executing it is undefined behavior; it is not error recovery, a return, or a C++ exception. The state-machine invariant must prevent a bad stored ID from taking this default path.

blocks.text: Keep address, contents, and loaded value separate. For example, an alloca result is the address of a slot; a store writes an integer into that slot; a later load defines a new SSA name for the integer read back. The pointer name does not become the stored number. A value slot preserves program data, whereas ms.state (when present) stores a control-flow destination encoding.
Walk one concrete execution

Call merge with condition = true: take left and obtain 10; with false, take right and obtain 20. In a PHI listing join chooses the incoming constant using the predecessor edge. In a demoted listing only the executed path stores its constant, and join reads that value. In the complete machine entry selects state 0 or 1, the chosen path writes its data value then state 2, and dispatch enters join. The stored state number 2 means “run join”; it is not the result 10 or 20.

blocks.title: Read the complete before-and-after LLVM modules

blocks.text: Before — phi original

define i32 @merge(i1 %condition) {
entry:
  br i1 %condition, label %left, label %right

left:                                             ; preds = %entry
  br label %join

right:                                            ; preds = %entry
  br label %join

join:                                             ; preds = %right, %left
  %value = phi i32 [ 10, %left ], [ 20, %right ]
  ret i32 %value
}
After — phi full

define i32 @merge(i1 %condition) {
entry:
  %ms.state = alloca i32, align 4
  %value.reg2mem = alloca i32, align 4
  %ms.next = select i1 %condition, i32 0, i32 1
  store i32 %ms.next, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

left:                                             ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  store i32 10, ptr %value.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 2, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

right:                                            ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  store i32 20, ptr %value.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 2, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

join:                                             ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  %value.reload = load i32, ptr %value.reg2mem, align 4
  ret i32 %value.reload

ms.dispatch:                                      ; preds = %right, %left, %entry
  %ms.current = load i32, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  switch i32 %ms.current, label %ms.invalid [
    i32 0, label %left
    i32 1, label %right
    i32 2, label %join
  ]

ms.invalid:                                       ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  unreachable
}

Both listings are complete LLVM modules defining the example function, not fragments with omitted blocks. They have no main driver unless one is explicitly included; opt can parse and verify them, while execution requires a caller. Names, alignments, and printer annotations may differ in your own output. These listings were generated and verified with the isolated LLVM 23.1.5 teaching references, not copied from an assumed completed learner implementation.
Follow the values and edges: True still reaches left’s store of 10, false reaches right’s store of 20, and both eventually return the selected value.

quiz.q: Why prepare SSA values before adding dispatcher edges?
choices: Extra edges can break definition-to-use dominance
The verifier requires every function to use memory
PHIs are forbidden in all LLVM programs
quiz.why: PHIs are valid LLVM IR. It is our planned CFG restructuring that can invalidate existing SSA relationships.

lessons.title: Collect PHIs without changing them
lessons.summary: Understand why SSA needs a path-dependent value at a join, why changing predecessors threatens that choice, and why we collect PHIs before rewriting them.
lessons.takeaway: Preserve the incoming path’s value choice before replacing its edges.

blocks.text: Why a compiler needs a PHI at a join
Start with a familiar source-language variable. A conditional can assign that variable on either path, and code after the conditional must use whichever assignment actually happened:

LLVM commonly represents computed values in static single assignment form, or SSA: each named instruction result has one defining instruction; a function argument is a value supplied at function entry. This makes dependencies explicit. An optimizer can follow a name back to one definition instead of searching through every possible reassignment of a mutable variable. One static definition can execute many times in a loop; “single assignment” describes the IR definition, not a promise to execute it only once.

At a join, however, the available value depends on the path taken. We cannot give one SSA name two separate defining assignments. A PHI expresses that choice in one definition. In tests/ir/phi.ll, the relevant instruction is:

join:
  %value = phi i32 [ 10, %left ], [ 20, %right ]
  ret i32 %value

Read each bracket as “value, incoming predecessor.” If execution enters join from left, value is 10; if it enters from right, value is 20. The predecessor is the block whose edge was just taken. The PHI does not rerun the condition, execute both paths, or take whichever value appears first in the text. This example uses constants; real incoming values can be results computed on the different paths.
Why PHIs matter to our flattening pass

Before: left  ───────→ join     PHI can distinguish left from right.
        right ───────→ join

Later:  left/right → dispatcher → join
                               The last predecessor is now dispatcher.

If we change the edges but keep the old PHI unchanged, its incoming labels no longer describe the predecessors of join. The PHI is both a useful account of the original value choice and a dependency on the original graph. We need to preserve that choice in another form before replacing those edges.

This lesson only finds those instructions and records their addresses. The next lessons use that worklist to replace predecessor-based choices with explicit memory transfers. A count of zero means this preparation step has nothing to do; it does not mean the function has no other data-flow constraints.
Checkpoint: If join is entered from right, why must the PHI select 20? What information would disappear if the immediate predecessor became dispatcher?

items: The two paths compute different values: `left` stores 10 and `right` stores 20, and the join block's `phi i32 [ 10, %left ], [ 20, %right ]` resolves that choice by the edge actually used to enter. When join is entered from `right`, the program's answer is 20, so the PHI must select the `%right` incoming value.

A PHI's value is a function of which predecessor executed. If the immediate predecessor became `ms.dispatch`, every arrival would look like it came from the same block and the predecessor-identity information would vanish from the CFG — exactly what the demotion slot (the predecessor's store and the join's load) exists to preserve.

blocks.text: Task: Collect PHI nodes in the existing FlatteningPass::run(), after the eligibility guard. This lesson does not modify IR.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Include the types and container
Instructions.h defines PHINode and other instruction subclasses. Casting.h supplies LLVM’s type checks. std::vector is a growable collection; this vector’s element type is PHINode*, not Instruction*.
Step 2 — Traverse existing instructions by reference

F is a mutable Function&. Therefore auto &BB and auto &I refer to mutable existing blocks and instructions. Plain auto would try to copy objects; const auto & would prevent collecting the mutable PHI pointers needed by the later utility.
Step 3 — Keep the result of dyn_cast

dyn_cast returns a PHINode* when the instruction is a PHI, or nullptr otherwise. The if tests that pointer. push_back copies the pointer into the vector; it does not copy or take ownership of the instruction.
Step 4 — Print and preserve
llvm::errs() << "Number of PHIs: " << phis.size() << "\n";
Keep PreservedAnalyses::all(): collecting pointers and printing a count leave IR unchanged. The existing function declaration and rejection returns also remain unchanged.
Study-session walkthrough — collect a worklist before calling a mutating helper

Gather PHI nodes before calling helpers that erase or replace them. The vector is a worklist of existing instruction addresses, separating discovery from mutation rather than changing the target program immediately.
Before writing, answer: Why save addresses in a vector instead of immediately changing each PHI as the instruction loop visits it?

F contains blocks and each block contains instructions. The references BB and I name existing mutable objects. dyn_cast checks the instruction class and returns a typed borrowed pointer, or nullptr. push_back saves that pointer; it does not copy or own a PHI. Keeping mutation outside this traversal avoids invalidating the instruction-list iterator when the later helper erases a PHI.
Task: Small writing step: Write only the collection and count first. Keep the preservation result all() while no IR changes.

Checkpoint: Predict one PHI for phi.ll and one for loop.ll. Then run the inspection checkpoint and compare canonical IR: it should be unchanged. Counting the object is not yet lowering its predecessor-dependent choice.

items: `phi.ll` has exactly one PHI: the join block's merge value with incoming values `[10, %left]` and `[20, %right]`. `loop.ll` has exactly one PHI: the loop counter with incoming value `0` on the first entry (from `%entry`) and the body's incremented value on the back edge.

The inspection run only counts and prints the PHIs, so the emitted canonical IR must be byte-identical to the input; counting (or printing) a PHI's incoming values reads the object without touching it, and the predecessor-dependent choice — which incoming value is live — is lowered only when a later lesson replaces the PHI with a slot load.

blocks.text: The full implementation of this insertion
Verify

cmake --build build
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -disable-output tests/ir/phi.ll
Checkpoint: What does the vector own? Why do we retain pointers rather than copies? What changes when a later utility deletes a PHI?

items: The vector owns its own contiguous array of pointer values (the addresses); the `PHINode` objects themselves are owned by their parent basic block, and ultimately by the function.

IR objects such as `PHINode` are non-copyable, so there is no meaningful copy to store — a vector of `PHINode` values would not compile — and a pointer to the live instruction is the only handle that lets the pass act on the real object in place.

When a later utility (for example `DemotePHIToStack`) erases a PHI from its parent block, the vector's stored pointer still holds the old address but the object at that address no longer exists — the entry dangles, which is why the day's rule is to collect all pointers first, then mutate, and never read or iterate entries after erasure.

quiz.q: Why prepare PHIs before routing incoming paths through one dispatcher?
choices: Their value choice refers to incoming edges that the rewrite will change
PHIs are invalid in every ordinary LLVM function
The dispatcher can infer the old predecessor from the order of cases
quiz.why: A PHI associates incoming values with predecessor edges. Preserve that association before replacing those edges.

lessons.title: Keep the typed pointer from dyn_cast
lessons.originalTitle: Keep the typed pointer from dyn_cast
lessons.summary: Understand the actual push_back error: a successful type test does not change the declared type of the original instruction.
lessons.takeaway: A type check is useful only if you keep the typed result you need.

blocks.text: Why the worklist needs a more specific kind of instruction

The previous lesson identified PHIs as the operations whose incoming choices must be preserved. But the loop visits every instruction: arithmetic, loads, branches, returns, and PHIs. The later PHI-demotion helper accepts a PHINode*, so the worklist must contain instructions proven to be PHIs.

A typed pointer records that knowledge in C++. Testing whether an instruction is a PHI does not change the declared type of the original loop variable. Keeping the pointer returned by dyn_cast carries the successful check into the vector and then into the transformation call. This is how the conceptual selection becomes a type-safe worklist; it creates no new IR object.
Task: Fix the pointer-type mismatch encountered while collecting PHIs. Work in the inner instruction loop from the previous lesson.
The failing template
Step 1 — Read the declared types

A PHINode derives from Instruction. Converting PHINode* to Instruction* is an upcast. The reverse needs a check: an arbitrary Instruction* might identify an add, branch, load, or return. A condition does not automatically narrow the C++ type of I.
Step 2 — Name the cast result
auto *phi = llvm::dyn_cast<llvm::PHINode>(&I);
This does not allocate a PHI. It gives a more specific pointer to the same instruction if the type matches. The draft discarded this pointer and then pushed the original, less-specific &I.
Step 3 — Append only a successful cast
Use an if-initializer-style declaration in the condition so the typed pointer is available inside the body. A null pointer skips the body.
Study-session walkthrough — the push_back mismatch is about the static pointer type

A dyn_cast check can succeed while push_back still receives the wrong static pointer type. If you discard the typed result and append &I, vector<PHINode*> receives the more general Instruction*. Keep the checked pointer instead.
Before writing, answer: If the if-condition proved this instruction is a PHI, why does phis.push_back(&I) still fail?

The test does not rewrite I’s C++ declaration. &I still has type Instruction*. A PHINode is an Instruction, so a PHINode* can be used where Instruction* is expected, but an arbitrary Instruction* is not automatically a PHINode*. The pointer returned by dyn_cast carries the successful check in its static type. Both pointers identify the same existing IR object.
Task: Small writing step: Change only the if initializer and the argument passed to push_back; do not cast away the type error with a C-style cast.
Checkpoint: Rebuild, then check the same PHI counts as the previous lesson. The emitted IR must still match the input; fixing the host C++ type does not replace a target instruction.

items: The rebuilt pass must print the same PHI counts as lesson 1 — one for `phi.ll`, one for `loop.ll`, zero for `minishield-input.ll` — and the emitted canonical IR must be byte-identical to the input, because this step still performs no mutation.

The fix changed only a host-side C++ type (the worklist now stores the typed `PHINode*` obtained from `dyn_cast` instead of a base `Instruction*`), so no target instruction was replaced; the first actual IR edit still happens only when demotion runs in a later lesson.

blocks.text: The full corrected fragment
Observed error: phis.push_back(&I) fails because the vector needs PHINode* but &I remains Instruction*. Saving the result as phi makes the argument type match.
Verify

cmake --build build
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -disable-output tests/ir/phi.ll
Compilation should succeed and the phi.ll count should still be 1. We have changed C++ bookkeeping, not LLVM IR.

blocks.title: LLVM casts refine a borrowed pointer’s static type

blocks.text: A PHINode inherits from Instruction, but a vector<PHINode*> cannot accept an arbitrary Instruction*. dyn_cast<PHINode>(&I) asks LLVM’s class hierarchy whether the existing instruction is a PHI. Success returns a PHINode* to that same object; failure returns nullptr. No PHI is allocated or copied.

This is LLVM’s classof-based casting machinery, not C++ dynamic_cast and not a request to enable compiler RTTI. cast<T> asserts that the type is appropriate; dyn_cast<T> handles a possible mismatch. Use isa<T> when you only need a yes/no answer. See [LLVM casting](https://llvm.org/docs/ProgrammersManual.html#the-isa-cast-and-dyn-cast-templates).
Checkpoint: After a successful cast, do base and phi refer to two instructions or one? Who owns that instruction?

items: One: a successful `dyn_cast` allocates or copies nothing — it returns a `PHINode*` to the same instruction that `base` (an `Instruction*`) already points at, so the two pointers are different static types naming a single object.

That instruction is owned by its parent `BasicBlock` and, through it, by the function and the module: the cast and the `phis` worklist only hold borrowed addresses, and since no new PHI is ever created, neither the cast nor the vector owns the instruction.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: Why is &I later valid for a vector<Instruction*> but invalid here? Explain the difference between a runtime type test and the static type of an expression.

items: `&I` — the address-of operator applied to the `Instruction&` loop variable — is statically an `Instruction*`. A base pointer is accepted wherever an `Instruction*` is expected, so `vector<Instruction*>` works, but `vector<PHINode*>` needs the more-derived pointer type, and C++ never inserts a downcast automatically, so the bare expression `&I` cannot produce one.

The static type of an expression is fixed by its syntax and declarations (here `Instruction*`), while the runtime type is which concrete class the pointed-to instruction actually is; a runtime type test (`dyn_cast<PHINode>`) asks the second question and returns a typed `PHINode*` or null, so the worklist can store a correctly typed pointer without assuming the cast is safe.

lessons.title: Demote PHIs after collection
lessons.summary: Replace a predecessor-dependent value choice with explicit writes and reads, so the choice can survive the coming CFG rewrite.
lessons.takeaway: Demotion changes how a value travels, while preserving which path supplies it.

blocks.text: What demotion changes, and why we want it

We have located the places where the old graph chooses a value by predecessor. Before routing those paths through a shared dispatcher, we need another way to communicate that choice. PHI demotion replaces the implicit “which incoming edge?” selection with explicit writes and reads of a shared storage slot.

Path from left:  write 10 into slot ─┐
                                    ├→ join: read slot → return result
Path from right: write 20 into slot ─┘

Only the executed path writes its incoming value for this diamond. join reads the stored value. Thus the path still determines the result, but join no longer needs a PHI mentioning left and right as its direct predecessors. This prepares the value transport for later edge changes; demotion itself does not create or connect the dispatcher.

“Demote” means lowering a selected SSA value into memory-based storage. The slot can be written on different paths; each load from it still defines its own SSA result. We are not switching LLVM out of SSA, deleting the selected computation, or merely renaming a variable.

rows: One PHI defines the selected result.
An entry-allocated slot carries the selected value.
The predecessor edge identifies the incoming value.
Incoming paths arrange the writes; users read the slot.
The PHI must agree with the old incoming edges.
The PHI is removed, and its users receive loaded values.

blocks.text: This representation can add memory operations and make optimization harder. For this prototype, that cost buys a simpler foundation for CFG rewriting. A later optimizer may eliminate some storage again; the word “stack” here does not guarantee that every slot survives into machine code.
Checkpoint: Why is removing a PHI without replacing its users and incoming-value selection insufficient?

items: A PHI has users: instructions in the join block consume its value, so erasing the node without replacing those uses leaves dangling SSA values that the verifier rejects.

The PHI's real job is the predecessor-dependent choice (left delivers 10, right delivers 20); simply removing the node throws that selection away, so demotion must reproduce it in memory — a stack slot, a store of the incoming value in each predecessor, and a load replacing the PHI's uses — so the chosen value still depends on which path executed.

blocks.text: Task: After collecting PHIs, replace each PHI with stack-based data flow. This is the first lesson that actually changes the program’s IR.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Include the transformation helper
#include "llvm/Transforms/Utils/Local.h"

The installed LLVM 23 API is a free function: DemotePHIToStack(PHINode*, optional insertion point). There is no DemotePHIToStack::runOnFunction(F) method. The default insertion behavior is enough for these study fixtures.
Step 2 — Process the saved pointers
llvm::DemotePHIToStack(phi);

The utility allocates stack storage, arranges stores of incoming values and loads for users, and deletes the PHI. Do not dereference phi after this call. The vector still contains that address, but the instruction it identified no longer exists.
Step 3 — Invalidate after a change

Return PreservedAnalyses::none() after demotion. Return all() if there were no PHIs and nothing changed. This early return is correct for this PHI-only checkpoint; a later lesson removes it when a second transformation stage must run even without PHIs.
Study-session walkthrough — demotion replaces a choice, not merely a line of text
Use PHI demotion to preserve the incoming path’s value choice through explicit storage. Replacing users and arranging writes/reads are the purpose; simply making the PHI line disappear is not enough.
Before writing, answer: Where does the selected value go after the PHI itself has disappeared?

For the diamond, an entry slot exists before either path. left writes 10, right writes 20, and join reads the value written by the executed path. Both stores appear in the IR, but only the selected path runs. The helper erases the PHI, which is why collection must finish first and why saved pointers become unsafe to use afterward. The vector still exists; its size is not an access to the erased objects.
Task: Small writing step: Add the demotion loop after collection, and return none() after this stage actually changes IR. Do not call a nonexistent DemotePHIToStack::runOnFunction method.

Checkpoint: On phi.ll expect stores and a load with the original branches still present. Trace both conditions. Later preparation must remove the old empty-PHI early return, because it cannot skip all subsequent work.

items: The demoted `phi.ll` shows a new slot `alloca` in entry, `store i32 10, ptr %value.reg2mem` in left, `store i32 20, ptr %value.reg2mem` in right, and a load in join replacing the PHI, while the original branches (entry to left/right, left/right to join) remain: with a true condition, left stores 10 and join loads 10; with false, right stores 20 and join loads 20.

The old `if (phis.empty()) return all();` guard assumed “no PHI means nothing to do”, but a later fixture (`cross_block`) shows a function with zero PHIs can still have a value crossing block boundaries that must be demoted — so preparation must drop that early return and let every eligible function reach the escaping-value stage.

blocks.title: A worklist survives erasure; its pointed-to objects may not

blocks.text: Collecting pointers separates traversal from mutation. vector<PHINode*> retains pointer values when LLVM erases a PHI, but that erased pointer becomes dangling. Iterating to the next vector element is safe; calling a method through the erased pointer is not. size() counts stored elements, including dangling pointer values, rather than querying the deleted instructions.
Checkpoint: Why is reserving vector capacity unrelated to preventing an erased instruction pointer from dangling?

items: Capacity only sizes the vector's own storage — the C++ heap array that holds the pointer values — while whether a pointer dangles depends on who owns the `PHINode` it points to and when that object is destroyed: `DemotePHIToStack` erases the PHI from its parent block, and the block and function (not the vector) own and free the instruction, so reserving extra slots for addresses does nothing for the lifetime of the object a saved address points at after erasure.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: Trace both outcomes of the condition. Which store executes? What does join load? Why must changing IR invalidate cached analyses?

items: With a true condition, left's store executes (writing 10) and join's load reads 10; with a false condition, right's store executes (writing 20) and the load reads 20 — exactly one store runs per execution, and the load always returns what the executed path wrote.

LLVM analysis results are cached against the IR as it was when computed; once a pass inserts slots or erases the PHI, those cached results no longer describe the current IR — referenced instructions may be gone and dataflow has changed — so a mutating pass must not trust a cache computed before the mutation (or must re-fetch it afterward).

lessons.title: Find values that cross block boundaries
lessons.originalTitle: Find values that cross block boundaries
lessons.summary: Ordinary values can cross blocks without any PHI. Understand why new edges threaten those definitions before collecting the remaining dependencies.
lessons.takeaway: Removing PHIs does not remove every dependence on the old graph.

blocks.text: Why removing PHIs is only half of preparation

A PHI is one way blocks exchange values, but ordinary instructions can also define a value in one block that another block uses. For example, entry can calculate sum, branch to exit, and have exit return sum. That function has no PHI at all.

LLVM requires an ordinary definition to dominate its uses: every entry-to-use path must pass through the definition. Think of a receipt that must be written before any reader can refer to it. Adding a dispatcher edge to the reader can create a graph route that bypasses the writer. The verifier checks the graph relationship; it does not accept “our state IDs will never choose that order” as a replacement for SSA dominance.

PHI demotion can itself produce a load whose result is used in another block. We therefore inspect ordinary cross-block dependencies after the PHI stage. This worklist finds remaining value transport to prepare, rather than assuming “no PHIs” means “safe to rewire.” Here “escaping” means crossing a block boundary, not escaping to another function or heap object.
Checkpoint: Can a two-block function with no merge point still have a value dependency that flattening must prepare? Give an example.

items: Yes: the `cross_block` fixture is a two-block function with no PHI at all, in which entry computes `%sum = add i32 %x, 1` and exit executes `ret i32 %sum` — the add's result is defined in one block and used in another, so it is a cross-block value that flattening must prepare (demote to a slot) even though no block has multiple predecessors.
That is exactly why the collection rule is “defined in block A, used in block B” rather than “has a PHI”: the absence of a merge point does not imply the absence of a cross-block dependency.

blocks.text: Task: After PHI demotion, collect remaining instruction results used outside their defining block. Do not demote this new collection yet.
Before you begin — definition versus use

header:
  %i.reload = load i32, ptr %i.reg2mem
  ; ...
body:
  %next = add i32 %i.reload, 1
exit:
  ret i32 %i.reload

The load defines i.reload in header, while body and exit use it. That is a cross-block dependency. The current CFG makes header dominate those uses. A dispatcher can add a path that bypasses header, so the dependency needs preparation.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Use the right vector element type

This worklist may contain loads, arithmetic, or other value-producing instructions. Use Instruction*, the common base type, rather than PHINode*. Function arguments and constants are not instructions in these block lists; they are not collected here.
Step 2 — Filter unsuitable candidates

if (I.getType()->isVoidTy() || llvm::isa<llvm::AllocaInst>(I))
    continue;

A void instruction has no result to spill. The alloca is the storage object itself and is excluded in this exercise. Lessons 05 and 06 explain both tests. This is the study-fixture preparation policy, not a claim that every possible allocation or instruction type is supported by the final flattener.
Step 3 — Test where the result is used

if (I.isUsedOutsideOfBlock(&BB))
    escapingValues.push_back(&I);

The method is called on the defining instruction and asks whether its result is used outside BB. Here &I has exactly the vector’s Instruction* element type. Only record pointers during this traversal.
Step 4 — Inspect the collection

for (const auto *value : escapingValues)
    llvm::errs() << "cross-block value: " << value->getName() << "\n";

Remove the old PHI-empty early return so this stage is reached even without PHIs; lesson 07 explains the change-tracking detail. LLVM values need not have names, so these names are a learning diagnostic rather than a general test interface.

After PHI preparation, inspect ordinary instruction results used in another block. A reload introduced by the first helper may still have nonlocal users, so removing every PHI does not complete value preparation.
Before writing, answer: What exactly am I collecting now: every instruction, every pointer, or only results with a cross-block user?

This code is a fragment inside the existing instruction traversal. First exclude operations with no result and the storage allocations used by our strategy. Then ask whether this result has a user outside its defining block. &BB is the current block’s address; &I is the address of the candidate instruction. “Escaping” here means crossing a block boundary, not heap escape or leaving the function.

The original direct use was sound because the header dominated those blocks: by the time they ran, the header had always executed. The dispatcher edge (`ms.dispatch` to `header`) changes how the loop is entered and can invalidate that dominance, so the direct use can no longer assume the defining load has run; this checkpoint only collects the dependency — the escaping-value demotion in a later lesson repairs it with a second slot.

blocks.title: SSA dominance is a graph property, not your expected runtime path

blocks.text: For an ordinary use, a definition must dominate that use: every entry-to-use path passes through the definition. A dispatcher adds graph paths even when a state variable is intended to make some paths infeasible. LLVM’s SSA verifier does not infer your entire state-machine invariant to excuse missing dominance. Demotion changes value transport to memory, but the allocation pointer still has to dominate its uses.

A PHI incoming operand is special: its use occurs on the corresponding incoming edge. That is why “used in another block” is not the complete story for repairing PHIs; use the PHI-specific helper before ordinary escaping-result demotion. See [LLVM IR dominance and PHIs](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#phi-instruction).
Checkpoint: Why does “we never choose that state first” fail to repair a direct SSA use that no longer dominates?

items: Dominance is checked on the graph, not on the values the state machine stores: every entry-to-use path must pass through the definition, and the new dispatcher edge creates a graph path that reaches the use without passing through the definition — even if the stored state IDs make that order infeasible at runtime. The SSA verifier does not infer the state-machine invariant that would excuse the missing dominance: "we never choose that state first" is a claim about runtime values, not about the graph, so the direct use stays invalid until it is demoted to memory, where the entry allocation — which dominates every use — carries the value.

items: In the `cross_block` example the defining instruction is entry's `%sum = add i32 %x, 1` and the use in a different block is exit's `ret i32 %sum`.

PHI demotion inserts new instructions (the slot `alloca`, the predecessor stores, the join load) and erases the PHI, so a traversal before demotion would miss the cross-block uses that demotion itself creates and would still reference a PHI about to disappear; traversing after demotion sees the final value flow, with demotion's loads and stores included and nothing stale.

Reserve storage for the shown element type in this function invocation and produce its address, not the stored integer. `alloca i32` reserves one i32 slot. The allocation does not initialize its contents; a store must supply a value before an intended read.

`br label %B` always transfers control to block B. `br i1 %C, label %A, label %B` goes to A for true and B for false; their order matters. A branch is the block’s final instruction and produces no result. It does not execute both destinations.

Compare two same-typed integers and produce i1, which can feed br or select. `slt` asks whether the left operand is smaller using signed integer interpretation, so a negative i32 is below zero. The comparison computes a condition; it does not jump by itself.

Read left-to-right: compare the first integer operand with the second, then use the resulting i1 as a condition. For the loop it compares the current counter with the bound; for the discount kernel it checks whether the amount is negative.

Read a value from memory: in `load i32, ptr %slot`, i32 is the loaded value’s type and %slot is its address. The left-hand result gets the current contents, not another copy of the address. Each load defines a new SSA value; it does not compute the value that a missing earlier store should have supplied.

End this function invocation and return the typed operand to its caller. `ret i32 %v` returns the integer value, while `ret ptr ...` returns a pointer. A return does not proceed to the next printed block or automatically go back to dispatch.

Write memory: in `store i32 VALUE, ptr ADDRESS`, the first operand is the value and the second is the destination address. A store has an effect but no result name. Writing a state slot changes the next routing choice; writing a demotion slot transports an original program value.

Call count_to with limit = 2. The initial counter is 0; the signed-less-than test is true for 0 and 1, so the body increments it to 1 and then 2. At 2 the test is false and exit returns 2. lessons.title: Ask whether an instruction produces a value
lessons.originalTitle: Ask whether an instruction produces a value
lessons.summary: Distinguish an instruction’s result type from its operands and from the function’s return type.
lessons.takeaway: ret i32 returns from the function, but the ret instruction itself has no result.

blocks.text: An operation can have an effect without producing a value

Instructions do different jobs. add computes a result that later instructions can consume. store changes memory but supplies no result value. ret ends a function invocation; a call can either return a value or be void. These effects matter, even when the operation has no result.

Our current question is narrow: which instruction results need a different way to reach another block? A void-result instruction has no such result to spill. Filtering it out means “leave this operation out of the value worklist,” not “delete the operation” or “ignore its side effects.” We will handle branch terminators separately when changing control flow.

rows: Keep the effect; do not demote a nonexistent result.
Needs the separate storage filter in the next lesson.

blocks.text: Task: Fill in the void-result filter inside the inner instruction loop. This prevents collecting operations that produce no value.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Ask the instruction for its result type
I.getType()
This returns an llvm::Type*. It describes the value produced by this instruction, not the type of its first operand. Use -> to call a method on that type pointer.
Step 2 — Test the type
I.getType()->isVoidTy()
void means the instruction does not produce a value for another instruction to use. The name isVoidTy is an LLVM type predicate; it returns a boolean.
Step 3 — Skip this inner-loop iteration

if (I.getType()->isVoidTy())
    continue;
continue advances to the next instruction. It does not return from run(), skip the rest of the function, or mark the IR changed.
Read these examples
In ret i32 %x, i32 is the type of the value returned by the function. The ret instruction itself produces no SSA result. There is no %new = ret ... value for later instructions to consume.
Study-session walkthrough — void describes a result, not whether an operation matters
Ask about the instruction’s result type separately from its effect. A store, branch, or return can be essential even though it produces no SSA result for the ordinary-value worklist.
Before writing, answer: Does skipping a void instruction mean I should delete its memory or control-flow effect?

if (I.getType()->isVoidTy())
    continue;

I.getType() asks LLVM for the result type; isVoidTy() tests it. This is compiler-side C++ inspection. continue skips this iteration of the collection loop, leaving the target instruction untouched. A store, branch, or return can remain essential even though its result type is void. Conversely a call might return i32 or might be void, so checking only whether an instruction is a call would not answer the question.
Task: Small writing step: Write the result-type filter before the cross-block-use check. Keep it a collection filter, not a rejection of every function containing a void instruction.

Checkpoint: On the demoted loop, stores and branches must still appear in output, but they must not be reported as values to spill. The new load results do produce i32 values and can still be candidates.

items: The demoted `loop.ll` still contains stores (the demotion stores and the original ones) and branches (the original branches, plus the new dispatcher hops) — all void-typed instructions that must appear in the output IR but are excluded from the spill candidates because they produce no value.

The filter keys on the instruction's result type: `getType()->isVoidTy()` is true for stores and branches, so they are skipped, while the loads that demotion inserted have type `i32` (the loaded type), so they do produce a value and remain candidates for the escaping-value analysis.

blocks.text: The full filter

if (I.getType()->isVoidTy())
    continue;
Verify

Rebuild and inspect loop.ll’s collection. Its stores, branches, and return should not enter escapingValues. Its load can still be a candidate. The alloca is not void, so it needs the next lesson’s separate filter.
Checkpoint: Why does ret i32 %x have void instruction type? Why does checking I.getOperand(0)->getType() answer a different question?

items: `ret` produces no SSA value at all — its result type is `void` — so `ret i32 %x` has void instruction type; the `i32` in the syntax is the type of the operand being returned, not of the instruction.

`I.getOperand(0)->getType()` asks for the type of the value the instruction takes (here `i32`), which is a different question from the type of the value the instruction produces; the spill analysis needs the latter (void, hence not a candidate), and answering with the former would classify every `ret i32` as a value producer.

lessons.title: Recognize the stack allocation itself
lessons.summary: Use isa when you only need a yes/no answer. Understand why alloca survives the void filter.
lessons.takeaway: The storage pointer is not the value we are trying to spill into storage.

blocks.text: Why the storage itself is a different kind of result

The demotion strategy gives a value a storage slot, writes its value into that slot, and loads it where needed. alloca creates the slot and returns its address. That address naturally appears in stores and loads in several blocks, so a generic “used outside its block” test would select the allocation too.

For this preparation algorithm, storage pointers are the stable foundation we rely on. Adding another slot just to transport the address of the first slot is not the intended repair. We exclude AllocaInst from the ordinary value worklist and require supported storage allocations to remain in the original entry, where they dominate all the later memory accesses.

Skipping an alloca is not proof that every allocation is safe. A non-entry alloca might be bypassed by a new edge; a variable-sized or repeated allocation may have meaningful execution/lifetime behavior. The stricter eligibility lesson rejects those cases before full rewriting. A normal entry slot is allocated once per function invocation, not once for the whole program.
Task: Add an AllocaInst filter alongside the void-result filter. Keep the worklist focused on values to demote, not their storage allocations.
The template to start with

if (I.getType()->isVoidTy() || /* TODO: recognize alloca */)
    continue;
Step 1 — Recall what alloca returns
%slot = alloca i32
This allocates space for an i32 and returns a pointer to that space. The result type is ptr, not i32 and not void. Consequently isVoidTy() does not exclude it.
Step 2 — Use a type predicate
llvm::isa<llvm::AllocaInst>(I)
isa<T> returns whether the instruction belongs to that class. We only need to skip the instruction; we do not need an AllocaInst* or any alloca-specific methods. Therefore isa is enough.
Step 3 — Combine the filters
The || operator means either condition is sufficient. Short-circuit evaluation stops after a true first condition, though both checks here are read-only.
Study-session walkthrough — an allocation produces an address, not its stored integer

Recognize an allocation separately from the void-result filter: alloca produces a pointer. Its address naturally reaches loads and stores in several blocks, but that storage foundation is not an ordinary scalar result to re-spill in this strategy.
Before writing, answer: Why does alloca i32 pass the non-void test, and why do we nevertheless skip it in this worklist?

if (I.getType()->isVoidTy() || llvm::isa<llvm::AllocaInst>(I))
    continue;

isa asks only whether the existing instruction belongs to the allocation class; no typed pointer is needed just to skip it. In alloca i32, i32 is the storage element type, while the instruction result has LLVM type ptr. Our memory-transport strategy relies on entry-allocated slot addresses being available everywhere. Re-spilling the address of a slot is not the intended repair for each original scalar value.
Task: Small writing step: Add the allocation filter beside the void filter. Explain both halves before testing them together.

Checkpoint: The allocation must stay in the IR and out of escapingValues. A reload from its slot can still be collected. This skip does not make non-entry or dynamic allocas safe: the later eligibility lesson imposes a separate support rule before full rewriting.

items: The demotion slot itself is an `alloca`, and if the collection reported it as an escaping value, the next demotion would allocate a slot for the slot — a regressive double demotion — so the `alloca` is filtered out with `isa<AllocaInst>`; the reload (the load from the slot) does produce a value and can still be collected as a candidate.

The collection filter only keeps the analysis from re-demoting the slots; it does not approve `alloca`s that are non-entry or variable-sized, because the eligibility lesson imposes a separate support rule (“only static entry allocas are supported”) before any full rewrite — hoisting such an alloca could change allocation frequency or lifetime.

blocks.text: The full filter

if (I.getType()->isVoidTy() || llvm::isa<llvm::AllocaInst>(I))
    continue;
isa versus dyn_cast

rows: Recognize an alloca to skip it.
Collect a PHINode* or inspect intrinsic-specific information.

blocks.text: Keep stack slots in the actual entry/setup block when designing the dispatcher. Excluding allocas from this worklist does not make arbitrary non-entry or dynamic allocations automatically safe to flatten.
Verify
Rebuild and inspect the cross-block worklist for the demoted loop. The slot pointer crosses blocks, but the allocation should not appear in escapingValues. The i.reload instruction result should.
Checkpoint: Why would skipping only void instructions leave alloca in consideration? When would you choose dyn_cast instead of isa?

items: An `alloca`'s result type is a pointer to the allocated type (the slot's address), not `void`, so the void-type filter alone does not exclude it — an explicit `isa<AllocaInst>` check is required to keep the slot out of `escapingValues`.

`isa<T>` is a boolean runtime test (“is this a T?”), which is enough for a filter that only needs to skip; `dyn_cast<T>` is the same test but returns the typed `T*` (or null), which is what you need when you want to call a method on the derived type — so a collection loop that only filters can use `isa`, while the PHI loop that calls `DemotePHIToStack` needs `dyn_cast`.

lessons.title: Finish collection without a premature return
lessons.originalTitle: Finish collection without a premature return
lessons.summary: Review the two missing pieces found in the draft: appending candidates and reaching this stage when the PHI list is empty.
lessons.takeaway: Zero PHIs does not imply unchanged IR or no remaining work.

blocks.text: Why each preparation stage must get a chance to run

The earlier PHI-only exercise could stop when its PHI worklist was empty. The pass now has another responsibility: ordinary values crossing block boundaries. An empty first worklist says nothing about whether the second one is empty.

entry: compute %sum → exit: return %sum
No PHI, but %sum still travels between blocks.

Think of this as a sequence of independent inspections. Each stage can do zero edits without cancelling the remaining stages. The final changed flag summarizes whether any stage edited the IR. This distinction prevents a function that happens to lack PHIs from skipping all later preparation and construction.
Task: Review the complete preparation flow so every eligible function reaches cross-block inspection.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Remove the old early return

A PHI-only transformation could stop immediately when its PHI worklist was empty. The expanded pipeline cannot: a PHI-free function can still have an add used in another block. An empty range naturally performs zero iterations, so the PHI loop needs no special guard.
Step 2 — Actually append candidates

Observed error: The reviewed draft created escapingValues and applied the filters, but did not push any instruction. A filter rejects unsuitable values; it does not automatically collect the suitable ones.
Step 3 — Report only real mutation

This is the end of a collection-only checkpoint: only PHI demotion has modified IR so far. The next mutation stage will add escapingValues to this decision. Querying phis.empty() is safe even after the instructions were deleted; do not dereference their stored pointers.
Study-session walkthrough — a filter does not append, and an empty first stage is not the end

Review two independent collection mistakes: an early return on phis.empty() can bypass the new stage, and filtering escapingValues does not append suitable candidates automatically. Make both continuation and insertion explicit.
Before writing, answer: Why is the second worklist empty even though I can see a value used in another block?

A for-loop over an empty vector naturally performs zero iterations and then continues. That is different from returning from run(), which cancels every later phase. Likewise, continue rejects a candidate; it does not automatically collect whatever remains. push_back is the explicit action that grows the worklist.
Task: Small writing step: Remove the PHI-only early return and make the append visible after the two filters. At this collection-only stage, report mutation only for edits already performed.

Checkpoint: Use the complete cross_block example below: it has zero PHIs but sum is defined in entry and consumed in exit. It should reach collection. Write the suggested fixture yourself; the reference in the book does not create a test file.

items: The `cross_block` fixture — entry computing `%sum = add i32 %x, 1` and exit returning it — has zero PHIs, so before the fix the early return on empty PHIs short-circuited the whole pass and the escaping-value stage never ran; after removing the premature return, the function reaches collection, `sum` lands in `escapingValues` (and is printed as a cross-block value), and at this collection-only stage the module stays unchanged.

The checkpoint asks you to write the fixture file yourself (`tests/ir/cross-block.ll`): the book's reference section shows the expected input and output IR, but it does not create the test file — your own file is what the inspection run exercises.

Verify the path with no PHIs

define i32 @cross_block(i32 %x) {
entry:
  %sum = add i32 %x, 1
  br label %exit
exit:
  ret i32 %sum

Checkpoint: Why is &I the right type for this vector but not the PHI vector? Why must success in the eligibility checker and preservation information remain separate decisions?

items: The escaping-values worklist holds a mix of instruction kinds (`add`, `load`, ...), so its element type is the base `Instruction*` and `&I` fits; the PHI worklist holds only PHIs and the demotion helper takes a `PHINode*`, so that vector needs the typed pointer — an `Instruction*` there would not compile without a cast at every use.

Eligibility (is this function supported at all?) and the preservation set (which cached analyses does my mutation invalidate?) answer different questions with different consequences: a rejected function mutates nothing and preserves everything, while a transformed function must declare exactly the analyses it broke; entangling the two decisions either leaks a stale cached analysis into a later pass (an `all()` that should not have been returned) or rejects a function that could have been transformed, and neither failure shows up in the verifier.

blocks.text: The helper interface connects our worklist to the edit

The worklist stores handles to existing IR objects. The utility must receive the actual object it will modify, rather than a copy of an arithmetic result in the program being compiled. This is why reading the C++ parameter type matters: Instruction& and PHINode* are two ways these APIs borrow mutable IR objects.

Dereferencing an Instruction* to bind an Instruction& does not execute the target instruction or load its runtime value. It gives the C++ helper access to that IR object. Both demotion utilities change the function’s representation; the signature tells you how to pass the object, while the helper’s semantic contract tells you what edits and lifetime changes to expect.
Task: Read both helper declarations in llvm/Transforms/Utils/Local.h before adding the next call.
The template to complete
Step 1 — Compare the first parameters
These lines explain the API shape; the comments stand for optional parameters, so they are not a replacement header to paste into your source. The real functions are already declared by Local.h.
Step 2 — Dereference the stored pointer
llvm::DemoteRegToStack(*value);

value is Instruction*. The expression *value refers to the existing Instruction object, matching Instruction&. This does not copy the instruction. Contrast DemotePHIToStack(phi), whose parameter is already a pointer.
Step 3 — Understand the result

Both helpers return a pointer to the created stack allocation. The current exercise can ignore that pointer. The function’s IR owns the inserted allocation; ignoring the return value does not delete it.
Study-session walkthrough — the argument type tells you whether to pass the pointer or the object

Read each helper’s first parameter before writing the call. The PHI helper accepts a pointer; the ordinary-value helper accepts an instruction reference. Both borrow mutable LLVM-owned IR rather than receive a copied runtime value.
Before writing, answer: Why did the PHI helper take phi directly, while the ordinary-value helper needs *value?

llvm::DemoteRegToStack(*value); // value: Instruction*; *value: Instruction lvalue

These are call fragments, not replacement declarations. The PHI parameter is PHINode*, so its saved pointer already matches. The ordinary helper’s parameter is Instruction&; *value names the existing instruction so the reference can bind to it. Neither expression copies an instruction or executes its runtime arithmetic. &value would instead take the address of the pointer variable, producing Instruction**, which is the wrong object and type.
Task: Small writing step: Read the installed Local.h declaration and write only the correctly typed call inside the saved-pointer loop. Keep optional arguments at their defaults for these fixtures.

Checkpoint: Ignoring the returned AllocaInst* does not delete the slot: the function owns inserted IR. Explain separately which helper erases its original PHI and which retains the original ordinary calculation.

items: The instructions the helpers create are inserted into the function's blocks, and the function (through its blocks) owns them, so ignoring the returned `AllocaInst*` merely loses the handle — the slot stays in the IR.

`DemotePHIToStack` erases the original PHI: the predecessor-dependent choice is reproduced by the slot stores and the PHI node itself is removed (a stored pointer to it dangles afterward), while `DemoteRegToStack` retains the original ordinary calculation — the instruction still executes — and adds the slot, a store of its result, and a reload at the uses.

blocks.text: Read DemoteRegToStack’s Instruction& and DemotePHIToStack’s PHINode* as distinct C++ contracts. Given Instruction *I, *I is an lvalue naming the existing instruction and binds to Instruction&. Given PHINode *phi, phi already has the required pointer type. Neither expression copies an LLVM instruction.

Default arguments do not create overloads with fewer parameters. They provide omitted argument expressions where the declaration is visible. Check the installed LLVM 23 Local.h rather than copying a signature from an older tutorial.
Checkpoint: What would happen if you passed &I when I is already an Instruction*? Name the resulting type.

items: `&I` takes the address of the pointer variable `I` itself, producing an lvalue of type `Instruction**` — the address of the handle, not the instruction. Because `DemoteRegToStack` expects an `Instruction&` and no implicit conversion exists from `Instruction**` to `Instruction&`, the call does not compile; and even in a function that did take a double pointer, you would be passing the wrong object and the wrong type.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: Explain what *value does here, why phi previously needed no dereference, and why the vector is a worklist rather than an owner of LLVM instructions.

items: `DemoteRegToStack` declares its parameter as `Instruction&` (a reference), so the call passes `*value` — the dereference binds the reference to the instruction the pointer points at; `DemotePHIToStack` declares its parameter as `PHINode*` (a pointer), so the loop passes the `phi` pointer directly with no dereference — each helper's declared parameter type determines what you hand it.

The vector is a worklist of borrowed pointers: it owns its own array of addresses, but every instruction it points at is owned by the parent block and function; the vector never deletes or moves an instruction, and the moment a helper erases one, the corresponding entry becomes a dangling pointer.

lessons.title: Demote the escaping values
lessons.summary: Keep each original calculation while changing how its result reaches another block. Understand what memory transport solves and what the state machine must still guarantee.
lessons.takeaway: Values move through slots; execution must still produce the right value before each read.

blocks.text: What ordinary-value demotion preserves

For an ordinary instruction, the calculation is already in the right block. The problem is how a later block obtains its result. DemoteRegToStack keeps the defining calculation, stores its result into entry-allocated storage, and supplies loads for uses. The direct SSA connection across blocks becomes explicit communication through memory.

Before: calculate %sum ─────────────→ another block uses %sum
After:  calculate %sum → store slot → another block loads slot → uses load

The name “Reg” refers to LLVM’s register-like SSA results, not a physical CPU register we are choosing. This step can add instructions; it is preparation for changing the graph, not a speed optimization.

Memory transport does not make arbitrary execution orders correct. The final state machine must still arrange for the appropriate store to execute before its corresponding load, preserving the original computation’s behavior. Preparation makes the IR representation suitable for that later rewrite; it does not prove the rewrite correct.
Task: Add cross-block value demotion after escapingValues collection. The eligibility guard still runs before either transformation.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Transform only after collection ends

for (auto *value : escapingValues)
    llvm::DemoteRegToStack(*value);

The helper adds an allocation, a store of the computed result, and loads for its uses. The defining calculation remains. Do not insert and rewrite instructions while discovering candidates with an ordinary traversal.
Step 2 — Combine the change conditions
const bool changed = !phis.empty() || !escapingValues.empty();
A function with zero PHIs can still be transformed by the second loop. Preserving analyses in that case would leave stale cached results available to later passes.
Study-session walkthrough — demote the collected result, then track the actual edit

Demote collected ordinary results only after discovery ends. Their calculations remain; the helper replaces cross-block transport with storage and reloads. Track this stage’s edits as well as PHI demotion.
Before writing, answer: If the add still exists, what has DemoteRegToStack accomplished?

The loop is placed after candidate discovery. Each saved pointer names an instruction whose result needs transport. The helper adds a slot, a store of the calculated value, and reloads at uses. bool changed summarizes either preparation stage; a PHI-free function may still change here. Returning all() after that change would make a false promise about cached analyses.

Task: Small writing step: Add only this second mutation stage after collection, then use the combined changed decision for the preservation return. Do not append duplicate copies of the earlier loops.

Checkpoint: In the cross_block example, sum = x + 1 must remain in entry and exit must return a loaded result. In the loop, inspect the extra slot carrying the header reload to other blocks. Memory transport does not permit arbitrary state execution order.

items: In `cross_block`, entry still executes `add i32 %x, 1` (`DemoteRegToStack` retains the original calculation), then stores the result into the new slot, and exit's `ret i32 %sum` becomes a load from the slot followed by a return of the loaded value; in `loop.ll` the header's counter reload is itself a cross-block value, so it gets an extra slot — the header stores the reloaded counter, and the body and exit load it.

Once a value travels through memory, the store must happen before the load in execution order, and the original dominance-based guarantee no longer holds; the state machine's dispatch order is what enforces that ordering, because memory transport itself permits no arbitrary state execution order.

The preservation result must be `none()` because the function was modified — the escaping-value stage inserted instructions — so any cached analysis computed before the mutation is now stale; only a function that both stages left untouched reports `all()`.

  br i1 %continue, label %body, label %exit

body:                                             ; preds = %header
  %next = add i32 %i.reload, 1
  store i32 %next, ptr %i.reg2mem, align 4

exit:                                             ; preds = %header

blocks.text: Use a small trace to see what the helper is responsible for

The utility call is short enough to hide its purpose. This two-block example makes the value’s journey visible: compute x + 1 in entry, then return that same result from exit. For input x = 4, both versions must return 5.

Trace where the calculation happens, where its result is written, and what the return reads. The arithmetic stays in entry. Only the way its result reaches exit changes. A new load has a new SSA name because it is a separate definition; matching the old name is not the correctness condition.

After this exercise you should be able to explain an unfamiliar demotion dump from the data path, even if LLVM has chosen different temporary names. That skill will matter when a later verifier error points to an old direct cross-block use.
Task: Trace the cross-block example by hand, then compare its generated IR. This is a reading exercise, not another transformation to add.
The input to start with

define i32 @cross_block(i32 %x) {
entry:
  %sum = add i32 %x, 1
  br label %exit
exit:
  ret i32 %sum
}
The template to fill in

entry:
  %sum.slot = alloca i32
  %sum = add i32 %x, 1
  ; TODO: store the computed value before leaving entry.
  br label %exit
exit:
  ; TODO: load the saved value and return that load.
Step 1 — Keep the calculation
The add still computes x+1. We are not replacing arithmetic with a different algorithm. “Demote” changes how the SSA result is carried between blocks.
Step 2 — Store after definition
store i32 %sum, ptr %sum.slot
The value operand and the pointed-to storage are different things. sum is an i32 result; sum.slot is a pointer. The store instruction itself has void type.
Step 3 — Load where the consumer needs the value

%sum.loaded = load i32, ptr %sum.slot
ret i32 %sum.loaded
The return now uses a value defined by a load in its own block. The allocation pointer still crosses blocks, so keep its allocation in the true entry block that dominates these accesses.

Trace a tiny calculation to understand the helper rather than inferring behavior from its name. This illustrative exercise follows one value through calculation, storage, reload, and return; it does not require a second demotion loop.
Before writing, answer: For x = 4, where does the number 5 exist before and after preparation?

Before preparation, exit directly refers to the SSA sum defined in entry. After preparation, the defining add still computes the same result, but a store/load pair makes transport explicit. The slot address and the integer stored there are different values. Each load has a new SSA name, so the new name does not mean a different mathematical answer. Generated suffixes such as reload are descriptive, not correctness guarantees.
