items: With `x = 4`: entry computes `add i32 4, 1` = 5, stores 5 into the slot, and exit loads 5 and returns 5. With `x = 0`: entry computes `0 + 1` = 1, stores 1, and exit loads 1 and returns 1 — both paths confirm the demotion preserved the value, since the stored value equals the original `sum` and the loaded value equals what exit returns.

The module only defines the function (with an argument) — it has no `main` that calls it with concrete arguments — so an actual runtime check would need a caller the fixture does not provide; the check at this checkpoint is a manual trace of the IR over the bounded pair of inputs.

blocks.text: The full conceptual result

define i32 @cross_block(i32 %x) {
entry:
  %sum.slot = alloca i32
  %sum = add i32 %x, 1
  store i32 %sum, ptr %sum.slot
  br label %exit
exit:
  %sum.loaded = load i32, ptr %sum.slot
  ret i32 %sum.loaded
}
This is illustrative IR. LLVM’s generated names may differ. For x=4, the add computes 5, the store writes 5, and the load supplies 5 to the return.
What the vector does
escapingValues is a C++ worklist of instruction pointers. DemoteRegToStack rewrites the IR those pointers identify; it does not convert the C++ vector into a stack slot.
Verify

Generate cross-block.ll’s output with the pass followed by verify. Locate the add, its store, the slot allocation, and the load used by the return. A valid result alone is not proof that every future dispatcher preserves the store-before-load order.

blocks.title: A host C++ pointer and an IR pointer live in different worlds

blocks.text: AllocaInst *slot is an address in the compiler process pointing to an IR object. That IR object represents a target-program instruction whose result type is ptr. When the generated program runs, the alloca result denotes its stack storage. Calling slot->getType() inspects a type in the compiler; it does not load the program’s stack slot.

LLVM opaque pointers do not encode a pointee type as ptr<i32>. Supply the memory access type to CreateLoad and maintain correct size/alignment/address-space assumptions. See [LLVM opaque pointers](https://llvm.org/docs/OpaquePointers.html).
Checkpoint: Which pointer is dereferenced when the pass evaluates slot->getName(), and which is used when the target executes load i32, ptr %slot?

items: `slot->getName()` dereferences the host C++ pointer — the `AllocaInst*` whose address lives in the compiler process and points at the IR object — so that call inspects the IR inside the compiler.

The target's `load i32, ptr %slot` uses the IR pointer value — the `alloca`'s result, of LLVM type `ptr` — which denotes the stack storage when the generated program runs: one pointer is a handle to an object the compiler inspects, the other is a value of the program being compiled.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: For x=4, what is stored and what is returned? Which object is the pointer, which is the i32, and which is just C++ bookkeeping?

items: For `x = 4`, the value stored into the slot is 5 and the value returned is 5 (the loaded value): the store writes the add's result, and the load defines a new SSA name for the integer read back.

The pointer is the slot itself — the `alloca`'s result, a `ptr` value in the IR that the store and load address; the i32 is 5 itself, the store's operand and the load's result, the program's actual data; and the C++ `AllocaInst*` that `DemoteRegToStack` returns is just host-side bookkeeping — a C++ pointer to the alloca instruction object in the IR, used by the pass and invisible to the executed program.

lessons.title: Trace PHI demotion by predecessor
lessons.summary: See how stores on incoming paths replace predecessor-based selection. Compare it directly with ordinary instruction demotion.
lessons.takeaway: A PHI disappears; the path taken determines which store supplies its former users.

blocks.text: A PHI carries a choice, not just one calculation

Ordinary-value demotion moves the result of one defining calculation through memory. PHI demotion has a different source of truth: the executed incoming path decides which of several incoming values should be carried. Preserving a PHI therefore requires preserving the path/value association.

condition=true  → left  → choose 10 → join returns 10
condition=false → right → choose 20 → join returns 20

In the demoted diamond, each chosen path writes its own incoming value and join reads the slot. Writing both 10 and 20 unconditionally before join would always leave the last write; allocating a slot without the path-specific writes would not encode any choice. The memory operations are a replacement for the PHI’s meaning, not merely a way to make the PHI instruction disappear.

Loops use the same abstraction to choose an initial value on entry and a carried value on later iterations. More complex edges and interacting PHIs make placement subtle. The hand trace below explains this diamond; the LLVM utility is responsible for the general mechanics used by the prototype.
Task: Trace the phi.ll diamond on both paths. Do not add a second demotion loop—this lesson explains the utility already used.
The PHI to start with

join:
  %value = phi i32 [ 10, %left ], [ 20, %right ]
  ret i32 %value
Arriving from left selects 10; arriving from right selects 20. A PHI is an SSA merge, not an ordinary instruction that explicitly executes an if statement.
The template to fill in

left:
  ; TODO: store the value associated with the left incoming edge.
  br label %join
right:
  ; TODO: store the value associated with the right incoming edge.
  br label %join
join:
  ; TODO: load the shared slot and return the loaded value.
Step 1 — Allocate one slot in entry
The shared slot must exist before either incoming path uses it. For this simple fixture, one alloca in entry serves both paths.
Step 2 — Replace selection with incoming-path stores

; In left:
store i32 10, ptr %value.slot
; In right:
store i32 20, ptr %value.slot
Only the path chosen by the condition executes. We do not execute both stores every time. In this fixture the stores belong before each predecessor’s branch to join.
Step 3 — Replace the PHI’s use with a load
join loads the slot. The utility replaces the old PHI’s uses and deletes the PHI. Do not access the deleted PHI through a pointer saved in the C++ vector.
Study-session walkthrough — trace a choice through PHI demotion
Trace PHI demotion by path, not by textual store order. A PHI can select different incoming values, so replacement storage must preserve which executed path supplies the value.
Before writing, answer: Why are there two stores in the module if only one value should be returned?

left path:  write 10 → join reads 10
right path: write 20 → join reads 20

This is a path sketch, not standalone LLVM syntax. Both possible stores are present statically; execution selects only one incoming path for this diamond. If both stores were executed unconditionally, the last write would win and the original choice would be lost. The PHI helper instead supplies storage and rewires users while preserving the selected incoming value.
Task: Small writing step: Read the complete modules below twice: once with condition true and once with false. Name the writer and reader on each path.

Checkpoint: True must still produce 10 and false 20. Compare this with ordinary demotion: there the original calculation remains; here the PHI is erased. In both cases, loads/stores replace a dependence on the previous value representation, not the need to execute the correct path.

items: True: entry branches to left, left stores 10, and join's load reads 10. False: entry branches to right, right stores 20, and join's load reads 20 — the demoted diamond still returns the right answer for each outcome.

In ordinary (escaping-value) demotion the original instruction still executes and the slot merely transports its result, while in PHI demotion the PHI itself is erased — the “calculation” is the predecessor-dependent selection, and the two predecessor stores reproduce it; in both cases the load/store pair replaces the value's representation (a direct SSA use becomes a memory round trip), not the need to execute the correct path, which still runs and whose store determines the value.

define i32 @merge(i1 %condition) {
entry:
  %value.slot = alloca i32
  br i1 %condition, label %left, label %right
left:
  store i32 10, ptr %value.slot
  br label %join
right:
  store i32 20, ptr %value.slot
  br label %join
join:
  %value.loaded = load i32, ptr %value.slot
  ret i32 %value.loaded
}
Compare the two utilities

rows: The result computed by that instruction.
The incoming values selected by the executed control-flow path.

blocks.title: Loop PHIs describe parallel values, not sequential assignments

blocks.text: Two PHIs can represent a swap: on a back edge, next a receives old b and next b receives old a. Naively emitting store b into a-slot and then loading a-slot for b loses old a. Correct lowering must preserve the incoming-edge values as a group. LLVM’s helper handles the relevant uses and placement; do not replace it with an unexamined hand-written pair of assignments.

; Conceptual loop fragment: both right-hand sides use the old iteration.
%a = phi i32 [ 1, %entry ], [ %b, %latch ]
%b = phi i32 [ 2, %entry ], [ %a, %latch ]
; This is a fragment, not a complete runnable function.
Checkpoint: Trace the first two swaps by hand. What temporary values would a correct sequential implementation need?

items: Entry gives `a = 1`, `b = 2`; the first back edge sets new `a` to old `b` (2) and new `b` to old `a` (1), so after the first swap `a = 2`, `b = 1`, and the second swap restores `a = 1`, `b = 2` — the values swap on every back edge, and both right-hand sides must use the old iteration's values. A correct sequential implementation therefore needs a temporary that preserves one of the old values (for example `tmp = a; a = b; b = tmp;`), because naively "store `b` into `a`'s slot, then load `a`'s slot for `b`" overwrites the old `a` and leaves both variables holding the old `b`.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: Why does each path load the right value? Why can PHI demotion still leave a new load result used outside its defining block, as in loop.ll?

items: Each path stores its own incoming value into the single slot before reaching join, and join's load executes after the taken path's store, so the load always reads what the executed path wrote — 10 on the true path, 20 on the false one — even though the load lives in one shared block.

In `loop.ll` the PHI demotion inserts the counter load in the header, but that load's result is used by the body and exit — blocks outside the header — so the demotion itself creates a new cross-block value that the escaping-value stage must demote again (an extra slot); demotion can move a dependence, not always eliminate it.

lessons.title: Assign states before changing edges
lessons.summary: Encode the original next-block decision as a state number, and understand why one-time entry setup is excluded from recurring states.
lessons.takeaway: A state ID encodes a destination; it does not decide the program’s behavior by itself.

blocks.text: Why blocks become states

An original branch names its next block directly. A shared dispatcher needs a value it can inspect to choose that next block. A state ID is our encoding of the next block’s identity: store a number, reach dispatch, and let its switch decode the number back to a destination.

Original intention: run left next.
Encoded intention:  next state = 0.
Dispatcher rule:    state 0 means left.

The numbers have no intrinsic meaning. Any unique, consistently used assignment would work. Mapping the prepared blocks in function order gives us deterministic dumps and a simple table to inspect. Mapping after demotion also includes any blocks introduced during preparation.

The original entry is setup rather than a recurring state: its allocations must execute once per invocation, and the entry block cannot acquire predecessors. Excluding it keeps dispatcher cycles from re-entering setup. We assign IDs before appending dispatch/invalid so the machine’s own machinery does not accidentally become an original program state.
Task: After both demotion stages, map the original non-entry blocks to unsigned state IDs. Do not create dispatcher blocks during this traversal.
Before you begin — what a state represents

A state number identifies which original block the future dispatcher should run next. It is not an instruction count, a block name, or a new block. In this design, entry stays setup and is excluded from the switch’s ordinary state cases.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Include the map type
#include "llvm/ADT/DenseMap.h"
DenseMap maps a key to a value. Here the key is BasicBlock* and the value is unsigned. The vector keeps the order; the map supports looking up a destination’s ID when rewriting a branch.
Step 2 — Keep setup out of the state loop

if (&BB == entry)
    continue;

The entry block must execute once, particularly its stack allocations. Dispatching through setup repeatedly could allocate storage or repeat initialization on each transition. The pointer returned by &F.getEntryBlock() identifies the actual entry regardless of its name.
Step 3 — Record a block and its ID
Take the address because BB is a reference to the block. The next lesson revisits the pointer and pair-construction errors found in the first draft.
Step 4 — Print in vector order
Iterate stateBlocks to print deterministic output. DenseMap iteration order is not a stable display order. Do not rely on LLVM block names as unique persistent IDs.
Study-session walkthrough — give a next-block decision an integer encoding
Map prepared original non-entry blocks before adding dispatcher machinery. Keep the state list and encoding deterministic, and exclude one-time entry setup from the recurring states.
Before writing, answer: Is state 0 a new block, the entry block, or just a number associated with an existing destination?

The vector preserves a deterministic list; the map records which unsigned integer represents each block address. The expression id++ uses the current number for this assignment, then increments it. Entry stays one-time setup, so it gets no ordinary state. The map lives in the C++ transformer; it is not itself emitted into the target module.
Task: Small writing step: Print each state/block association after mapping and before creating new blocks. Use the block pointer as the key and a readable name only for the report.

Checkpoint: For the prepared diamond, expect left 0, right 1, join 2. The module stays unchanged at this checkpoint. Later dispatch must decode those same associations; storing zero universally is not a substitute for consulting the intended destination.

items: For the prepared diamond the assignment is left 0, right 1, join 2 (entry is excluded from the state IDs — one-time setup, and its allocations must not re-run), and at this checkpoint the pass only computes and prints the table, so the emitted module is byte-identical to the input.

The later dispatcher decodes exactly these associations: each terminator's store writes the destination block's ID into the state slot and the dispatch switch jumps on the loaded ID, so a universal zero (a default-initialized entry, or a missing lookup treated as 0) would route every transition to the same block — which is why the checked `find`-based lookup must distinguish “no state” from “state 0”.

blocks.text: The full mapping fragment
Verify

cmake --build build
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -disable-output tests/ir/phi.ll
No entry state is assigned. Mapping IDs changes C++ bookkeeping only; it does not itself invalidate analyses. Keep the existing changed decision from demotion.
Checkpoint: Why are a vector and a map both useful? Why does entry not get a state? Why can state zero be an incorrect universal initialization value for a conditional entry?

items: The `stateBlocks` vector preserves a deterministic order — the assignment order that printing and later construction rely on — while the `DenseMap` `stateIDs` gives fast block-pointer-to-ID lookup, which each terminator's store needs for its destination; together they provide order for iteration and lookup for addressing.
Entry is one-time setup: it runs exactly once, before the state is first loaded, and its allocations must not re-run on every transition, so there is no state to dispatch back to it.

For a conditional entry the first state (left 0 or right 1) depends on the condition, so a universal “start at state 0” — a default slot value or a missing-lookup default — would assert that left always comes first and misroute the machine whenever the condition first takes right.

lessons.title: Fix pointer keys and pair insertion
lessons.originalTitle: Fix pointer keys and pair insertion
lessons.summary: Translate the state-map compiler errors into exact C++ types, and distinguish copying a pointer from copying a block.
lessons.takeaway: Use &BB over block objects, but BB over a vector of block pointers.

blocks.text: The map must identify the exact destination object

The state table connects a block object to its encoding. When we later read an old branch’s successor, LLVM gives us a BasicBlock*. Using block addresses as map keys lets us find the encoding of that exact destination without relying on a display name.

Names may be absent or changed. Numbers may be reused accidentally if a lookup silently inserts an entry. A correct mapping must give every supported original destination one unique state ID and let missing destinations be recognized as a violated assumption. The C++ pointer and pair syntax in this exercise implements that semantic relationship.
Task: Review the state-mapping draft and fix its three type/syntax errors before building a dispatcher.
The failing template
Step 1 — Compare addresses

if (entry == &BB)
    continue;
entry is BasicBlock*. BB is BasicBlock&. Comparing entry with &BB compares pointer identity.
Step 2 — Append an address, not an object
stateBlocks.push_back(&BB);
The vector stores BasicBlock*. BB is not already a pointer merely because a reference may be implemented internally using an address.
Step 3 — Use map assignment or a brace-constructed pair

Angle brackets delimit template arguments in DenseMap<...>. Braces construct the key/value pair passed to insert. For this collection every block key is new; bracket assignment is a straightforward choice.
Step 4 — Print the name, not a pointer address
In this loop BB is already a pointer because that is the vector’s element type. lookup receives the pointer key, while -> accesses a block member.
Study-session walkthrough — object, address, and key/value pair are separate C++ ideas

Follow the declared C++ types to fix state-table expressions. Comparing a pointer to a block object, appending an object to a pointer vector, and using angle brackets as a key/value pair constructor are different mistakes.
Before writing, answer: Where do I need BB, where do I need &BB, and what does DenseMap insertion actually receive?

BB is a reference alias for an existing block, not already a pointer. &BB obtains its address. Both the vector element and the DenseMap key are BasicBlock*. Braces can form the key/value pair expected by insert; angle brackets normally introduce template arguments, not runtime pair values. operator[] assigns through the mapped value but also inserts a missing key, so later destination validation needs care.
Task: Small writing step: Correct one expression at a time, rebuild, and keep mapping separate from IR construction. Do not fix a mismatch by trying to copy a BasicBlock.

items: After the pointer-key fix the printed table matches the intended associations (left 0, right 1, join 2), and the emitted canonical IR is still byte-identical to the input, because this stage only computes and prints the table without touching the IR.

`0` is a real state (left's), so a missing key that silently returns the default 0 is indistinguishable from “the destination is left” — a misspelled or unregistered block would misroute the machine with no error; the later checked `find`-based reference makes the invariant explicit by treating a missing key after successful preflight as a fatal internal-contract error (“state destination missing after valid-input preflight”) rather than a fallback to 0.

blocks.text: The full corrected loop

Observed error: const auto *BB would be a pointer to const BasicBlock and would not implicitly convert to the map’s BasicBlock* key. const auto BB instead makes the copied pointer itself const. These are different declarations.
Verify

Rebuild and compare the phi.ll state order with lesson 12. lookup returns a default zero for a missing key; in this prototype all original destination blocks must already be mapped, so do not treat lookup as validation that a key exists. Use find() when validating membership.

blocks.title: DenseMap lookup, accidental insertion, and iterator lifetime

blocks.text: operator[] inserts a missing key with a default value. For unsigned, that value is zero, which is also a legitimate state ID. lookup returns a default value for a missing key without inserting, but still cannot distinguish “missing” from “state zero.” Use find and check end() when absence means an invariant failure.

DenseMap can rehash when entries are added, invalidating references/iterators into its storage. It does not move the BasicBlock objects whose pointer values are stored as keys. Finish constructing the map before relying on its iterators during rewriting.
Checkpoint: Why can stateIDs[target] make a broken target lookup appear to work?

items: `operator[]` inserts a missing key with a default value, and for an unsigned state ID that default is zero — which is also a legitimate state ID (the first state, `left` in this lesson's table of left 0, right 1, join 2). So a broken or unregistered target does not error: it silently returns 0 and routes to that state's block, indistinguishable from a lookup of a block that really is state 0, and as a side effect it pollutes the map with an entry for the wrong key that later lookups will "find" — which is why the checked `find`/`end()` form treats a miss after preflight as an internal-contract failure instead of a fallback to 0.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: Why is copying a pointer element okay here even though for (auto BB : F) would try to copy a noncopyable block?

items: `for (auto BB : F)` declares the loop element as a `BasicBlock` value, so the loop would copy each block — and `BasicBlock` is noncopyable, so that form fails to compile; a pointer element is a different type: copying a `BasicBlock*` copies only the address (a word-sized value), and every copy still refers to the same single original block, so the worklist can hold many copies of the address without ever copying the block.

lessons.title: Construct a complete dispatcher block
lessons.summary: Build the shared block that decodes next-state choices, and distinguish valid disconnected machinery from a live transformed program.
lessons.takeaway: Write a state, reach dispatch, decode it to the intended original block.

blocks.text: What the dispatcher adds to the program

A dispatcher is a shared decision block. Instead of every original branch choosing another program block directly, each rewritten transition will write the desired state and jump to this block. The dispatcher reads the state and uses its switch to choose the corresponding original block.

entry setup → [write next state] → dispatch
                                  read state
                                  switch 0 → left
                                         1 → right
                                         2 → join

We use one i32 memory slot because many different blocks must update the same next-state information. A single SSA name cannot be repeatedly assigned by all those transitions. Its alloca lives in entry so the address is available everywhere; the stored contents change as execution moves between states. An alternative design could maintain SSA PHIs for state, but this course chooses memory so we do not have to repair those PHIs while restructuring the graph.

This lesson deliberately constructs complete but disconnected machinery. It separates “can we build a valid load/switch/case structure?” from “have we redirected execution correctly?” An unreachable dispatcher does not demonstrate flattening yet, and its uninitialized slot must not be read on a live path. The next connection lesson supplies the first write before making it reachable.

The invalid default expresses the invariant that our own transitions store only mapped state IDs. Ending it with unreachable makes that assumption explicit to LLVM; it is not a safe fallback if the assumption is broken.
Task: After state mapping, add an i32 state slot and two complete new blocks. Preserve the old branch structure at this construction checkpoint.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Choose an insertion point

IRBuilder is a helper for inserting instructions. getFirstInsertionPt() returns an iterator to the first legal insertion position; * obtains the instruction and & takes its address. The builder inserts before that instruction. This expression differs from &*dispatcher, which just recovers a pointer you already had.
Step 2 — Allocate the state once
auto *stateSlot = setup.CreateAlloca(setup.getInt32Ty(), nullptr, "ms.state");

getInt32Ty() returns the LLVM i32 type. CreateAlloca returns the storage pointer. nullptr supplies no array-size operand, meaning the default single element in this overload. The final string is the IR result name. No store is added yet because the dispatcher is deliberately unreachable.
Step 3 — Append the two blocks

LLVMContext owns shared IR context such as uniqued types. &F attaches each block to this function. With no insertion-before argument, the blocks are appended; the original entry remains first. stateBlocks was collected before creation, so neither new block receives a normal state ID.
Step 4 — Terminate the invalid-state path

llvm::IRBuilder<> invalidBuilder(invalidBlock);
invalidBuilder.CreateUnreachable();

unreachable ends the block and declares that this path must never execute in a valid run. It is not a runtime exception handler or a recovery return. Correct state writes must prevent invalid values from selecting it.
Step 5 — Load and switch
CreateLoad needs the loaded value type and pointer. CreateSwitch creates the terminator and sets its default destination. Its third argument reserves case capacity; it does not add case edges.
Step 6 — Populate the cases and mark the mutation

getInt32(ID) creates an i32 integer constant, unlike getInt32Ty(), which supplies a Type*. Keep changed declared before construction so the final preservation result includes the new instructions and blocks.
Study-session walkthrough — construct valid machinery before making it live

Construct the state slot, dispatcher, and invalid block while leaving original branches intact for this checkpoint. Complete disconnected machinery can verify without yet demonstrating live dispatcher routing.
Before writing, answer: What do CreateLoad and CreateSwitch add, and why does an unreachable new block still need a terminator?

This is a construction fragment after block creation. CreateLoad needs the integer value type and slot address. CreateSwitch sets a default and reserves case capacity; separate addCase calls create the mappings. The invalid block needs its own ending even while unreachable. unreachable is an assertion that no defined execution gets there, not a recovery return. Append both blocks after the original entry.
Task: Small writing step: Build and terminate the two blocks, then add one case per previously mapped state. Leave the original edges alone for this checkpoint.

Checkpoint: In the resulting dump dispatch should have no predecessors yet. Its slot has no initialization store because that load is not executed. The next lesson must arrange a valid store before adding a live edge.

items: The constructed `ms.dispatch` block (its load plus switch) is inserted but nothing branches to it yet, so the dump shows it with no predecessors — it is dead code until the entry connection in the next lesson makes it reachable.

The state slot has no initialization store yet because its only load (inside dispatch) is not executed by any live path; the moment the next lesson adds a live edge, a valid store must happen before that load, so the dispatcher cannot read an uninitialized slot.

blocks.text: The full construction stage

Place this after the demotion and state-mapping stages. It replaces the old final preservation return. The variable entry is the BasicBlock* saved during mapping; if your source calls it entry_ptr, use that spelling consistently.
Verify

cmake --build build
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/phi.ll -o build/phi-dispatcher.ll
cat build/phi-dispatcher.ll

Expect a state slot, a dispatcher load and switch with 0→left, 1→right, 2→join, and an invalid block ending in unreachable. ms.dispatch has no predecessors at this checkpoint. Its load is not executed, so no initialization store is needed yet.

blocks.title: IRBuilder is a template whose methods can return different value kinds

blocks.text: IRBuilder<> uses default template parameters for folding and insertion behavior. A method such as CreateSelect can fold constant operands and return a Constant rather than a newly inserted SelectInst. auto* preserves the method’s declared pointer result type; it does not promise a particular concrete instruction subclass.

Use the common Value* interface when either a constant or instruction is legal. Use dyn_cast<Instruction> only when you need to test whether a runtime instruction was inserted. Constant folding can change printed instruction counts without changing semantics.
Checkpoint: Why is “every Create... call adds exactly one instruction” an unsafe testing assumption?

items: `IRBuilder<>` folds by default: when the operands allow it (for example a `CreateSelect` or `CreateAdd` over constants), the method returns a `Constant` and inserts no instruction at all, so printed instruction counts can change without any semantic change. `auto*` only preserves the method's declared pointer result type and does not promise a concrete instruction subclass, so tests that count instructions or assume every builder result is an `Instruction` are unsafe — the safe interface is the common `Value*`, with `dyn_cast<Instruction>` used only when you actually need to test whether an instruction was inserted.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: Which block executes the allocation? Why is a switch destination not a substitute for that destination block’s own terminator? Why must new blocks not enter stateBlocks?

items: The entry block executes the allocation: the `ms.state` `alloca` is placed in entry (the eligibility rule requires static entry allocas), and entry runs once before any dispatch.

A switch case only routes control into its destination block; it does not replace that block's own terminator — once control is inside the block, the block still executes its own branch or `ret` to leave, so the switch answers “which block next” for its own block only.

`ms.dispatch` and `ms.invalid` are the machine's routing machinery, not original program states; if they entered `stateBlocks` (and the ID map), the snapshot and rewrite would treat the dispatcher's own switch as an original terminator to lower and assign states to the machine's own blocks — the rewrite would end up rewriting its own routing.

lessons.title: Separate block names from C++ variables
lessons.originalTitle: Separate block names from C++ variables
lessons.summary: Fix the creation errors from the first dispatcher draft and explain exactly why a block pointer is the right return type.
lessons.takeaway: dispatcher is a C++ identifier; "ms.dispatch" is an LLVM name string.

blocks.text: A block has an identity, a label, and an ending

Three different ideas appear when we create a block. The C++ variable lets the pass refer to the block object. The IR name makes printed output readable. The block’s instructions and final terminator determine what the generated program actually does. Spelling a block ms.dispatch does not give it dispatcher behavior.

Likewise, naming a block invalid does not make it an exception handler or give it an implicit exit. LLVM requires a terminator even in a currently unreachable block. The default case needs a defined IR structure that accurately states our invariant, rather than an empty block that merely has a plausible label.
Task: Review the BasicBlock creation statements and the empty invalid block found in the first draft.
The failing template
Step 1 — Use a legal C++ identifier
A dot is member access in C++, not part of an identifier. Writing ms.dispatch makes the parser look for a member named dispatch on an object named ms. Use dispatcher as the variable name.
Step 2 — Keep the returned pointer
BasicBlock::Create returns BasicBlock*. The function owns the attached block. Do not try to construct a local BasicBlock value from that pointer or take the address of an invented local object.
Step 3 — Pass the IR name as a string

    F.getContext(), "ms.dispatch", &F);

The placeholder name in the teaching signature meant “supply a name here”; it was not a predefined variable. Quoted "ms.dispatch" is the block’s display name and may contain a dot even though the C++ identifier cannot.
Step 4 — Finish the invalid block
After the declaration errors are fixed, an empty invalid block would still fail LLVM verification. Compilation checks C++ syntax and types; verify checks the IR your C++ creates.
Study-session walkthrough — the C++ handle is not the IR label

Distinguish the C++ variable, the LLVM block object, and its printed name. A declaration using ms.dispatch as a variable or treating BasicBlock::Create as returning a block value fails at C++ checking; an empty block without a terminator fails LLVM verification.

The quoted string is an argument naming an LLVM block; a dot inside it is ordinary text. The unquoted C++ dot is member access. Create returns BasicBlock*, so dispatcher is a pointer to an object attached to F, not a local block copy. Finishing that declaration does not automatically fill another block’s terminator. A previous .so can still load after a failed build, but it cannot prove the revised draft compiled.

Once compilation succeeds, the emitted module must be verified separately: the two error domains have different owners, a C++ declaration or identifier error is the compiler's problem and stops the build, while a missing terminator or an invalid block is an IR problem reported by the LLVM verifier when the module is checked or printed.

items: The pointer variable (for example a `BasicBlock*` named `dispatch`) is a C++ identifier holding an address; the object it identifies is the `BasicBlock` in the IR, owned by the function; and its IR name (`"ms.dispatch"`) is the block's label string set via `setName` — a dot is legal inside that quoted name and is what appears in the dump.

define i32 @merge(i1 %condition) {

lessons.title: Connect an unconditional entry branch
lessons.summary: Translate the original entry branch’s intention into a stored state, making the first dispatcher hop live without changing its destination.
lessons.takeaway: Initialize the state from the real successor before dispatch reads it.

blocks.text: Why the first state must come from the old entry edge

The dispatcher exists, but the original entry still follows its old branch. To make execution use the new route, we must translate that branch’s intention into a stored state ID, then send control to dispatch. For loop.ll, the old destination is header, so the first stored state must decode to header.

Before: entry ─────────────────────────────→ header
After:  entry → store ID(header) → dispatch → header

The order is essential: dispatch loads the slot, so entry must write it first. A universal store of zero would be correct only if the actual destination happened to have ID zero. We read the destination and consult the map because the mapping, not the numeric spelling, defines the meaning.

This first connection handles an unconditional branch: there is one intended successor. It leaves header/body loop edges direct, so it demonstrates only the first dispatcher hop. A conditional entry needs to encode a choice, and full flattening must translate the other original transitions as well.
Task: Connect only an unconditional entry branch first. Use loop.ll, whose entry branches to header, mapped to state 0. This is still a partial transformation.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Save the original terminator

The old branch identifies the real first destination. It also provides an insertion point so replacement instructions can be inserted before it. Keep this code inside the construction block where stateSlot and dispatcher are in scope.
Step 2 — Look up its destination state

auto *destination = entryTerminator->getSuccessor(0);
auto *initialState = entryBuilder.getInt32(stateIDs.lookup(destination));

An unconditional branch has one successor, at index 0. For the loop fixture this is header with ID 0. The lookup must use the destination block, not the entry itself: entry intentionally has no state ID.
Step 3 — Store, branch, then erase

The store runs before the dispatcher’s load. Emit replacements before deleting the old instruction: the builder’s insertion point and the original successor information are still needed. The brief intermediate state with two terminators must not survive to verification. Do not dereference entryTerminator after eraseFromParent().
Step 4 — Leave other entry forms unchanged for now

default: break leaves conditional, switch, return, and unreachable entries untouched at this checkpoint. Do not invent a universal store of zero for them. Later lessons must select the state corresponding to the actual path.
Study-session walkthrough — initialize the state before the first dispatcher read

Translate only the unconditional entry branch for the first live dispatcher hop. Use its original successor to choose the initial state; keep header/body loop branches direct until their own transitions are deliberately rewritten.
Before writing, answer: Why must I read the old successor and emit the replacement before erasing the old branch?

Place this fragment inside the UncondBr case and construction scope. The builder inserts before term. The store must execute before dispatch loads the slot; its integer comes from the actual destination’s map entry, not from the entry block itself. Erasing too early destroys information and invalidates the insertion anchor. Do not access term afterward.

`phi.ll`'s conditional entry (a `br i1` to left or right) is still unchanged at this stage — this lesson handles only the unconditional entry, and the conditional entry's state selection belongs to a later lesson — and the remaining loop transitions (header to body/exit, body back to header) are not yet flattened: the original-terminator rewrite comes in the later rewrite lesson.

items: Until the replacement exists, the old branch is the entry block's only terminator; erasing it first would leave the block without a terminator (an invalid IR state the verifier rejects) and would destroy the builder's insertion anchor and the successor information it still needs, so the pass emits the store and the new branch before `entryTerminator->eraseFromParent()`.

A conditional entry's first state is not a constant: it is left's ID (0) or right's ID (1) depending on the condition, so entry must select the first state from the condition (for example a `select` of the two state IDs) and then store it; storing one universal ID would hard-code one path and misroute the other, which is why the lesson's `UncondBr`-only case deliberately leaves conditional entries untouched.

lessons.title: Define the supported input before mutation
lessons.originalTitle: Define the supported input before mutation
lessons.summary: Tighten the Day 1 guard before turning the prototype into a complete dispatcher. Scope is a correctness decision.
lessons.takeaway: Reject unsupported input before the first edit.

blocks.text: Why a transformation needs a support contract

A read-only pass can inspect instructions without taking responsibility for new execution paths. A transformation has a stronger obligation: every accepted case must still mean the same thing after our edits. The fact that LLVM accepts an input does not mean this particular algorithm knows how to transform it.

For example, an allocation in a later block may be valid in the original graph because every use follows that block. Dispatching directly to a use can bypass the allocation. Simply skipping alloca during value collection does not repair that relationship. Other constructs have special calling, exception, or value-type rules that our simple rewrite does not maintain.

Preflight makes these assumptions executable: unsupported input is rejected before the first edit. This keeps a rejected function intact instead of leaving it half-demoted or half-rewired. A narrow accepted subset is a deliberate semantic boundary, not a claim that rejected LLVM features are generally invalid.
Task: Future exercise: expand FunctionEligibility before enabling the complete rewrite below. These chapters are a book draft; your working implementation has not been updated for you.
Why the old guard is not enough

The earlier guard supported inspection and a limited prototype. A new dispatcher edge can bypass a non-entry alloca, making its pointer fail dominance. Some LLVM instruction results cannot be spilled as ordinary scalars. Special call semantics can forbid the control-flow changes we are proposing.
The template to start with
Step 1 — State a narrow contract

This teaching implementation accepts valid, ordinary scalar LLVM IR: integers, floating-point values, pointers, supported branch terminators, and static entry allocations. It is conservative. It rejects explicit intrinsic calls for now rather than assuming every llvm.* operation is safe. This is narrower than “all C++ functions.”
Step 2 — Reject non-static allocation

isStaticAlloca() encodes LLVM’s entry/constant-size rule, including restrictions such as inalloca. Do not simply move a loop’s alloca into entry: changing how often storage is allocated may change behavior.
Step 3 — Reject exceptional result and call forms

The full reference rejects non-scalar instruction results, naked functions, inline assembly calls, convergent calls, operand bundles, returns_twice, musttail, and intrinsic calls. Explain the reason for each before relaxing it; rejection is a defined limitation, not a bug to hide.
Study-session walkthrough — operation, result, and storage are different

Build these guards incrementally inside the existing instruction loop in FunctionEligibility::check, and test each before adding the next. Eligibility inspects original IR without changing it; the flattening pass must call it before demotion.

%sum = add i32 %x, 1
%slot = alloca i32
store i32 %sum, ptr %slot
%loaded = load i32, ptr %slot

This is an illustrative instruction fragment, not a complete function. add computes a 32-bit integer. alloca reserves storage for an i32 but produces a pointer to that storage. store writes an integer through the pointer and produces no result. load reads an integer through the pointer and defines a new i32 result. The memory contents can change, although each named SSA instruction result still has one static definition.

rows: What element does this allocation reserve?

blocks.text: Do not confuse I.getType() with the allocated element type. For %slot = alloca i32, I.getType() is ptr. Integer arithmetic and an integer load can both produce i32 while being different operations.
Study-session walkthrough — why an allocation must dominate its uses

define i32 @nonentry_alloca() {
entry:
  br label %allocate
allocate:
  %slot = alloca i32
  store i32 7, ptr %slot
  br label %read
read:
  %value = load i32, ptr %slot
  ret i32 %value
}

define starts a function returning i32; the empty parentheses mean no arguments. Each colon starts a basic block. br label %allocate transfers execution to that block. %slot names the address returned by alloca; store i32 7, ptr %slot writes 7 into that address. The next branch reaches read, where load reads the stored integer. ret returns it, so the original program returns 7.

Originally every route to read passes through allocate. Dispatcher edges can create a route to read that bypasses allocate, so the pointer definition no longer dominates its use. Excluding allocations from the ordinary value-demotion worklist does not repair this relationship. Our prototype rejects allocations that are not supported static entry allocations.

dyn_cast returns a typed pointer to the existing instruction, or nullptr for another instruction class. isStaticAlloca checks LLVM’s static-entry allocation classification; it is not merely a test for the word alloca. Entry storage executes once per function invocation. Hoisting arbitrary allocations yourself could change allocation frequency or lifetime, so rejection is the current policy.
Study-session walkthrough — build the result-type guard

LLVM supports more value types than this prototype promises to transform. We deliberately accept ordinary integer, floating-point, and pointer results, plus operations with no result. This is a conservative support boundary, not a claim that LLVM cannot store structures or vectors.

Each method returns a C++ bool. The || operators mean any one category is allowed; !supported means no category matched. const auto * borrows the LLVM Type object without allowing mutation through that pointer. This is compiler-side inspection, not a target-program instruction.

rows: Accept here; the separate allocation guard still applies.
Accept the operation, although it has no result to demote.

blocks.text: Eligibility and worklist filtering answer different questions. A void store is an allowed operation, so eligibility accepts it. During ordinary value demotion we skip it because there is no produced value to spill. Rejecting every void result would incorrectly reject stores, branches, and returns.

The braces { i32, i32 } describe a structure with two integer fields, not a control-flow block. zeroinitializer supplies zero for both fields. insertvalue creates a new aggregate with field 0 replaced by x; extractvalue reads field 0 from that aggregate, without a pointer or memory load. The original function returns x. Our guard rejects %pair because the result is a structure, even though %first and the function’s return type are i32.
Study-session walkthrough — an intrinsic is a special operation expressed as a call

An LLVM intrinsic has semantics defined by LLVM rather than an ordinary user-supplied function body. Many are represented with call instructions naming llvm.* functions. The call is the instruction; the intrinsic identifies the operation it invokes. Intrinsics can describe arithmetic, memory, lifetime, coroutine, and other operations with different constraints.

declare supplies a signature without a body. @llvm.ctpop.i32 is a module-level name for the intrinsic that counts set bits in an i32. define starts our ordinary wrapper function. Its i32 %x argument is supplied by a caller; call passes that value to the intrinsic and binds the returned i32 to %count. ret returns that result. For x = 7, binary 111, the answer is 3.

A scalar result does not establish that every operation is supported by our control-flow rewrite. We reject explicit intrinsic calls conservatively until their individual semantics are covered. This does not mean every intrinsic is unsafe. The ordinary recursive call in recursion.ll remains outside this blanket intrinsic restriction.

Keep the specific coroutine diagnostic first, then reject the other intrinsic calls. This incremental version uses IntrinsicInst; the full reference below recognizes intrinsic callees within its broader CallBase checks. Both implement the conservative policy, while the full version also checks other special call forms.
Study-session walkthrough — musttail is a requirement, not a hint

Here @callee is an ordinary declared function, not an intrinsic. musttail modifies the call and requires a tail-call transfer under LLVM’s rules. The function returns its result immediately. This is a stronger contract than an ordinary call that can return to surrounding code and continue doing work.

The required call/return relationship constrains the instructions permitted between them, with limited exceptions in LLVM’s rules. A generic spill or CFG rewrite must not insert arbitrary work there. Our prototype rejects musttail before any edit instead of promising to preserve those constraints. The unchanged example is valid; the rejection is about the transformation’s scope.

CallInst recognizes the call instruction class; isMustTailCall asks whether this particular call carries the mandatory marker. An ordinary call passes this check. This is separate from the intrinsic check because an ordinary function can be the target of a musttail call.
Study-session walkthrough — inspect inline-assembly calls through CallBase

Keep the musttail rule separate from the following call-form checks. A focused musttail fixture should produce “musttail calls are unsupported” and unchanged canonical IR; test that reason rather than accepting any rejection.

Add the inline-assembly predicate to the CallBase block and check it with tests/ir/inline_assembly.ll. With the diagnostic shown in this exercise, expect “inline assembly is not supported” and unchanged canonical output. Then test convergent calls independently.

Place this fragment in the existing instruction loop before any transformation. CallBase is the common LLVM base for CallInst, InvokeInst, and CallBrInst; it lets this guard inspect the shared call-like interface. The earlier musttail check used CallInst because that marker belongs to ordinary call instructions. dyn_cast returns a borrowed pointer to the existing instruction when it matches; isInlineAsm asks whether the callee is embedded assembly rather than a normal function target.

This is a complete input module. define void starts a function with no returned value; its empty parentheses mean no arguments. entry names its first block. call void has no result to bind to an SSA name, but still executes an operation. asm embeds target assembly text, and sideeffect says it can have effects even without a used output. The first quoted string is the assembly text; the second is the operand-constraint string. Both are empty here, and the final () supplies no operands. ret void ends the function without returning a value.

The prototype rejects this call form conservatively even for an empty assembly string: accepting one visually harmless spelling would not establish correct handling of arbitrary target assembly, constraints, or hidden effects. This is a support-policy choice, not a claim that the input is invalid LLVM IR. Its void result also does not make the call irrelevant; skipping void results in the spill worklist and rejecting an unsupported operation answer different questions.
Task: Write the CallBase/isInlineAsm guard and the separate tests/ir/inline_assembly.ll fixture. Keep the intrinsic and musttail checks; do not replace the entire checker with this one rule.

cmake --build build
opt -passes=verify -disable-output tests/ir/inline_assembly.ll
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/inline_assembly.ll -o build/inline_assembly-checked.ll

Checkpoint: Expect “inline assembly is not supported” and unchanged canonical output for the focused fixture. Explain why call void can matter even without a produced value, and why CallBase is broader than CallInst. Verify the convergent rule separately.

items: The focused fixture (a function containing inline assembly) is rejected by the guard with “inline assembly is not supported”, and the emitted canonical IR is byte-identical to the input, because rejection happens before any mutation.

A `call void` produces no SSA value but can still have side effects — memory writes or other observable effects — that the state machine's reordering must respect, so the guard cannot ignore value-less calls; and `CallBase` is broader than `CallInst` because it is the shared base of `CallInst` and `InvokeInst`, so checking `CallBase` catches both ordinary and EH calls.
The convergent rule (“convergent calls are not supported”) is a separate guard check with its own fixture, so it must be verified separately rather than inferred from the inline-assembly result.

blocks.text: Study-session walkthrough — a convergent call has participation constraints

Inspect the convergent marker on the existing CallBase pointer before mutation. Use tests/ir/convergent.ll as a focused input, expect “convergent calls are not supported,” and compare canonical output. A rejection caused by another rule does not establish this predicate’s coverage.

In grouped execution, such as GPU work, an operation can involve communication among participating threads. Which threads participate can depend on control flow. Convergent describes constraints on preserving that participation; it does not mean every thread takes the same path or simply that a function eventually returns. Routing through a shared dispatcher changes the graph, so this prototype excludes marked calls until it has a suitable correctness argument. This is conservative policy, not a rule that every CFG transformation is forbidden. See LLVM’s [Convergent Operation Semantics](https://llvm.org/docs/ConvergentOperations.html).

call is the already-checked borrowed pointer to a call-like instruction; use your existing variable name if it differs. isConvergent() returns a C++ bool for that call’s semantic marker. It is not a target-program test of how many threads arrived. Returning the rejection before demotion keeps the original function intact. This guard is separate from intrinsic recognition: an ordinary external function call can also be marked convergent.

Read the complete module locally: declare gives group_operation an i32 result and one i32 input without defining a body. Its convergent suffix marks the declared function. define creates use_group, whose caller supplies i32 %x. The call passes %x to that ordinary external name and binds its returned integer to %r; its own explicit convergent suffix marks the call site. ret returns %r. @ names the module-level functions; % names the wrapper’s local argument/result. The markers describe a contract, not an extra argument, branch, or arithmetic instruction.

group_operation is a placeholder, not an LLVM intrinsic and not an implemented GPU primitive. This fixture isolates recognition of the convergent call marker. It is valid input for parsing/guard checks, but has no main or implementation of the external callee, so it is not a standalone executable or a behavioral simulation of thread communication.
Task: Write the isConvergent guard inside the CallBase block and the focused tests/ir/convergent.ll input. Keep the inline-assembly rule. Check the intended reason as well as unchanged output.

cmake --build build
opt -passes=verify -disable-output tests/ir/convergent.ll
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/convergent.ll -o build/convergent-checked.ll

Checkpoint: Expect “convergent calls are not supported” with identical canonical output. Explain why a scalar result and an ordinary external callee do not remove the participation contract. Keep this rule distinct from the operand-bundle check.

items: The convergent-call fixture is rejected with “convergent calls are not supported” and the canonical output is identical to the input, because the guard rejects before any mutation.

The `convergent` attribute is a participation contract — every call to that function within a loop must reach the same convergence point together — and it is a control-flow obligation that holds whether the result is a plain scalar and whether the callee is an ordinary external function; neither fact removes the contract, which the machine's reordering cannot preserve.

This rule is distinct from the operand-bundle check: bundles are attached call metadata with their own rejection message (“operand bundles are unsupported”), and a call can be convergent without bundles and vice versa.

blocks.text: Study-session walkthrough — an operand bundle is part of call semantics

Reject calls carrying operand bundles before any transformation. Use tests/ir/operand_bundle.ll to exercise that predicate independently; expect “operand bundles are unsupported” and unchanged canonical output. The next sections explain the payload syntax and why an ordinary argument count is a different question.

getNumOperandBundles() returns the number of attached bundle groups. != 0 is a C++ comparison meaning at least one is present. It does not count ordinary callee arguments or count the values inside one bundle; even a bundle with no payload values is still a bundle. hasOperandBundles() is the installed API’s equivalent yes/no helper. Keep this check inside the successful CallBase cast and use your existing pointer variable name.

Read the complete module: declare void @observe(i32) describes an external function taking one i32 and returning no value. define void @with_bundle(i32 %x) defines our wrapper. Its call passes %x as the ordinary argument inside @observe(i32 %x). Because the call returns void it has no named SSA result, but it still executes an operation; ret void then ends the wrapper.

The separate square-bracket suffix [ "deopt"(i32 %x) ] attaches one operand bundle to that call site. The quoted string deopt is its tag; the typed %x is state payload carried by the bundle. This is not array indexing and not a second ordinary argument in observe’s function signature. The same local value happens to appear in both places, but those two uses have different semantic roles.

Bundles are semantically meaningful, not disposable comments. For deopt, a suitable runtime can use attached state for an alternative continuation or reconstruction when deoptimizing compiled execution; attaching the bundle does not directly invoke deoptimization on every call. Different tags have different requirements. Our prototype excludes bundled calls conservatively until it preserves those requirements; this does not mean every bundle is inherently unsafe. See the primary [LLVM operand-bundle reference](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#operand-bundles).

observe is an ordinary external placeholder, not an intrinsic or a supplied deoptimization runtime implementation. This fixture is for parsing and guard recognition. It has neither a main function nor a body for observe, so it is not a standalone executable demonstration of deoptimization behavior.
Task: Write the operand-bundle predicate inside CallBase and the focused tests/ir/operand_bundle.ll input. Preserve the earlier call checks and reject before PHI or ordinary-value demotion.

cmake --build build
opt -passes=verify -disable-output tests/ir/operand_bundle.ll
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/operand_bundle.ll -o build/operand_bundle-checked.ll

Checkpoint: Expect “operand bundles are unsupported” with unchanged canonical output. Identify the ordinary argument, bundle tag, and payload separately; explain why counting arguments would test the wrong property.

items: The operand-bundle fixture is rejected with “operand bundles are unsupported” and the canonical output is unchanged (rejection before mutation).

In `call void @observe(i32 %x) [ "deopt"(i32 %x) ]` the three roles are separate: the ordinary argument is `i32 %x` (a value of the callee's type), the bundle tag is the quoted string `deopt`, and the payload is the typed `(i32 %x)` state the bundle carries — the same local value may appear in both places, but the two uses have different semantic roles.

Counting arguments would test the wrong property: a legitimate multi-argument call with no bundle would trip a count, while a one-argument call with a bundle would slip past it — the guard must ask specifically whether the call carries an operand bundle, not how many arguments it has.

blocks.text: Study-session walkthrough — returns_twice can resume one continuation again

Add the returns_twice predicate to the CallBase checks and isolate it with tests/ir/returns_twice.ll. Expect “returns_twice calls are unsupported” and unchanged canonical output. The function-level naked rule is a separate check because it concerns the containing function rather than one call.

The C setjmp/longjmp mechanism is a useful conceptual example: setjmp first returns normally while recording context; a later nonlocal transfer can make execution continue as though that same call had returned again. This is not two result operands produced at once, and not merely an ordinary loop calling a function twice. A transformation relying only on a single forward return path has not established correct handling of this reentry, so this prototype rejects it conservatively. See LLVM’s [function attributes](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#function-attributes).
#include "llvm/IR/Attributes.h"

Add the include explicitly at the top of FunctionEligibility.cpp; it declares the LLVM attribute identifiers used by the guard. This is a C++ compilation dependency, not an instruction inserted into the input program. Then use the following predicate inside the existing successful CallBase cast.

if (call->hasFnAttr(llvm::Attribute::ReturnsTwice))
    return {false, "returns_twice calls are unsupported"};

hasFnAttr asks about the call’s function attribute contract and returns a C++ bool. llvm::Attribute::ReturnsTwice is the C++ identifier; returns_twice is the spelling printed in LLVM IR. This does not count result values, count dynamic calls, or run the target function. Use your existing CallBase pointer name and reject before any demotion or graph change.

Read the complete module: declare describes resume_point as taking no arguments and returning i32, without providing its body. Its suffix marks the declared contract. define creates the ordinary wrapper use_resume_point. The call’s empty () passes no arguments; its own explicit returns_twice marker states the call-site contract. %result is the local name for the integer returned by that call, and ret returns that integer to the wrapper’s caller. @ identifies functions; % identifies the local SSA result.

resume_point is an ordinary external placeholder, not an intrinsic or an implementation of setjmp. The attribute itself does not manufacture a second return. This module isolates the guard’s recognition of the marker; with no main or callee implementation it is not a standalone executable demonstration of a nonlocal return.
Task: Add the explicit Attributes.h include and ReturnsTwice predicate inside CallBase. Write tests/ir/returns_twice.ll and retain the earlier call checks.

cmake --build build
opt -passes=verify -disable-output tests/ir/returns_twice.ll
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/returns_twice.ll -o build/returns_twice-checked.ll

Checkpoint: Expect “returns_twice calls are unsupported” and identical canonical output. Explain why one static SSA call/result can need special control-flow handling without producing two simultaneous result values.

items: The `returns_twice` fixture is rejected with “returns_twice calls are unsupported” and the canonical output is identical to the input (rejection before mutation).

A `returns_twice` call (the setjmp/longjmp family) can resume control at the call site more than once at runtime, so the same SSA result may be read on more than one pass with different values and control can flow backward to a point before the call — yet statically the IR shows one call instruction and one result value, never two simultaneous results; the state machine's snapshot assumes forward-only control flow, so the guard rejects the function even though the static IR looks ordinary.

blocks.text: Study-session walkthrough — naked changes the function’s low-level entry/exit contract

Check the function-level Naked attribute before traversing instructions. Save the focused module below as tests/ir/naked.ll, or pass it through standard input for the same guard test. Expect “naked functions are unsupported” and unchanged canonical output; test that specific reason.

For an ordinary function, the backend manages entry/exit machine-code work such as stack-frame setup and restoration when needed. Those sequences are the prologue and epilogue; they are not LLVM blocks automatically named prologue or epilogue. naked disables the usual prologue/epilogue emission and places the function under a special low-level contract. Our dispatcher and demotion add stack storage under ordinary assumptions, so we reject this case conservatively. See LLVM’s [function attributes](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#function-attributes).

F is the function being inspected. hasFnAttribute asks whether this function carries the Naked attribute; it is not a question about one instruction or a call’s result. This is why the predicate belongs outside the instruction loop, unlike the preceding CallBase checks. Reuse the explicit llvm/IR/Attributes.h include from the previous step for the attribute identifier.

Read the complete structural input: define starts a function body, void says there is no returned value, @naked_example names the function, and () means no arguments. The naked suffix is a function attribute, not a block label or an instruction. entry names the first block. unreachable is its terminator and asserts that defined execution never reaches that point; actually executing it is undefined behavior, not a normal void return or recovery action.

This fixture exists only to test attribute rejection. It is not an executable demonstration of a functioning naked routine or target-specific prologue behavior. There is no inline-assembly call, so a different call guard cannot substitute for the missing naked rule and accidentally make the negative test appear successful. Parser/verifier validity and the existence of a defined runtime behavior are different questions.
Task: Put the function-level Naked predicate before block/instruction traversal and write tests/ir/naked.ll. Keep every preflight decision before the first transformation edit.

cmake --build build
opt -passes=verify -disable-output tests/ir/naked.ll
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/naked.ll -o build/naked-checked.ll

Checkpoint: Expect “naked functions are unsupported” with identical canonical IR. Explain why the predicate is on F rather than CallBase, and why this non-executable structural fixture can test a guard without demonstrating a working naked backend routine.

items: The naked-function fixture (a function carrying the `naked` attribute) is rejected with “naked functions are unsupported” and the canonical IR is identical to the input.

`naked` is a function attribute — it suppresses the compiler's prologue and epilogue, so the body must satisfy the whole calling convention itself — which describes the function being processed, so the predicate is on `F` (`F.hasFnAttribute(llvm::Attribute::Naked)`), checked before the block/instruction traversal rather than on a `CallBase` inside it; the machine's state slot and dispatcher are added under ordinary frame assumptions that a naked function does not honor.

The guard is a structural, attribute-based check that fires on the attribute alone before any code generation or execution, so a fixture that merely carries the `naked` attribute can test that the guard rejects and leaves the IR unchanged, without needing a working naked backend routine that actually executes prologue-less code.

Create one valid focused input for each restriction, then check the rejection reason and canonical before/after equality. For the naked case you can save naked.ll or supply the complete module through stdin. Use the table as expected outcomes, not as a substitute for running your own checks.

blocks.title: Dominance applies to allocation pointers too

blocks.text: Demoting arithmetic removes direct cross-block data uses, but the alloca result is itself an SSA pointer. If a dispatcher reaches a use without passing through that allocation, the IR is still invalid. Preserving entry storage and rejecting non-entry allocations are separate pieces of the design.
Checkpoint: Why does putting values in memory not eliminate every SSA dominance requirement?

items: Demotion removes the direct cross-block data use, but the `alloca`'s result is itself an SSA pointer: every store into the slot and every load from it uses that pointer as an operand, and each such use must be dominated by the allocation. If the dispatcher can reach a use without passing through the allocation — a non-entry allocation, or a graph path that bypasses entry — the pointer use still violates dominance even though the original value now travels through memory, which is why the eligibility rule keeps only static entry allocas.

blocks.title: Why special call semantics constrain CFG rewriting

blocks.text: An ordinary call is not the whole story. musttail requires strict call/return structure; inserting a spill reload or transition between the call and return can violate its contract. returns_twice marks calls that can return more than once, so an apparently single forward path does not capture their control effects. A convergent operation has additional constraints on how control flow may be transformed around participating operations. Operand bundles carry semantic information beyond ordinary operands, such as deoptimization or funclet context.

These features are not inherently untransformable. This small pass lacks a feature-specific proof and implementation, so preflight rejects them before editing. In contrast, a normal recursive scalar call can remain in place if its result is prepared correctly. “Do not modify calls” is not enough: moving surrounding control flow or inserting value transport can still change a call contract.
Checkpoint: Why can a musttail call become invalid even when its opcode and callee are unchanged?

items: `musttail` requires a tail-call transfer — the function returns the call's result immediately, and LLVM's rules constrain the instructions permitted between that call and its return. The rewrite inserts spill reloads and state stores and reroutes control through `ms.dispatch` between the call and the return: same opcode, same callee, but the required call/return relationship is broken, so the prototype rejects `musttail` before any edit — "do not modify calls" is not enough, because moving the surrounding control flow or inserting value transport changes the call's contract.

blocks.text: See the [LLVM call instruction reference](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#call-instruction) and the specific attributes/bundles involved before relaxing a rejection.
Checkpoint: Name a source feature rejected by this prototype and the invariant the rejection protects. Why must every rejection happen before the first demotion?

items: For example: a function with the `naked` attribute is rejected (“naked functions are unsupported”) because the machine's assumptions about entry setup (static entry allocas, inserted instructions) do not hold for a function that suppresses its prologue/epilogue; a `musttail` call is rejected (“musttail calls are unsupported”) because `musttail` constrains what may appear between the call and the following return, and an inserted spill or dispatcher hop would break that promise; a non-entry or variable-size `alloca` is rejected (“only static entry allocas are supported”) because hoisting it into the one-time setup could change allocation frequency or lifetime.

The pass promises that a rejected function comes back untouched; if any mutation — even the first demotion — happened before a later check failed, the function would be left half-transformed and that promise would break, so the guard scans the whole function first and only when every check passes does any demotion begin.

blocks.text: LLVM program before and after this checkpoint
This valid function contains a variable-size alloca. The stricter guard rejects it before preparation or construction.
The program is unchanged at this checkpoint. The output is identical: no partial spills, state slot, or new edges. Being valid LLVM IR is separate from being supported by this pass.
Reading this LLVM program from zero

Do not read every displayed block as one straight-line script. A call supplies the function inputs and starts its first block. Within the selected block, follow the written instructions until a terminator chooses another block or returns to the caller. A label names a block; it does not execute an operation by itself.

rows: `define` starts a function body. `@dynamic` is the module-level function name; `i32` immediately before it is the return type. Parentheses contain typed inputs supplied by the caller; braces contain its blocks.

i8 means an 8-bit integer; an alloca of i8 reserves one byte per element here; i32 means a 32-bit integer bit pattern; signed interpretation comes from operations such as slt or sdiv, not from a separate signed i32 type.

The left side names the result of this instruction. Each SSA result has one static defining instruction; input arguments are values supplied at function entry. A name is a handle for a value, not a mutable source variable or a guaranteed CPU register.

The colon defines a block label; the label operand names a jump destination. `%` is also used for local result/argument names, so use the type/context to distinguish a value from a block target. `@` instead identifies a module-level symbol.

Everything after a semicolon on that line is a comment for the reader. The printer lists incoming blocks after preds; it is not an instruction, an execution order, or a separate edge definition. Branch/switch operands actually define the edges.

Alignment is in bytes, not elements, bits, or a value to store. An aligned alloca provides suitably aligned storage; an aligned load/store promises that its pointer meets that alignment. It does not initialize memory or change the integer read/written.

blocks.text: Every instruction used in this pair

rows: Meaning and operand order in these listings

`alloca i8, i32 %n` reserves n i8 elements and produces their address. It does not store n into the storage. This size depends on a runtime input, so it is not a static entry allocation and the guard intentionally rejects it unchanged.
`br label %B` always transfers control to block B. A branch is the block’s final instruction and produces no result. It does not execute both destinations.

End this function invocation and return the typed operand to its caller. `ret i32 %v` returns the integer value, while `ret ptr ...` returns a pointer. A return does not proceed to the next printed block or automatically go back to dispatch.

blocks.text: Walk one concrete execution

For an illustrative valid call with n = 4, alloca reserves four i8 elements, br goes to done, and ret returns the input integer 4, not the allocated address. This lesson’s guard rejects the variable-sized allocation before editing the IR, so both printed versions remain identical; rejection is a pass decision, not an instruction inserted into the program.

blocks.title: Read the complete before-and-after LLVM modules

blocks.text: Before — dynamic original

define i32 @dynamic(i32 %n) {
entry:
  %storage = alloca i8, i32 %n, align 1
  br label %done

done:                                             ; preds = %entry
  ret i32 %n
}

This listing is a complete LLVM module defining the example function, not a fragment with omitted blocks. It has no main driver unless one is explicitly included; opt can parse and verify it, while execution requires a caller. Names, alignments, and printer annotations may differ in your own output. This listing was generated and verified with the isolated LLVM 23.1.5 teaching references, not copied from an assumed completed learner implementation.
Follow the values and edges: The allocation count is n, not a constant static entry allocation. The refusal is intentional, not a verifier failure.

quiz.q: Can you safely hoist every non-entry alloca into entry?
choices: No; allocation frequency and lifetime can affect behavior
Yes; all pointers are equivalent
Yes, if verify passes
quiz.why: Hoisting can change program semantics. The prototype rejects these allocations until a sound handling strategy is designed.
