lessons.originalTitle: Give state-machine construction its own class
lessons.summary: Extract the builder from the orchestrating pass and make its preconditions explicit.
lessons.takeaway: A small interface separates policy, preparation, and construction.

blocks.text: Why separate the builder from the pass

The transformation now has three distinct questions: may we edit this function, have its values been prepared, and how do we construct the new graph? Mixing all three in one long run() makes it harder to identify which assumption a failure violates.

StateMachineBuilder gives graph construction one boundary. Its input is a valid, accepted, prepared function; its job is to translate that function’s control flow. This separation lets us test a prepared graph directly while keeping rejection and preparation in the orchestration pass.

A precondition is an obligation on the caller, not an automatic check performed by a C++ class. Extracting the code does not make unsafe input safe. Naming those obligations is what lets another reader understand when this helper may be used.
Task: Future exercise: declare StateMachineBuilder and move dispatcher construction into it. Keep eligibility and value preparation in FlatteningPass.
Study-session walkthrough — declare the builder interface first

Begin with include/minishield/StateMachineBuilder.h. Eligibility defines the support boundary; preparation transports values; construction changes the graph. Give construction a named interface before moving the implementation, so you can state its contract without rewriting the pass all at once.

pragma once prevents repeated inclusion in one translation unit; the include makes llvm::Function known. The namespace gives the class its minishield:: name, and public permits callers outside the class. static means callers will use StateMachineBuilder::build(F) without constructing an object. Function& borrows mutable existing IR; it does not copy or own the function. bool reports whether construction changed IR, not whether input was eligible.

Before calling the implementation, the caller must supply valid IR that passed strict preflight and had PHIs/escaping results prepared. A declaration documents that contract; it does not execute the checks or perform construction.

Task: Write only the header for this step and fill its public static declaration. Leave graph code and CMake unchanged until you write the later .cpp definition. Use the implementation scaffold as the next exercise after checking the interface.
Check the declaration without needing its definition

A normal build may report no work because an unused header is not compiled on its own. Once you have written it, this optional syntax-only caller checks visibility and the static call form without linking the not-yet-written definition:

Checkpoint: A header declaration alone should cause no LLVM program change. Explain why a static method needs no builder object, why Function& is mutable but borrowed, and why the declaration cannot supply a linked implementation by itself.

items: A non-static member is called through an object, and an object exists to hold state. `build` has no state: everything it needs arrives through `F`, and everything it computes (the entry block, the snapshots, the state IDs) is fresh per call and dies with it. A `this` pointing at zero bytes of state would only suggest a per-builder configuration that does not exist. `static` says the class is only the name that owns the function, so callers write `StateMachineBuilder::build(F)` without constructing anything. `FunctionEligibility::check` is static for the same reason; if a design had state to carry between calls, that would be the moment to make it non-static.

The reference copies nothing and owns nothing: it binds to the caller’s existing `Function`, whose lifetime belongs to the caller (ultimately the `Module` and `LLVMContext`). Mutability lives in the reference’s type, not in the object: `Function &` lets the body rewrite the CFG in place, while `check`’s `const Function &` forbids it. The same object can be reached read-only or read-write through different declarations.

A declaration is a promise about a symbol; the definition is the machine code. The compiler type-checks against the promise, but a real program also needs the linker to resolve the call: without the `.cpp` definition, linking fails with `undefined reference to 'minishield::StateMachineBuilder::build(llvm::Function&)'`. The header is the shared contract, included by many translation units that each compile only the promise; the `.cpp` is the single implementation, compiled once and linked into every consumer. A header no `.cpp` includes compiles to nothing, which is why `ninja: no work to do` was the honest report for the declaration-only step.

blocks.text: The template to start with
Step 1 — Define the contract

build receives a mutable function with valid IR that passed the strict guard and has already had PHIs and cross-block results prepared. It returns whether it changed the CFG. It does not own the function and must not be called on rejected input.
Step 2 — Snapshot only original blocks and terminators
Capture the entry terminator too: it must choose the first state. Snapshot before creating dispatch/invalid so the later rewrite does not accidentally rewrite the dispatcher’s own switch.
Step 3 — Skip functions with no dispatchable entry path
For this design, build returns false if there is only one block or entry has no successors. Do not construct an unused state machine just to satisfy a block-count expectation.
The full header
Study-session walkthrough — define the first implementation body

After declaring the interface, write lib/StateMachineBuilder.cpp with this small body. Include your own header so the compiler checks the definition against the declaration. DenseMap, Instructions, and vector support the upcoming state/terminator snapshots; leave those snapshots as the next writing step.

The header declares a public static method; this file defines it. Do not repeat static on an out-of-class member definition. StateMachineBuilder::build selects the class member, and the enclosing minishield namespace matches the header. Function& borrows mutable existing IR. The returned bool reports a construction edit, so this no-edit scaffold truthfully returns false.

The caller must already exclude declarations so getEntryBlock has a body to inspect. auto &entry aliases that first block. F.size() counts blocks, while getNumSuccessors() counts the entry terminator’s outgoing destinations. Skip a function with fewer than two blocks or no outgoing entry edge: there is no live next-block route for this dispatcher design to construct. The || expression accepts either reason and short-circuits after a true first condition.

Task: Write only the file, method body, and early guard for this checkpoint. Leave the snapshot TODO in place. Once the .cpp file exists, add lib/StateMachineBuilder.cpp to the existing target’s source list; do not replace the other sources. Rebuild after that source-list edit.

A header declaration is sufficient to compile a call, but linking that call requires the matching definition. Missing definitions or a source omitted from the target can therefore produce undefined-reference errors later. For now keep the placeholder disconnected: do not call it from FlatteningPass or remove the existing construction code until the helper implements the complete intended behavior.

Checkpoint: Expect the new source to compile and the current pass’s emitted LLVM program to stay unchanged, because it still uses the existing implementation. The scaffold itself contains no mutation and returns false. Why must the snapshot of prepared blocks, IDs, and terminators be taken before any dispatcher block is created?

items: The new `StateMachineBuilder` source compiles and the current pass's emitted program stays byte-identical, because the placeholder is deliberately left disconnected — `FlatteningPass` still calls the existing construction code, and the scaffold's `build()` contains no mutation and truthfully returns `false`.

The snapshot (the original blocks, the assigned state IDs, and every original block's terminator, including entry's — it must choose the first state) must be taken before `ms.dispatch` and `ms.invalid` are created; otherwise the later terminator-rewriting traversal would include the newly created blocks and treat the dispatcher's own switch as an original terminator to lower — the rewrite would end up rewriting its own routing machinery.

blocks.text: Verify

Add the implementation source to the existing CMake target after writing it. A helper header alone does not link a definition. Until the next lessons fill in rewriting, do not replace your working pass with an incomplete scaffold.

blocks.title: Static member functions and borrowed references

blocks.text: static here means the method needs no StateMachineBuilder instance or this pointer. It does not mean the function owns global state or that F is immutable. The Function& parameter borrows an object owned by LLVM; the bool reports mutation, not a newly allocated function.
Checkpoint: Why is a non-owning Function& preferable to new Function(...) for this interface?

items: The `Function` is already owned by the module (and the `LLVMContext`), and the pass manager hands the pass the very object it will run; `new Function(...)` would create a second copy outside the module whose edits the module, the pass manager, and later passes would never see, and whose lifetime you would have to manage yourself. `Function&` instead borrows the mutable, LLVM-owned object in place, and the returned `bool` reports whether that borrowed function was mutated — not a newly allocated function.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: Which responsibilities remain in the pass, which in eligibility, and which in the builder?

items: The pass (`FlatteningPass::run`) keeps the orchestration: it receives the function, runs the stages in order (eligibility, then value preparation, then construction), and reports the preservation result to the analysis manager.

Eligibility (`FunctionEligibility::check`) owns the support boundary alone: it decides whether the function is supported at all and rejects before any mutation, protecting the “rejected input comes back untouched” invariant.

The builder (`minishield::StateMachineBuilder::build`) owns graph construction: it takes a valid, accepted, prepared function and translates its control flow — state assignment, snapshot, dispatcher construction, and terminator rewriting — returning whether construction changed the IR; value preparation (demotion) stays in the pass, not the builder.

blocks.text: LLVM program before and after this checkpoint
This listing is the monolithic complete reference, emitted identically by the same algorithm behind StateMachineBuilder. It is a C++ responsibility split, not a new IR transformation.
The program is unchanged at this checkpoint. The helper boundary does not add another dispatcher or change any state choice. This is the final-shape reference, not an intermediate scaffold to run.
Reading this LLVM program from zero

Do not read every displayed block as one straight-line script. A call supplies the function inputs and starts its first block. Within the selected block, follow the written instructions until a terminator chooses another block or returns to the caller. A label names a block; it does not execute an operation by itself.

rows: `define` starts a function body. `@merge` is the module-level function name; `i32` immediately before it is the return type. Parentheses contain typed inputs supplied by the caller; braces contain its blocks.

i1 means one bit: 0 is false and 1 is true for a condition; i32 means a 32-bit integer bit pattern; signed interpretation comes from operations such as slt or sdiv, not from a separate signed i32 type.

An opaque pointer value: it can represent an address or the special handle returned in the coroutine example. It does not contain an i32 integer or encode a pointee type. A load/store spells out the type of value accessed separately from the pointer.

The left side names the result of this instruction. Each SSA result has one static defining instruction; input arguments are values supplied at function entry. A name is a handle for a value, not a mutable source variable or a guaranteed CPU register.

The colon defines a block label; the label operand names a jump destination. `%` is also used for local result/argument names, so use the type/context to distinguish a value from a block target. `@` instead identifies a module-level symbol.

This is a typed literal: the i-prefixed part specifies the bit width, and the decimal part is the constant value. For example, a case number or stored state ID is an integer value, unlike a `%name` or `name:` label.

Everything after a semicolon on that line is a comment for the reader. The printer lists incoming blocks after preds; it is not an instruction, an execution order, or a separate edge definition. Branch/switch operands actually define the edges.

Alignment is in bytes, not elements, bits, or a value to store. An aligned alloca provides suitably aligned storage; an aligned load/store promises that its pointer meets that alignment. It does not initialize memory or change the integer read/written.

blocks.text: Every instruction used in this pair

rows: Meaning and operand order in these listings

Reserve storage for the shown element type in this function invocation and produce its address, not the stored integer. `alloca i32` reserves one i32 slot. The allocation does not initialize its contents; a store must supply a value before an intended read.
`br label %B` always transfers control to block B. A branch is the block’s final instruction and produces no result. It does not execute both destinations.

Read a value from memory: in `load i32, ptr %slot`, i32 is the loaded value’s type and %slot is its address. The left-hand result gets the current contents, not another copy of the address. Each load defines a new SSA value; it does not compute the value that a missing earlier store should have supplied.

End this function invocation and return the typed operand to its caller. `ret i32 %v` returns the integer value, while `ret ptr ...` returns a pointer. A return does not proceed to the next printed block or automatically go back to dispatch.

Produce a value from `select i1 CONDITION, TYPE TRUE_VALUE, TYPE FALSE_VALUE`. A true condition chooses the first alternative, false the second; alternatives have the same type. This does not branch or conditionally execute the instructions that computed the operands. Here the chosen result is either a destination’s state number or the final return value.

Write memory: in `store i32 VALUE, ptr ADDRESS`, the first operand is the value and the second is the destination address. A store has an effect but no result name. Writing a state slot changes the next routing choice; writing a demotion slot transports an original program value.

Transfer control according to one integer value. The destination immediately after the condition is the default for no matching case. Each line inside `[...]` pairs a typed case constant with `label %DESTINATION`; only one destination is taken. An original switch chooses a program outcome; a dispatcher switch decodes the stored state ID. The brackets are a case list, not a runtime array.

End the block by asserting that execution never reaches this point on a defined run. Actually executing it is undefined behavior; it is not error recovery, a return, or a C++ exception. The state-machine invariant must prevent a bad stored ID from taking this default path.

blocks.text: Keep address, contents, and loaded value separate. For example, an alloca result is the address of a slot; a store writes an integer into that slot; a later load defines a new SSA name for the integer read back. The pointer name does not become the stored number. A value slot preserves program data, whereas ms.state (when present) stores a control-flow destination encoding.
Walk one concrete execution

Call merge with condition = true: take left and obtain 10; with false, take right and obtain 20. In a PHI listing join chooses the incoming constant using the predecessor edge. In a demoted listing only the executed path stores its constant, and join reads that value. In the complete machine entry selects state 0 or 1, the chosen path writes its data value then state 2, and dispatch enters join. The stored state number 2 means “run join”; it is not the result 10 or 20.

blocks.title: Read the complete before-and-after LLVM modules

blocks.text: Before — phi full

define i32 @merge(i1 %condition) {
entry:
  %ms.state = alloca i32, align 4
  %value.reg2mem = alloca i32, align 4
  %ms.next = select i1 %condition, i32 0, i32 1
  store i32 %ms.next, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

left:                                             ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  store i32 10, ptr %value.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 2, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

right:                                            ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  store i32 20, ptr %value.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 2, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

join:                                             ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  %value.reload = load i32, ptr %value.reg2mem, align 4
  ret i32 %value.reload

ms.dispatch:                                      ; preds = %right, %left, %entry
  %ms.current = load i32, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  switch i32 %ms.current, label %ms.invalid [
    i32 0, label %left
    i32 1, label %right
    i32 2, label %join
  ]

ms.invalid:                                       ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  unreachable
}

Because pointers automatically delete instructions

lessons.title: Choose states for conditional branches
lessons.summary: Use select to compute the next state without introducing another conditional branch.
lessons.takeaway: Condition, true destination, false destination: preserve their order.

blocks.text: A conditional transition chooses a number instead of an edge

An original conditional branch answers “which block next?” from an i1 condition. We want the same runtime decision to survive, but with both paths first going through dispatch. Replace the edge choice with a value choice: select the true destination’s state ID when the condition is true, otherwise the false destination’s ID.

LLVM select is an instruction/value in the generated program. The C++ pass constructs that decision; it does not execute the target program’s condition while building IR. Swapping the two state IDs preserves valid types but reverses behavior, so testing both outcomes is necessary.

Both select alternatives here are state constants. We are not moving the side effects of both original paths into one block; dispatch still executes only the selected destination. This distinction matters because select chooses already available values rather than making arbitrary computations conditional.
Task: Future exercise: replace a conditional original branch with a selected state, a store, and a branch to dispatch. This applies to conditional entries and conditional state blocks.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Read the original operands before erasing
getCondition() gives an i1 LLVM value. getSuccessor(0) is the true destination; getSuccessor(1) is the false destination. Use the pointer-to-state mapping built from original blocks.
Step 2 — Build an i32 state choice
CreateSelect produces an LLVM value, not a host C++ decision. Both alternatives are i32 state constants; the condition chooses which value will be stored when the target program executes.
Step 3 — Share the store-and-branch tail
Do this once after the opcode switch. ret and unreachable use continue to skip the shared tail. A plain break in those cases would reach the tail with next still null.
The full conditional case
Verify

For phi.ll, true must select left’s state and false right’s state. Inspect a select before the entry’s store/dispatch branch. Test both conditions with a wrapper calling merge; a verifier-only check cannot catch swapped destinations.

blocks.title: Switch scopes, break, and continue

blocks.text: Braces around a case introduce a C++ scope for local declarations. break exits the switch and proceeds to its shared tail. continue inside that switch applies to the surrounding terminator loop, skipping the tail. Confusing them can emit an invalid null store or accidentally rewrite a return.
Checkpoint: Trace execution after break and after continue in the complete helper.

items: After `break` (for example from the `CondBr` case, with `next` set to the selected state) control leaves the opcode switch and runs the shared tail — `b.CreateStore(next, slot)`, `b.CreateBr(dispatch)`, `T->eraseFromParent()`: the original terminator is replaced by a state store and a branch to dispatch. After `continue` (the `Ret`/`Unreachable` cases) the tail is skipped entirely and the outer terminator loop moves on to the next block's terminator, so the return/unreachable stays in place and the still-null `next` is never stored; confusing the two is exactly the warned failure — `break` on `ret` reaches the tail with `next` null (an invalid null store), and `continue` on a conditional branch leaves that transition unrewritten.

blocks.title: A select is an IR value, not a C++ if

blocks.text: The C++ builder runs while transforming the module. It constructs a target-program select; it does not know a runtime condition such as the input argument. Select chooses values, not which operand instructions execute. Here its operands are constants, so we are not speculatively executing side-effecting operations.
Checkpoint: Why would replacing arbitrary control-dependent operations with eager computations plus select require more care?

items: A `select` chooses between values, not between which instructions execute: eagerly computing both alternatives executes the instructions that produced them, so if either side has side effects (a call, a store, a trap) or its own control-flow semantics, running both changes the program's behavior where the original control dependency executed only one. Here the select's operands are state constants, so no side-effecting operations are being speculatively executed; generalizing the trick to arbitrary control-dependent operations would require proving that both sides are pure and safe to execute eagerly.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: How would a true/false state swap pass verify and still compute the wrong answer?

items: The swap only changes which i32 constants `CreateSelect` stores — `select i1 %condition, i32 1, i32 0` instead of `select i1 %condition, i32 0, i32 1` — and that is still a perfectly valid instruction: the types match, the store and the branch to dispatch are well-formed, and the dispatcher's switch still covers every state, so the verifier has nothing to flag; but at runtime a true condition now stores right's ID (1) and false stores left's ID (0), so dispatch routes each outcome to the opposite block and `phi.ll` returns 20 for true and 10 for false — swapping the constants preserves valid types but reverses behavior, and a verifier-only check cannot catch it.

lessons.title: Lower original switches to state selection
lessons.originalTitle: Lower original switches to state selection
lessons.summary: Preserve default behavior and each integer case while replacing the original multi-way terminator.
lessons.takeaway: Start from the default state, then override it on matching cases.

blocks.text: A switch still needs its complete decision rule

A source switch can have several named cases and a default for every other value. Flattening must preserve that entire mapping. We encode the original outcome as a next-state value instead of letting the old switch transfer control directly.

Start: next = ID(default destination).
For case value k: if input == k, choose ID(case destination).
Finally: store next and go to dispatch.

Starting from the default is what preserves unmatched inputs. Comparing every case to the same original condition preserves the case decisions; valid case values are distinct, although multiple values may share one destination. The condition’s integer type can differ from the i32 type chosen for state IDs.

There are now two different switches in the story. The original switch represents a program decision that this lesson translates into comparisons and selects. The new dispatcher switch decodes the state ID and must remain in place. Confusing the two can make the transformer rewrite its own routing machinery.
Task: Future exercise: handle original SwitchInst terminators, not the newly created dispatcher switch.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Make default explicit
next = stateOf(sw->getDefaultDest());
An input not matching any listed case must retain the original default destination. Initializing next to zero would silently change this behavior.
Step 2 — Compare using the original condition type
auto *matches = b.CreateICmpEQ(sw->getCondition(), oneCase.getCaseValue());
The switch’s integer condition is not necessarily i32. Its case constants already have the matching type. The generated comparison yields i1, while destination state constants remain i32.
Step 3 — Chain value selections
next = b.CreateSelect(matches, stateOf(oneCase.getCaseSuccessor()), next, "ms.next");

blocks.title: Value* may identify a constant, not an instruction

blocks.text: IRBuilder<> uses a constant folder by default. If a comparison or select can be folded, a Create* helper can return a Constant rather than insert an Instruction. This is why next is llvm::Value*, not Instruction*. Never blindly cast every builder result to Instruction just because the method starts with Create.
Checkpoint: How is a host C++ integer 3 different from an LLVM ConstantInt representing target value 3?

items: A host C++ integer 3 is a value in the compiler's own memory — data in the C++ program itself. An LLVM `ConstantInt` is a `Value` object in the target module's constant pool: a target-program constant of a specific LLVM type (`i32 3`), referenced as an operand by target instructions and printed in the IR. When the default folder folds `b.CreateAdd(b.getInt32(1), b.getInt32(2))`, the `Value*` result is that IR `Constant` inside the module — not a C++ `int` the compiler can use — which is why `next` is declared `llvm::Value*` rather than `Instruction*`, and why blindly casting builder results to `Instruction` is not a valid assumption.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: Why must default be initialized first? Why must the compare operands use the original switch type?

items: The default case is the destination for every input that matches no listed case, so initializing `next` to the default destination's state (`next = stateOf(sw->getDefaultDest())`) before the case loop is what preserves unmatched inputs; initializing `next` to zero (or leaving it unset) would silently reroute every unmatched input to block 0, changing the program's behavior on the default path.

The original switch's condition is an integer that is not necessarily `i32` (an `i64` or `i8` switch is legal), and `icmp eq` requires both operands to have the same type; the case constants already carry the condition's type, so comparing the condition against each case value in the original type is what keeps every case decision valid — the comparison yields `i1` to drive the chained selects, while the destination state constants remain `i32`, and those two roles must not be mixed.

lessons.title: Rewrite every original terminator
lessons.summary: Combine the branch forms into one complete, carefully bounded state-machine builder.
lessons.takeaway: Rewrite the snapshot, never the dispatcher’s new switch.

blocks.text: Full flattening is a repeated protocol, not just a new switch

Creating a dispatcher and connecting entry changes only one hop. The complete machine requires each original non-terminal transition to follow the same protocol: compute the intended next state, store it, then branch to dispatch. The switch chooses the next block, whose own transition repeats that process.

setup → choose/store state → dispatch → original block
                               ↑              |
                               └─ store next ─┘
An original return finishes the invocation instead of taking the loop back.

This is the key behavioral invariant: at each dispatcher visit, the slot encodes exactly the destination the original program would have chosen at that transition. A valid number is not enough; it must be the correct number for the original condition and path.

Snapshot original terminators before appending new blocks so the rewrite applies only to the old program’s transitions. Keep ret and unreachable terminal rather than manufacturing another state after they have already ended a path. The shared store/branch tail is appropriate only when a next state exists.
Task: Future exercise: complete StateMachineBuilder.cpp using the previous branch cases. This reference assumes the strict preflight and value-preparation stages.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Handle terminal paths
Return and unreachable terminate the current function path. Leave those instructions unchanged and continue the outer loop. Do not set a state and dispatch again after a return.
Step 2 — Validate state membership

Use find() rather than silently interpreting lookup’s default zero as a real state. Missing IDs here mean a bug in the snapshot/preflight contract for valid input. Unsupported user input should have been cleanly rejected before mutation.
Step 3 — Finish each replacement before verifying

Insert comparisons/selects, then the state store, then the dispatch branch, and erase the old terminator. Do not use an erased pointer or a builder insertion point that still refers to the erased instruction.
The full builder implementation
Verify

Build only after you have added the new helper source to CMake. Run the pass followed by verify over every positive fixture. At this final builder stage, each original nonterminal block—including entry—should store a destination state and branch to dispatch. The dispatcher still has its switch; terminal blocks still return or end in unreachable.

blocks.title: A structural invariant is measured at a particular stage

blocks.text: Count N immediately before building the dispatcher, after SSA preparation. This helper adds two blocks, so its result has N+2 blocks. Do not blindly assert input N+1 from the old roadmap: a different design or earlier preparation can change that count. A test must describe this algorithm, not a remembered number.
Checkpoint: Which stage’s block count does your test record?

items: The count N is taken immediately before building the dispatcher, after SSA preparation (PHI demotion and escaping-value demotion) has completed — the prepared function, before this helper's edits; because the helper adds exactly two blocks (`ms.dispatch` and `ms.invalid`), its result has N+2 blocks. The test must describe this algorithm (N before, N+2 after for this design), not a remembered number like input N+1 from the old roadmap, since a different design or earlier preparation can change that count.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: Which terminator is intentionally never in the snapshot? Why does the helper use a fatal internal-contract error rather than partially returning success?

items: The dispatcher's own switch terminator (`ms.dispatch`'s) is intentionally never in the snapshot: the `terminators` vector captures every original block's terminator — including entry's, since it must choose the first state — before `ms.dispatch` and `ms.invalid` are created, so the rewrite's input set contains only original terminators and the machine's own routing switch is never lowered as if it were one.

By the time the rewrite runs, successful preflight and the state assignment have guaranteed that every original terminator's destination has a state; a missing key (or an unknown terminator kind, “unsupported terminator escaped preflight”) therefore indicates an internal bug, not an unsupported input, and `report_fatal_error` stops cleanly while naming the violated contract — a partial success would leave a half-rewritten function with some terminators flattened and others still original, a worse and harder-to-diagnose state than an immediate, named failure.

lessons.title: Orchestrate policy, preparation, and construction
lessons.summary: Finish the pass as an ordered pipeline and account for every mutation in analysis invalidation.
lessons.takeaway: One pass coordinates; each helper has a focused job.

blocks.text: Why the order of phases is part of correctness

The pass is now a pipeline within a pipeline. Eligibility protects the input boundary; preparation changes how values travel; construction changes how blocks are reached; preservation reporting tells later passes which cached facts remain usable. Each phase establishes assumptions needed by the next.

reject unsupported input before edits
    ↓
prepare values for a different graph
    ↓
translate control-flow decisions into states
    ↓
report whether cached analyses became stale

Reordering these calls is not just a style change. Rewiring first can leave old PHIs and SSA uses invalid. Rejecting last leaves unsupported functions mutated. Reporting no change after demotion lets later passes reuse obsolete results. Track all phases’ changes without accidentally skipping a phase whose call has side effects.
Task: Future exercise: replace the prototype’s inline construction with the strict guard, preparation stage, and StateMachineBuilder call.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Keep rejection before modification
No demotion or state allocation should precede the decision. Rejection after a partial transformation violates the unchanged-input contract.
Step 2 — Combine change information without skipping work

bool changed = !phis.empty() || !escaping.empty();
changed |= StateMachineBuilder::build(F);

Here |= is boolean accumulation that evaluates the builder call even if changed was already true. Writing changed = changed || build(F) would short-circuit and skip construction whenever demotion changed the function. Alternatively call build first into a separate bool, then combine the results.
Step 3 — Preserve conservatively

Return none() after any mutation in this teaching implementation. Preserving a particular analysis is a claim you must justify and, for dependent cached analyses, implement correctly. “The graph still looks similar” is not enough.
The full pass reference
Verify
Run stats before and after flattening in the same pipeline so cached analysis invalidation is exercised. Expect the second stats pass to observe the new blocks and edges, not the original cached CFG.

  -passes='function(minishield-stats,minishield-flatten,minishield-stats),verify' \
  -disable-output tests/ir/loop.ll

blocks.text: This is C++ evaluation behavior, not an LLVM pass-manager feature. A change flag should summarize work, not accidentally control whether required work runs.
Checkpoint: How would you test that the builder runs when a PHI was already demoted?

items: Run a function whose PHIs are already gone but which still needs preparation — the `cross_block` fixture (zero PHIs; `sum` defined in entry and consumed in exit): its PHI worklist is empty, but its escaping values are not, so the change flag is already true before the builder call — exactly the case where a buggy `changed = changed || build(F)` would short-circuit and skip construction. Confirm the builder ran by checking that the machine's artifacts appear in the emitted IR (the `ms.state` alloca, the `ms.dispatch`/`ms.invalid` blocks, and the rewritten entry terminator) — equivalently, that the second `minishield-stats` in the verify pipeline observes the new blocks and edges; if the builder were skipped, the module would show only the demotion.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: Which helper owns policy? Which phase changes data flow? Which creates CFG edges? What exactly does the final bool summarize?

items: The eligibility guard owns the policy: it decides whether the function is supported at all, before any other phase runs.

The preparation phase (demoting PHIs and escaping values) changes data flow: values that were direct SSA uses now travel through stack slots via stores and loads, changing how data moves without yet changing control flow.
The construction phase (state-machine building) creates the CFG edges: the entry branch to `ms.dispatch`, the dispatcher's switch cases, and the rewritten original terminators.

The final `bool` summarizes whether any phase changed the function — which is exactly what the preservation result is keyed on (`none()` if the IR changed, `all()` if it did not) and what the pass reports to the analysis manager.

The PHI’s i32 type applies to every incoming value, so a literal inside a bracket does not repeat the type. PHIs go at the start of a block. On a loop’s first entry choose its entry value, and on a back edge choose its carried value. Multiple PHIs select incoming values together, rather than sequentially overwriting each other.

End this function invocation and return the typed operand to its caller. `ret i32 %v` returns the integer value, while `ret ptr ...` returns a pointer. A return does not proceed to the next printed block or automatically go back to dispatch.

Produce a value from `select i1 CONDITION, TYPE TRUE_VALUE, TYPE FALSE_VALUE`. A true condition chooses the first alternative, false the second; alternatives have the same type. This does not branch or conditionally execute the instructions that computed the operands. Here the chosen result is either a destination’s state number or the final return value.

Write memory: in `store i32 VALUE, ptr ADDRESS`, the first operand is the value and the second is the destination address. A store has an effect but no result name. Writing a state slot changes the next routing choice; writing a demotion slot transports an original program value.

Transfer control according to one integer value. The destination immediately after the condition is the default for no matching case. Each line inside `[...]` pairs a typed case constant with `label %DESTINATION`; only one destination is taken. An original switch chooses a program outcome; a dispatcher switch decodes the stored state ID. The brackets are a case list, not a runtime array.

End the block by asserting that execution never reaches this point on a defined run. Actually executing it is undefined behavior; it is not error recovery, a return, or a C++ exception. The state-machine invariant must prevent a bad stored ID from taking this default path.

blocks.text: Keep address, contents, and loaded value separate. For example, an alloca result is the address of a slot; a store writes an integer into that slot; a later load defines a new SSA name for the integer read back. The pointer name does not become the stored number. A value slot preserves program data, whereas ms.state (when present) stores a control-flow destination encoding.
Walk one concrete execution

Call count_to with limit = 2. The initial counter is 0; the signed-less-than test is true for 0 and 1, so the body increments it to 1 and then 2. At 2 the test is false and exit returns 2. A PHI selects initial 0 on entry and the previous body’s next value on a back edge; after demotion the loop-variable slot carries those same values. The complete after listing stores state 0 for header, 1 for body, or 2 for exit. State storage controls where to run; separate value slots carry the counter. The default unreachable path is never an intended outcome.

blocks.title: Read the complete before-and-after LLVM modules

blocks.text: Before — loop original

define i32 @count_to(i32 %limit) {
entry:
  br label %header

header:                                           ; preds = %body, %entry
  %i = phi i32 [ 0, %entry ], [ %next, %body ]
  %continue = icmp slt i32 %i, %limit
  br i1 %continue, label %body, label %exit

body:                                             ; preds = %header
  %next = add i32 %i, 1
  br label %header

exit:                                             ; preds = %header
  ret i32 %i
}
After — loop full

define i32 @count_to(i32 %limit) {
entry:
  %ms.state = alloca i32, align 4
  %i.reload.reg2mem = alloca i32, align 4
  %i.reg2mem = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 0, ptr %i.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 0, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

header:                                           ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  %i.reload = load i32, ptr %i.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 %i.reload, ptr %i.reload.reg2mem, align 4
  %i.reload.reload = load i32, ptr %i.reload.reg2mem, align 4
  %continue = icmp slt i32 %i.reload.reload, %limit
  %ms.next = select i1 %continue, i32 1, i32 2
  store i32 %ms.next, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

body:                                             ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  %i.reload.reload1 = load i32, ptr %i.reload.reg2mem, align 4
  %next = add i32 %i.reload.reload1, 1
  store i32 %next, ptr %i.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 0, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

exit:                                             ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  %i.reload.reload2 = load i32, ptr %i.reload.reg2mem, align 4
  ret i32 %i.reload.reload2

ms.dispatch:                                      ; preds = %body, %header, %entry
  %ms.current = load i32, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  switch i32 %ms.current, label %ms.invalid [
    i32 0, label %header
    i32 1, label %body
    i32 2, label %exit
  ]

ms.invalid:                                       ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  unreachable
}

They have no main driver unless one is explicitly included; opt can parse and verify them, while execution requires a caller. Names, alignments, and printer annotations may differ in your own output. It always calls build twice

lessons.title: Inspect the final shape with LLVM tools
lessons.originalTitle: Inspect the final shape with LLVM tools
lessons.summary: Learn to diagnose a transformation from IR, pass traces, and verifier errors before relying on runtime comparisons.
lessons.takeaway: The verifier catches structure; inspection explains how it was built.

blocks.text: What inspecting the final graph can establish

A compiler transformation has two separate obligations: produce well-formed IR and preserve intended behavior. Structural inspection addresses the first and checks our design invariants. We want to see a live entry-to-dispatch path, valid state storage, the intended cases, and the rewritten transitions.

The mere presence of a switch or a block named ms.dispatch is weak evidence: it might be unreachable while the original graph still runs unchanged. Follow actual successors from entry and verify the relations among blocks. LLVM’s verifier also checks rules such as types, terminators, and dominance; it does not prove our state IDs choose the right answers.

This is why the next lesson compares executions. A true/false ID swap can be structurally legal yet wrong. Keep structural checks and behavioral checks as complementary tests rather than expecting one to replace the other.
Task: Future exercise: establish structural evidence for the complete rewrite before measuring performance.
The template to start with

opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/loop.ll -o build/loop-flat.ll
# TODO: inspect setup, dispatch, state stores, and terminal paths.
Step 1 — Inspect invariants, not exact names

LLVM may uniquify names such as ms.dispatch. Use opcode/edge relationships for assertions. Text dumps remain useful for understanding, but a test that only greps for a name can pass with a dead or malformed intended structure.
Step 2 — Read an SSA dominance error

If a definition no longer dominates a use, locate both blocks and draw the new incoming edges. Do not hide the error by deleting verify. Check that a slot was allocated in preserved entry and that the use refers to a local reload, not an old cross-block definition.
Step 3 — Trace passes

opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -debug-pass-manager -disable-output tests/ir/loop.ll
Use the pass-manager trace to distinguish “loaded,” “scheduled,” “skipped,” and “ran.” Optional passes can be skipped on optnone functions; a missing diagnostic is not always a broken plugin.
Step 4 — Preserve a failing artifact
Keep the smallest failing input, the command, the compiler version, and stderr. Save generated IR under build/. Record which stage first breaks rather than changing several phases at once.
The full inspection checklist

items: Setup remains the first block and has no predecessors.
State allocation dominates every load/store using its pointer.
Every generated block has a terminator.
Dispatch cases reference the intended state blocks.
Original state transitions store a valid ID before dispatch.
The default invalid path must be unreachable under valid state transitions.

blocks.text: Verify
Repeat with the branch, switch, recursion, loop, and PHI fixtures. Structural checks must pass before behavior comparisons are useful.
Checkpoint: What would a correct-looking but unreachable dispatcher prove? Why must instructions and edges both be inspected?

items: A dispatcher whose load and switch cases all look correct but has no live predecessor proves only that the construction placed the right instructions — the machine was built but never entered, and whatever control flow remains is what actually executes; it is a built-but-unconnected machine that demonstrates nothing about behavior.

Instructions and edges are independent failure modes: a block can hold a perfect switch with no incoming branch (built but not connected), or an incoming edge with a wrong switch (connected but not built correctly); inspecting the instructions verifies the machine's parts, while inspecting the edges (predecessors, branches, switch destinations) verifies that control actually flows through them, and only both together confirm the final shape.

blocks.text: Before — phi original

define i32 @merge(i1 %condition) {
entry:
  br i1 %condition, label %left, label %right

left:                                             ; preds = %entry
  br label %join

right:                                            ; preds = %entry

define i32 @merge(i1 %condition) {
entry:
  %ms.state = alloca i32, align 4
  %value.reg2mem = alloca i32, align 4
  %ms.next = select i1 %condition, i32 0, i32 1
  store i32 %ms.next, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

left:                                             ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  store i32 10, ptr %value.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 2, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

right:                                            ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  store i32 20, ptr %value.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 2, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

join:                                             ; preds = %ms.dispatch

choices: No; the block could be unreachable or incorrectly wired
Yes; that name is reserved by LLVM

lessons.title: Compare observable behavior on a defined domain
lessons.originalTitle: Compare observable behavior on a defined domain
lessons.summary: Build original and transformed functions from the same front-end IR, then compare outputs for bounded inputs.
lessons.takeaway: Equivalent behavior is stronger than valid IR, but testing is still finite evidence.

blocks.text: Why valid IR is not enough

Imagine a rewrite that reverses the destinations of a conditional branch. The result can have correct types, terminators, and dominance, but return the wrong discount. To test meaning, run the original and protected versions on the same inputs and compare what a caller can observe.

This is differential testing: one implementation is the reference for the other. Our small driver exposes a numeric result on stdout and an exit status. The test domain must use defined arithmetic and valid arguments; otherwise a disagreement might come from a broken fixture rather than our transformation.

We compile one common input IR and vary whether MiniShield transforms it. Keeping the driver, compiler settings, and final optimization the same helps isolate that difference. Finite tests give evidence for the tested cases, not proof for all inputs. Also inspect the graph: a stub that does nothing can pass every output comparison.
Task: Future exercise: write a C input function and a separate driver. Transform the function’s IR, not the driver that parses arguments and prints results.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Bound the test domain

Use amounts from -1000 through 10000 and levels 0 through 5. The arithmetic below cannot overflow int on that domain. Comparing two programs that both have source undefined behavior is not a meaningful correctness test.
Step 2 — Write the function and driver
Save that as tests/cases/discount.c and the following as tests/cases/discount_driver.c. The command-line guard keeps executions inside the documented domain.
Step 3 — Create one common IR input

The front end emits unoptimized IR without the O0 optnone attribute so the optional pass will run. Both variants then use the same -O2 backend. This separates the tested transformation from accidental differences in front-end settings.

mkdir -p build/differential
clang -O0 -Xclang -disable-O0-optnone -S -emit-llvm \
  tests/cases/discount.c -o build/differential/common.ll
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -S build/differential/common.ll -o build/differential/protected.ll
clang -O2 tests/cases/discount_driver.c build/differential/common.ll \
  -o build/differential/original
clang -O2 tests/cases/discount_driver.c build/differential/protected.ll \
  -o build/differential/protected
Step 4 — Compare boundary and representative inputs

build/differential/original 1000 2
build/differential/protected 1000 2
# Expected stdout from each: 900
build/differential/original -1 0
build/differential/protected -1 0
# Expected stdout from each: 0
The full comparison contract

items: Same common input IR, driver, backend flags, toolchain, and inputs.
Both processes exit normally; compare exit status and stdout. Treat crashes/timeouts as failures.
Inspect transformed IR to ensure a transformation actually happened; equality is trivial if the pass skipped everything.
Passing examples provide evidence for this test domain, not a universal proof.

blocks.text: Verify
Start with amounts -1, 0, 1, 99, 100, 1000, 10000 and every level. Day 3 adds seeded randomized cases, CTest wiring, and diagnostics for the first mismatch.
Checkpoint: Why is -disable-O0-optnone present? Why transform the function module and link a common driver afterward?

items: `-disable-O0-optnone` is present because, without it, clang's `-O0` would attach the `optnone` attribute to the function and the optional pass would not run on it; the flag makes the front end emit unoptimized IR without that attribute, so the loaded `minishield-flatten` pass actually transforms the common `common.ll` input.

The fixture module defines only the function — no `main` — so to observe behavior you first transform it (`opt` with the pass plugin, producing `protected.ll`) and then link the resulting module against the common driver (`discount_driver.c`), a shared `main` that parses arguments, enforces the bounded domain, and prints the result; transforming first and linking afterward keeps the tested transformation isolated from the driver, which stays identical for the original and protected builds.

The other syntax printed around this function

rows: Module settings for the target machine and its data representation. The triple names the architecture/environment. The datalayout string describes details such as pointer sizes, integer alignment, native widths, and stack alignment; it is not a sequence of program instructions.

dso_local says the function symbol resolves locally in its linkage unit. noundef on the inputs requires a fully defined value, without undef/poison bits. These are semantic contracts and code-generation facts, not extra parameters or runtime tests.

The header’s #0 refers to the numbered attribute group below. noinline prevents inlining; nounwind says the function does not unwind; uwtable requests unwind-table information. These do not replace the body’s branches or arithmetic.

These are metadata names/references and tuple nodes. !"PIC Level" is a metadata string; typed i32 values inside a node describe settings. They are not runtime struct/array objects or executable assignments. For example, the module-flag tuple’s first integer controls how a setting merges when modules are linked; 8 means Min, 7 Max. The following string names the setting and the final integer gives its value.

These entries record position-independent code/executable settings and unwind/frame-pointer policy; !llvm.ident records compiler identity. They remain in the complete module for reproducibility while the lesson’s transformation changes function instructions.

lessons.title: Add difficult CFG fixtures deliberately
lessons.summary: Exercise nested loops, PHI cycles, multiple returns, shared switch destinations, and the unchanged rejection contract.
lessons.takeaway: One fixture should isolate one failure mode.

blocks.text: Why a simple diamond is not a sufficient test corpus

A diamond exercises one merge and two paths. It does not exercise a loop’s repeated value choices, two PHIs that depend on each other, a switch’s default, several returns, or an edge that needs special placement during demotion. A transformer can handle the first example perfectly and still break on these different relationships.

Choose each new fixture to stress one assumption. An initial/loop-carried value tests first versus later iterations. Shared switch destinations test whether values and destinations were confused. Parallel PHIs test whether old values are preserved before any replacement overwrites them.

The goal is not simply more lines of IR. Small focused fixtures let you predict the graph and results independently, recognize a specific failure, and keep a regression that explains the bug. Unsupported cases need equally deliberate rejection tests rather than being silently omitted.
Task: Future exercise: grow the fixture corpus before claiming the transformer handles general control flow.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Test parallel PHI selection

Two loop PHIs can exchange old values. Their incoming values are conceptually selected together. A naive hand-written sequence of stores and loads can overwrite an old value before the other PHI uses it; do not replace LLVM’s helper with that shortcut.

header:
  %x = phi i32 [ 0, %entry ], [ %y, %body ]
  %y = phi i32 [ 1, %entry ], [ %x, %body ]
  ; Complete the loop with a bounded induction counter before running it.
Step 2 — Test several shapes

rows: Repeated state transitions and multiple loop headers.
Loop count need not equal back-edge count.
Terminal states must not dispatch again.
Distinct values may map to one state.
The second preparation stage must run.

blocks.text: Step 3 — Make a test oracle

For each accepted fixture, use a bounded harness with known or original results. For rejected fixtures, compare canonical IR and the intended reason. Do not count an arbitrary early rejection as evidence that a later check works.
The full review procedure

items: Verify the input independently.
Predict accept/reject and expected outputs by hand.
Run the transform with verify.
Inspect structural relationships.
Execute both versions in the defined domain.
Keep a failing case as a regression test before attempting a fix.

blocks.text: Verify

Do not paste the partial PHI fragment above as a complete module; the loop counter and terminating path are an exercise. Finish it, validate it, then compare several iteration counts including zero and one.
Checkpoint: Why can preserving SSA validity still produce a wrong value when a hand-written PHI lowering overwrites an old incoming value?

items: SSA validity is structural — every use has a definition, every block has a terminator — so a hand-written lowering that pairs an incoming value with the wrong edge, or lets one path's store overwrite the slot before another path's load reads it, still produces perfectly valid IR that the verifier accepts; but the machine now delivers the wrong value on that path, because value correctness — which incoming value each transition must carry — is a semantic property the verifier does not check.

The parallel-PHI fixture makes this concrete: the two loop PHIs exchange old values (next `a` is old `b`, next `b` is old `a`) and their incomings are selected together; a naive sequential store sequence can overwrite one old value before the other PHI's store reads it, so the separate saved slots are what keep the old values available — which is why the lesson says not to replace LLVM's helper with that shortcut.

blocks.text: LLVM program before and after this checkpoint
This complete swap-loop fixture fills in the counter and exits missing from the earlier conceptual PHI fragment. It tests interacting loop-carried choices.
What changes: Three PHIs are prepared before dispatch rewriting. The next iteration must receive old b as a and old a as b, without sequential overwriting losing an old value.
Reading this LLVM program from zero

Do not read every displayed block as one straight-line script. A call supplies the function inputs and starts its first block. Within the selected block, follow the written instructions until a terminator chooses another block or returns to the caller. A label names a block; it does not execute an operation by itself.

rows: `define` starts a function body. `@swap_loop` is the module-level function name; `i32` immediately before it is the return type. Parentheses contain typed inputs supplied by the caller; braces contain its blocks.

i1 means one bit: 0 is false and 1 is true for a condition; i32 means a 32-bit integer bit pattern; signed interpretation comes from operations such as slt or sdiv, not from a separate signed i32 type.

An opaque pointer value: it can represent an address or the special handle returned in the coroutine example. It does not contain an i32 integer or encode a pointee type. A load/store spells out the type of value accessed separately from the pointer.

The left side names the result of this instruction. Each SSA result has one static defining instruction; input arguments are values supplied at function entry. A name is a handle for a value, not a mutable source variable or a guaranteed CPU register.

The colon defines a block label; the label operand names a jump destination. `%` is also used for local result/argument names, so use the type/context to distinguish a value from a block target. `@` instead identifies a module-level symbol.

This is a typed literal: the i-prefixed part specifies the bit width, and the decimal part is the constant value. For example, a case number or stored state ID is an integer value, unlike a `%name` or `name:` label.

Everything after a semicolon on that line is a comment for the reader. The printer lists incoming blocks after preds; it is not an instruction, an execution order, or a separate edge definition. Branch/switch operands actually define the edges.

Alignment is in bytes, not elements, bits, or a value to store. An aligned alloca provides suitably aligned storage; an aligned load/store promises that its pointer meets that alignment. It does not initialize memory or change the integer read/written.

blocks.text: Every instruction used in this pair

rows: Meaning and operand order in these listings

Add the two same-typed operands and define the sum. In these unflagged i32 examples, arithmetic is modulo 2^32; the test inputs stay in the small intended range. This calculates data, such as the next loop counter or x + 1, rather than choosing a block.

Reserve storage for the shown element type in this function invocation and produce its address, not the stored integer. `alloca i32` reserves one i32 slot. The allocation does not initialize its contents; a store must supply a value before an intended read.

`br label %B` always transfers control to block B. `br i1 %C, label %A, label %B` goes to A for true and B for false; their order matters. A branch is the block’s final instruction and produces no result. It does not execute both destinations.

Compare two same-typed integers and produce i1, which can feed br or select. `slt` asks whether the left operand is smaller using signed integer interpretation, so a negative i32 is below zero. The comparison computes a condition; it does not jump by itself.

Read left-to-right: compare the first integer operand with the second, then use the resulting i1 as a condition. For the loop it compares the current counter with the bound; for the discount kernel it checks whether the amount is negative.

Read a value from memory: in `load i32, ptr %slot`, i32 is the loaded value’s type and %slot is its address. The left-hand result gets the current contents, not another copy of the address. Each load defines a new SSA value; it does not compute the value that a missing earlier store should have supplied.

Define one value by the edge just used to enter this block. Each `[ VALUE, %PREDECESSOR ]` pairs an incoming value with its source block; it is not an array access. The PHI’s i32 type applies to every incoming value, so a literal inside a bracket does not repeat the type. PHIs go at the start of a block. On a loop’s first entry choose its entry value, and on a back edge choose its carried value. Multiple PHIs select incoming values together, rather than sequentially overwriting each other.

End this function invocation and return the typed operand to its caller. `ret i32 %v` returns the integer value, while `ret ptr ...` returns a pointer. A return does not proceed to the next printed block or automatically go back to dispatch.

Produce a value from `select i1 CONDITION, TYPE TRUE_VALUE, TYPE FALSE_VALUE`. A true condition chooses the first alternative, false the second; alternatives have the same type. This does not branch or conditionally execute the instructions that computed the operands. Here the chosen result is either a destination’s state number or the final return value.

Write memory: in `store i32 VALUE, ptr ADDRESS`, the first operand is the value and the second is the destination address. A store has an effect but no result name. Writing a state slot changes the next routing choice; writing a demotion slot transports an original program value.

Subtract the second operand from the first and define the difference. Operand order matters: a − b is not b − a. In the discount kernel it removes the computed discount; in the swap loop it makes the current ordering observable.

Transfer control according to one integer value. The destination immediately after the condition is the default for no matching case. Each line inside `[...]` pairs a typed case constant with `label %DESTINATION`; only one destination is taken. An original switch chooses a program outcome; a dispatcher switch decodes the stored state ID. The brackets are a case list, not a runtime array.

End the block by asserting that execution never reaches this point on a defined run. Actually executing it is undefined behavior; it is not error recovery, a return, or a C++ exception. The state-machine invariant must prevent a bad stored ID from taking this default path.

blocks.text: Keep address, contents, and loaded value separate. For example, an alloca result is the address of a slot; a store writes an integer into that slot; a later load defines a new SSA name for the integer read back. The pointer name does not become the stored number. A value slot preserves program data, whereas ms.state (when present) stores a control-flow destination encoding.
Walk one concrete execution

Use count = 1. The entry values are a = 1, b = 2, i = 0. The first loop test is true; one latch iteration makes the next a equal old b (2), next b equal old a (1), and i equal 1. The next test is false and exit returns a − b = 1. On the original back edge both PHIs use the old incoming values together. In the demoted listing, separate saved loads/slots keep old a available even after a’s destination slot is written.

lessons.title: Account for optimizers, debug data, and limitations
lessons.originalTitle: Account for optimizers, debug data, and limitations
lessons.summary: Understand where the transformation sits in a compilation pipeline and what the prototype does not guarantee.
lessons.takeaway: Measure the artifact you actually ship, not the intermediate picture you like.

blocks.text: The pass is one stage in a larger compiler

The IR we print immediately after flattening is not necessarily the code that ships. Later optimizations can remove redundant loads, simplify state choices, restructure loops, or eliminate some dispatcher machinery. Earlier optimization can introduce forms outside our prototype’s support contract.

We therefore need two kinds of observation: does the complete pipeline preserve results, and does the final artifact still have the structure we intend to study? A fast, correct executable may no longer demonstrate flattening if optimization simplified it away.

Debug locations and branch-weight metadata also describe program relationships. New instructions and edges do not automatically inherit all the old relationships correctly. Documenting what we preserve, reject, or leave unsupported keeps the technical claim aligned with the actual implementation.
Task: Future exercise: record the transformation’s placement relative to optimization and inspect both intermediate and final artifacts.
The template to start with

common IR → [optional optimization] → MiniShield → [backend optimization] → executable
# TODO: choose and record the exact pipeline for each experiment.
Step 1 — Expect simplification

An optimizer can simplify state dispatch or replace a branch-heavy function with straight-line code. A successful build or matching output does not prove that a dispatcher remains in the emitted binary. Inspect optimized IR and disassembly; report when a candidate fixture no longer demonstrates flattening.
Step 2 — Keep comparisons fair

Hold source, compiler, target, optimization level, driver, and input domain constant when comparing original and protected variants. Changing the transformation stage is an experiment to label, not an invisible adjustment to improve a result.
Step 3 — Treat metadata by meaning

Set the builder’s debug location from the original terminator for new transition instructions. Do not blindly copy branch-weight metadata to edges with a different meaning. The prototype does not promise fully preserved debug-variable locations or profile quality.
Step 4 — Describe invalid-state behavior accurately

The unreachable default is an internal invariant, not input validation. Loading an uninitialized state is not automatically zero, and executing unreachable is undefined behavior. A real robustness feature would require deliberate initialization and a defined failure policy, separately designed and tested.
The full limitations note to adapt

Prototype scope: ordinary scalar valid IR and static entry allocas.
Rejected: EH/personality, coroutines, block addresses, unsupported terminators,
          special call forms, explicit intrinsics, non-static allocas,
          non-scalar instruction results, and naked functions.
Not promised: formal behavior proof, arbitrary C++ support, anti-reversing
              guarantees, unchanged debug/profile quality, or immunity to
              later optimization simplifying the dispatcher.
Verify

Compare pre- and post-optimization IR for at least one fixture. Confirm the reported size/runtime refer to the final executable under the stated pipeline. Record both supported and rejected function counts.
Checkpoint: Why can stronger optimization improve runtime while weakening the intended obfuscation structure?

items: The state machine is an indirection — a dispatcher, a state slot, and a switch — that computes what a simpler expression could compute directly; a stronger optimizer recognizes and removes that indirection, so on the tiny merge fixture `-O2` eliminates the dispatcher and the stack slots entirely, leaving `%spec.select = select i32 10, i32 20` plus a return (with `range(i32 10, 21)` and the `mustprogress nofree norecurse nosync nounwind willreturn memory(none)` attributes).

The runtime improvement and the loss of obfuscation are the same transformation viewed twice: the optimizer removes exactly the machinery the flattening added, so a fast, correct executable may no longer contain the flattened structure — which is why the lesson says to inspect the optimized IR (and disassembly) and to report when a fixture no longer demonstrates flattening.
