Everything after a semicolon on that line is a comment for the reader. The printer lists incoming blocks after preds; it is not an instruction, an execution order, or a separate edge definition. Branch/switch operands actually define the edges.

Alignment is in bytes, not elements, bits, or a value to store. An aligned alloca provides suitably aligned storage; an aligned load/store promises that its pointer meets that alignment. It does not initialize memory or change the integer read/written.

blocks.text: Every instruction used in this pair

rows: Meaning and operand order in these listings

Reserve storage for the shown element type in this function invocation and produce its address, not the stored integer. `alloca i32` reserves one i32 slot. The allocation does not initialize its contents; a store must supply a value before an intended read.
`br label %B` always transfers control to block B. A branch is the block’s final instruction and produces no result. It does not execute both destinations.

Read a value from memory: in `load i32, ptr %slot`, i32 is the loaded value’s type and %slot is its address. The left-hand result gets the current contents, not another copy of the address. Each load defines a new SSA value; it does not compute the value that a missing earlier store should have supplied.

End this function invocation and return the typed operand to its caller. `ret i32 %v` returns the integer value, while `ret ptr ...` returns a pointer. A return does not proceed to the next printed block or automatically go back to dispatch.

Produce a value from `select i1 CONDITION, TYPE TRUE_VALUE, TYPE FALSE_VALUE`. A true condition chooses the first alternative, false the second; alternatives have the same type. This does not branch or conditionally execute the instructions that computed the operands. Here the chosen result is either a destination’s state number or the final return value.

Write memory: in `store i32 VALUE, ptr ADDRESS`, the first operand is the value and the second is the destination address. A store has an effect but no result name. Writing a state slot changes the next routing choice; writing a demotion slot transports an original program value.

Transfer control according to one integer value. The destination immediately after the condition is the default for no matching case. Each line inside `[...]` pairs a typed case constant with `label %DESTINATION`; only one destination is taken. An original switch chooses a program outcome; a dispatcher switch decodes the stored state ID. The brackets are a case list, not a runtime array.

End the block by asserting that execution never reaches this point on a defined run. Actually executing it is undefined behavior; it is not error recovery, a return, or a C++ exception. The state-machine invariant must prevent a bad stored ID from taking this default path.

blocks.text: Keep address, contents, and loaded value separate. For example, an alloca result is the address of a slot; a store writes an integer into that slot; a later load defines a new SSA name for the integer read back. The pointer name does not become the stored number. A value slot preserves program data, whereas ms.state (when present) stores a control-flow destination encoding.
The other syntax printed around this function

rows: The function’s address is not semantically significant within this module, which gives the optimizer extra freedom. This is an address-identity property, not removal of the @function name.

A return-value contract describing the half-open interval 10 ≤ result < 21. It is not a loop or a runtime bounds check; this function actually chooses 10 or 20. A result violating the contract would be poison.

The numbered group attaches facts to a function declaration/definition rather than executing them. `mustprogress`: Requires forward progress rather than an unobservable infinite computation; it is an optimizer contract, not an inserted progress check. `nofree`: The function does not deallocate memory. `norecurse`: The function is not recursive, directly or indirectly. `nosync`: The function does not perform synchronization. `nounwind`: The function does not unwind the stack. `willreturn`: The function must return control to its call site on defined execution. `memory(none)`: The function has no externally observable memory read/write effects under this attribute’s contract.

blocks.text: Walk one concrete execution

Call merge with condition = true: take left and obtain 10; with false, take right and obtain 20. In a PHI listing join chooses the incoming constant using the predecessor edge. In a demoted listing only the executed path stores its constant, and join reads that value. The optimized after listing replaces all this routing and memory with one select choosing 10 or 20 and one return; it does not execute both paths.

blocks.title: Read the complete before-and-after LLVM modules

blocks.text: Before — phi full

define i32 @merge(i1 %condition) {
entry:
  %ms.state = alloca i32, align 4
  %value.reg2mem = alloca i32, align 4
  %ms.next = select i1 %condition, i32 0, i32 1
  store i32 %ms.next, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

left:                                             ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  store i32 10, ptr %value.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 2, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

right:                                            ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  store i32 20, ptr %value.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 2, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

join:                                             ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  %value.reload = load i32, ptr %value.reg2mem, align 4
  ret i32 %value.reload

ms.dispatch:                                      ; preds = %right, %left, %entry
  %ms.current = load i32, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  switch i32 %ms.current, label %ms.invalid [
    i32 0, label %left
    i32 1, label %right
    i32 2, label %join
  ]

ms.invalid:                                       ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  unreachable
}
After — phi optimized

Both listings are complete LLVM modules defining the example function, not fragments with omitted blocks. They have no main driver unless one is explicitly included; opt can parse and verify them, while execution requires a caller. Names, alignments, and printer annotations may differ in your own output. These listings were generated and verified with the isolated LLVM 23.1.5 teaching references, not copied from an assumed completed learner implementation.
Follow the values and edges: Behavior can agree even when the intended flattened structure no longer survives. Inspect final code before claiming a final-artifact flattening demonstration.

quiz.q: Does an unreachable default provide safe error recovery?
choices: No; executing it is undefined behavior
Yes; it returns zero
Yes; it automatically throws a C++ exception
quiz.why: unreachable states an invariant to the optimizer. It is not a recovery routine or a runtime bounds check.

lessons.title: Close Day 2 with an evidence checklist
lessons.originalTitle: Close Day 2 with an evidence checklist
lessons.summary: Separate a completed book draft from a completed learner implementation, then prepare the handoff to the test-and-measurement work.
lessons.takeaway: A checklist is a claim only after its evidence exists.

blocks.text: What finishing Day 2 should mean

Reaching the last line of a builder is not the same as establishing a working transformation. We need an accepted-input boundary, correctly transported values, faithful state transitions, valid output IR, and tested behavior. The checklist turns those broad goals into evidence we can inspect.

Keep three states separate: a chapter is written, you have implemented its exercise, and its behavior has been checked. A full reference in the book establishes the first; it does not automatically establish the other two in your working tree. Day 3 makes the checks repeatable and measures the resulting artifacts.
Task: Future exercise: review the implementation and evidence before beginning Day 3. The chapters describe work to do; they do not mark it done for you.
The template to start with

[ ] Strict preflight rejects unsupported input before edits.
[ ] PHIs and suitable escaping values are prepared.
[ ] Entry is preserved as one-time setup.
[ ] Conditional/unconditional/switch transitions choose correct states.
[ ] Returns and unreachable remain terminal.
[ ] verify succeeds on the complete fixture set.
[ ] Accepted fixtures match original behavior on the defined test domain.
[ ] Rejected fixtures have intended reasons and unchanged canonical IR.
[ ] Limitations and optimizer placement are documented.
Step 1 — Name the unfinished item
If any box lacks evidence, keep it open and identify a smallest failing fixture or missing test. “The code compiles” does not fill the behavior boxes.
Step 2 — Save only source and reproducible fixtures

Commit the code, build configuration, documentation, and intentional test inputs. Keep build products and before/after generated IR in build/. The local table script remains excluded unless you explicitly decide to track it later.
Step 3 — Move into test infrastructure

Day 3 turns manual observations into repeatable unit, integration, and differential checks, then measures final artifacts. It adds evidence rather than assuming that many successful printouts are a test suite.
The full handoff record

Toolchain/version:
Commit tested:
Supported input contract:
Commands used:
Positive/negative fixtures:
Differential domain and seed:
Known limitations:
Open failures:
Verify
Have a reader reproduce one accepted case and one rejection from a fresh build directory using the recorded commands. Do not replace missing measurements with plausible-looking numbers.
Checkpoint: Which unchecked item currently limits your confidence most, and what concrete experiment would address it?

items: The item that usually limits confidence most is the one with no executed evidence yet — typically “accepted fixtures match original behavior on the defined test domain”, because verify and identical canonical IR prove form, not meaning; a plausible-looking output is not evidence, and “the code compiles” does not fill the behavior boxes.

The concrete experiment is the differential comparison from lesson 24: build the original and protected variants from the same common IR, run both with the same driver and backend flags over the bounded domain (for example amounts `-1, 0, 1, 99, 100, 1000, 10000` and every level for `discount`, both conditions for `phi.ll`, counts `0, 1, 2` for the swap loop), and compare exit status and stdout — any mismatch is a counterexample to keep as a regression, and full agreement upgrades that checklist item from “traced” to “verified on the domain”.

blocks.text: LLVM program before and after this checkpoint
Use the entire loop pair to review the Day 2 exit criteria. This is a reference endpoint, not a claim that the learner implementation has reached it.
What changes: Preparation and construction both contribute visible changes. No single grep for switch proves that all transitions or values are correct.
Reading this LLVM program from zero

Do not read every displayed block as one straight-line script. A call supplies the function inputs and starts its first block. Within the selected block, follow the written instructions until a terminator chooses another block or returns to the caller. A label names a block; it does not execute an operation by itself.

rows: `define` starts a function body. `@count_to` is the module-level function name; `i32` immediately before it is the return type. Parentheses contain typed inputs supplied by the caller; braces contain its blocks.

i1 means one bit: 0 is false and 1 is true for a condition; i32 means a 32-bit integer bit pattern; signed interpretation comes from operations such as slt or sdiv, not from a separate signed i32 type.

An opaque pointer value: it can represent an address or the special handle returned in the coroutine example. It does not contain an i32 integer or encode a pointee type. A load/store spells out the type of value accessed separately from the pointer.

The left side names the result of this instruction. Each SSA result has one static defining instruction; input arguments are values supplied at function entry. A name is a handle for a value, not a mutable source variable or a guaranteed CPU register.

The colon defines a block label; the label operand names a jump destination. `%` is also used for local result/argument names, so use the type/context to distinguish a value from a block target. `@` instead identifies a module-level symbol.

This is a typed literal: the i-prefixed part specifies the bit width, and the decimal part is the constant value. For example, a case number or stored state ID is an integer value, unlike a `%name` or `name:` label.

Everything after a semicolon on that line is a comment for the reader. The printer lists incoming blocks after preds; it is not an instruction, an execution order, or a separate edge definition. Branch/switch operands actually define the edges.

Alignment is in bytes, not elements, bits, or a value to store. An aligned alloca provides suitably aligned storage; an aligned load/store promises that its pointer meets that alignment. It does not initialize memory or change the integer read/written.

rows: Meaning and operand order in these listings

Add the two same-typed operands and define the sum. In these unflagged i32 examples, arithmetic is modulo 2^32; the test inputs stay in the small intended range. This calculates data, such as the next loop counter or x + 1, rather than choosing a block.

Reserve storage for the shown element type in this function invocation and produce its address, not the stored integer. `alloca i32` reserves one i32 slot. The allocation does not initialize its contents; a store must supply a value before an intended read.

`br label %B` always transfers control to block B. `br i1 %C, label %A, label %B` goes to A for true and B for false; their order matters. A branch is the block’s final instruction and produces no result. It does not execute both destinations.

Compare two same-typed integers and produce i1, which can feed br or select. `slt` asks whether the left operand is smaller using signed integer interpretation, so a negative i32 is below zero. The comparison computes a condition; it does not jump by itself.

Read left-to-right: compare the first integer operand with the second, then use the resulting i1 as a condition. For the loop it compares the current counter with the bound; for the discount kernel it checks whether the amount is negative.

Read a value from memory: in `load i32, ptr %slot`, i32 is the loaded value’s type and %slot is its address. The left-hand result gets the current contents, not another copy of the address. Each load defines a new SSA value; it does not compute the value that a missing earlier store should have supplied.

Define one value by the edge just used to enter this block. Each `[ VALUE, %PREDECESSOR ]` pairs an incoming value with its source block; it is not an array access. The PHI’s i32 type applies to every incoming value, so a literal inside a bracket does not repeat the type. PHIs go at the start of a block. On a loop’s first entry choose its entry value, and on a back edge choose its carried value. Multiple PHIs select incoming values together, rather than sequentially overwriting each other.

End this function invocation and return the typed operand to its caller. `ret i32 %v` returns the integer value, while `ret ptr ...` returns a pointer. A return does not proceed to the next printed block or automatically go back to dispatch.

Produce a value from `select i1 CONDITION, TYPE TRUE_VALUE, TYPE FALSE_VALUE`. A true condition chooses the first alternative, false the second; alternatives have the same type. This does not branch or conditionally execute the instructions that computed the operands. Here the chosen result is either a destination’s state number or the final return value.

Write memory: in `store i32 VALUE, ptr ADDRESS`, the first operand is the value and the second is the destination address. A store has an effect but no result name. Writing a state slot changes the next routing choice; writing a demotion slot transports an original program value.

Transfer control according to one integer value. The destination immediately after the condition is the default for no matching case. Each line inside `[...]` pairs a typed case constant with `label %DESTINATION`; only one destination is taken. An original switch chooses a program outcome; a dispatcher switch decodes the stored state ID. The brackets are a case list, not a runtime array.

End the block by asserting that execution never reaches this point on a defined run. Actually executing it is undefined behavior; it is not error recovery, a return, or a C++ exception. The state-machine invariant must prevent a bad stored ID from taking this default path.

blocks.text: Keep address, contents, and loaded value separate. For example, an alloca result is the address of a slot; a store writes an integer into that slot; a later load defines a new SSA name for the integer read back. The pointer name does not become the stored number. A value slot preserves program data, whereas ms.state (when present) stores a control-flow destination encoding.
Walk one concrete execution

Call count_to with limit = 2. The initial counter is 0; the signed-less-than test is true for 0 and 1, so the body increments it to 1 and then 2. At 2 the test is false and exit returns 2. A PHI selects initial 0 on entry and the previous body’s next value on a back edge; after demotion the loop-variable slot carries those same values. The complete after listing stores state 0 for header, 1 for body, or 2 for exit. State storage controls where to run; separate value slots carry the counter. The default unreachable path is never an intended outcome.

blocks.title: Read the complete before-and-after LLVM modules

blocks.text: Before — loop original

define i32 @count_to(i32 %limit) {
entry:
  br label %header

header:                                           ; preds = %body, %entry
  %i = phi i32 [ 0, %entry ], [ %next, %body ]
  %continue = icmp slt i32 %i, %limit
  br i1 %continue, label %body, label %exit

body:                                             ; preds = %header
  %next = add i32 %i, 1
  br label %header

exit:                                             ; preds = %header
  ret i32 %i
}
After — loop full

define i32 @count_to(i32 %limit) {
entry:
  %ms.state = alloca i32, align 4
  %i.reload.reg2mem = alloca i32, align 4
  %i.reg2mem = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 0, ptr %i.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 0, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

header:                                           ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  %i.reload = load i32, ptr %i.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 %i.reload, ptr %i.reload.reg2mem, align 4
  %i.reload.reload = load i32, ptr %i.reload.reg2mem, align 4
  %continue = icmp slt i32 %i.reload.reload, %limit
  %ms.next = select i1 %continue, i32 1, i32 2
  store i32 %ms.next, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

body:                                             ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  %i.reload.reload1 = load i32, ptr %i.reload.reg2mem, align 4
  %next = add i32 %i.reload.reload1, 1
  store i32 %next, ptr %i.reg2mem, align 4
  store i32 0, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch

exit:                                             ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  %i.reload.reload2 = load i32, ptr %i.reload.reg2mem, align 4
  ret i32 %i.reload.reload2

ms.dispatch:                                      ; preds = %body, %header, %entry
  %ms.current = load i32, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  switch i32 %ms.current, label %ms.invalid [
    i32 0, label %header
    i32 1, label %body
    i32 2, label %exit
  ]

ms.invalid:                                       ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  unreachable
}

Both listings are complete LLVM modules defining the example function, not fragments with omitted blocks. They have no main driver unless one is explicitly included; opt can parse and verify them, while execution requires a caller. Names, alignments, and printer annotations may differ in your own output. These listings were generated and verified with the isolated LLVM 23.1.5 teaching references, not copied from an assumed completed learner implementation.

lessons.summary: A compact reference for the general compiler and project vocabulary used in Day 2; LLVM-specific and C++-specific terms each have their own document.
lessons.takeaway: Look up the word, then return to the concrete IR example.

blocks.text: Use terms to recover the reason for an operation

Definitions are most useful when they reconnect a word to the problem it solves. If “PHI” is unclear, revisit lesson 1’s path-dependent choice. If “demotion” is unclear, compare the value transport in lessons 3, 9, and 11. If “state” is unclear, follow the original destination through its encoding in lesson 12 and its decoding in lesson 14.
This glossary is a reminder rather than a prerequisite to understanding the main lessons. Each concept is introduced in context before the exercise that depends on it.
Task: Use this reference when a term interrupts your progress. The [Day 1 glossary](#lesson-26) remains available under the Day 1 tab.
Terms in this document

rows: SSA, Dominance, Demotion (as a technique), Cross-block / escaping value, Worklist, Constant folding, Tail call, Undefined behavior, Differential test
State ID, Dispatcher, Setup / entry, Support contract, Prototype checkpoint, Prototype scope, Where to return

blocks.text: General CS and compiler concepts

The compiler-background terms the Day 2 lessons build on: the representation invariants (SSA, dominance), the techniques the pass uses (demotion, worklists), and the safety vocabulary (undefined behavior, differential tests) used when judging what a check proves.
SSA

See the [Day 1 glossary](#lesson-26) entry "SSA (static single assignment)": every value in LLVM IR is defined exactly once and used only after that definition; merges are handled by PHI nodes instead of redefining names, and `verify` checks the constraint.

Day 2 adds dispatcher edges that can reach a use without passing through its definition, which is why value preparation happens before the state machinery exists (lesson 0). The verifier checks the relationship; a passing verify is the evidence that dominance still holds.
See [static single assignment on Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Static_single_assignment_form).
Dominance

See the [Day 1 glossary](#lesson-26) entry "Dominator": a block B dominates a block A when every path from the function entry to A passes through B; dominance underpins the back-edge definition and the `DominatorTreeAnalysis`.
Lesson 0 states the rule and lesson 23 reads the verifier’s dominance error; the dispatcher’s new edges are exactly the kind of addition that can invalidate an originally satisfied dominance.
See [the dominator tree on Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominator_tree).
Demotion (as a technique)

Replace SSA value transport with explicit stack storage: allocate a slot, store the value, and load it at its uses. The motive is control-flow robustness — a value carried in memory can be read by any block, so new edges that bypass the original definition no longer break the data flow.

define i32 @merge(i1 %condition) {
entry:
  %value.reg2mem = alloca i32, align 4
  br i1 %condition, label %left, label %right
left:
  store i32 10, ptr %value.reg2mem, align 4
  br label %join
right:
  store i32 20, ptr %value.reg2mem, align 4
  br label %join
join:
  %value.reload = load i32, ptr %value.reg2mem, align 4
  ret i32 %value.reload
}

Day 2 performs the demotion mechanically: DemotePHIToStack in lesson 3 and DemoteRegToStack in lessons 8–9. The gotcha: demotion does not remove every dominance requirement, because the alloca’s result is itself an SSA pointer that must dominate its uses.
The technique is implemented by the free functions in the [Local.cpp source](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/main/llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/Local.cpp).
Cross-block / escaping value

An instruction result used outside the block that defines it. The pass must prepare these values before changing the graph, because a new edge can reach a use without passing through the definition. “Escaping” here means crossing a block boundary, not heap escape or leaving the function.
Collected in lesson 4, demoted in lesson 9. The gotcha: no PHI does not mean no cross-block value — a reload introduced by PHI demotion can still be used outside its defining block.
Introduced in lessons 04–05; see the collection fragment in lesson 04 and the demotion loop in lesson 09.
Worklist

A C++ collection of pointers to IR instructions, discovered during one traversal and processed later. The motive is ordering: the pass must not use an instruction after mutating the IR, so it collects first and acts second, and the traversal and the mutation never touch the same object at the same time.
Lessons 1–3 build the PHI worklist. The gotcha: the vector owns pointers, not instructions — after DemotePHIToStack the stored pointer dangles (lesson 3).
Worklists are the standard machinery of iterative [dataflow analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dataflow_analysis).
Constant folding

Evaluate a constant expression during IR construction or optimization and replace it with the computed constant. In Day 2 it appears through the builder: when a Create* helper can fold, it returns a Constant instead of inserting an Instruction, which is why a builder result is typed llvm::Value*, not Instruction*.
Lesson 19 meets this when lowering a switch: a comparison or select over state constants folds to a value unless an operand still depends on runtime input.
See [constant folding on Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constant_folding).
Tail call

A call positioned so the caller can hand its frame to the callee. The reason it matters here is the marker: LLVM’s tail and musttail flags promise structural properties, and musttail constrains what may appear between the call and the following return — an inserted spill or dispatcher hop can silently break that promise.
Lesson 17 rejects musttail calls before any edit, because the prototype does not preserve the constrained region around the call.
See [tail call on Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tail_call).
Undefined behavior

A state the language or IR contract leaves undefined. From there anything may happen, which is why one observed successful run is not evidence of correctness and why naive equivalence arguments fail: a program may be valid on paper and still sit on undefined behavior.
In Day 2, unreachable marks the ms.invalid destination: the state-machine invariant keeps execution off it, and reaching it would be undefined behavior, not error recovery (lessons 14–15).
See [undefined behavior on Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undefined_behavior).
Differential test

Run the original and the transformed program on the same defined inputs and compare observable results. The motive: structural checks (verify, identical canonical printing) prove form, not meaning; only paired execution catches a rewrite that is well-formed but computes the wrong answer.

./original 3 > /tmp/out.orig
./flattened 3 > /tmp/out.new
diff /tmp/out.orig /tmp/out.new
Day 2 compares executions in lesson 24 over a defined input domain and records the limits of that comparison in lesson 26.
See [differential testing on Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_testing).
Project vocabulary
The names this project gives its own machinery — state IDs, the dispatcher, the support contract — so the book, the code, and the terminal output refer to the same objects.
State ID

An integer naming a destination block in the dispatcher’s switch. The switch needs an integer condition while block identity is a C++ object, so a DenseMap converts the block pointer into a small stable number that can be stored in memory and decoded later. It is not the block’s printed name.
Assigned in lessons 12–13, decoded by the dispatcher’s switch in lesson 14. The gotcha: DenseMap iteration order is not a display order, so reports iterate the stateBlocks vector instead.
See the assignment in lesson 12 and the decoding in lesson 14.
Dispatcher

A single block that loads the current state ID and switches to the corresponding original block. Centralizing every transition through one place is what flattens the CFG: an original block no longer names its successor directly; it stores the next state and hops to the dispatcher.

define void @dispatch_example(i32 %start) {
entry:
  %ms.state = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 %start, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch
ms.dispatch:
  %ms.current = load i32, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  switch i32 %ms.current, label %ms.invalid [
    i32 0, label %a
    i32 1, label %b
  ]
a:
  ret void
b:
  ret void
ms.invalid:
  unreachable
}
Built in lesson 14, its first unconditional entry connection in lesson 16, and the original terminators rewritten into it in lesson 21.
See the construction in lesson 14 and the first hop in lesson 16.
Setup / entry

The preserved original entry block, which runs exactly once. Its stack allocations and initialization must not re-run on every transition, so the state machine never loops back through it: the entry performs its setup and hands control to the dispatcher instead.

define i32 @setup_once(i1 %condition) {
entry:
  %slot = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 7, ptr %slot, align 4
  br label %work
work:
  %v = load i32, ptr %slot, align 4
  ret i32 %v
}
Lesson 12 excludes entry from state assignment; keeping the one-time work out of the recurring dispatch is the invariant that makes entry setup rather than state 0.
See the exclusion in lesson 12 and the setup block in lesson 14.
Support contract

The explicitly documented subset of inputs the pass accepts before any mutation. Naming it makes every guard rejection a testable design boundary — the rejected LLVM construct is still valid IR, it is simply outside the documented subset.
The full contract — declarations, allocas, result types, intrinsics, special calls, EH/coroutines, block addresses, terminators, and naked functions — is enumerated in lesson 17.
See the contract and its rejections in lesson 17.
Prototype checkpoint

A deliberately limited stage whose output can be verified without implementing every supported case or the complete flattening. Freezing one invariant per checkpoint (no PHIs, values in memory, first hop connected) makes progress testable before the pipeline is complete.

checkpoint 1: PHIs collected, IR unchanged
checkpoint 2: PHIs demoted, values flow through memory
checkpoint 3: state IDs assigned, dispatcher connected
Lessons 3, 9, and 16 are checkpoints of this kind; each ends with an expected output and a changed-or-unchanged module.
See the checkpoints in lessons 03, 09, and 16.
Prototype scope

The deliberately limited support domain this pass claims. A rejection such as “intrinsic calls are outside this prototype’s scope” is a scope statement, not a claim that the input is invalid; the distinction keeps a rejected input from being misread as a bug in the IR.
Lesson 17 defines the scope one rejection at a time; lesson 26 records its limits.
See the scope in lesson 17 and the recorded limits in lesson 26.

LLVM-specific terms — printed IR, memory, control flow, calls, and the C++ API: lesson 29, the Day 2 LLVM document.
C++-specific terms — pointers, references, casts, classes, and translation units: lesson 30, the Day 2 C++ document.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: Choose one unfamiliar term, find its example, and explain it using the actual instruction or C++ expression rather than only repeating the definition.

items: Take “demotion (as a technique)”: the glossary's merge example shows it concretely — entry declares `%value.reg2mem = alloca i32, align 4`, left executes `store i32 10, ptr %value.reg2mem`, right executes `store i32 20, ptr %value.reg2mem`, and join executes `%value.reload = load i32, ptr %value.reg2mem` followed by `ret i32 %value.reload`.

Instead of a PHI that picks `[10, %left]` or `[20, %right]` by the predecessor edge, the value now lives in memory: whichever path executes writes its own constant, and join reads back what the executed path wrote — so demotion is the replacement of SSA value transport with explicit stack storage, exactly what `DemotePHIToStack` performs mechanically in lesson 3 and what lets new dispatcher edges stop breaking the data flow.

quiz.q: A load reads %slot, but nothing in the function ever stored to it. What does the load read?
choices: Whatever the slot happened to contain
Zero, because LLVM zero-initializes every stack slot
A verifier error, because every load requires a store
quiz.why: A load is just a memory read: it returns whatever bytes the slot currently holds. The verifier checks types and dominance, not that the slot was written first.

lessons.title: Glossary. LLVM terms used in Day 2
lessons.originalTitle: Glossary. LLVM terms used in Day 2
lessons.summary: The LLVM-specific terms of Day 2: the IR constructs the pass reads and writes, the call and function properties the guard checks, and the C++ API surface the pass uses.
lessons.takeaway: Name the construct, then name the API that reads or writes it.

blocks.text: Read the term, then find the construct

Each entry names an LLVM construct, the problem it serves in Day 2, and the API that reads or writes it. The groups follow where you meet the terms: the printed IR you read, the memory and control-flow constructs, the call and function properties the guard checks, and the C++ side of the pass.
Task: Use this document when an LLVM term interrupts your progress. General compiler and project vocabulary lives in the Day 2 glossary, and C++ language terms have their own document.
Terms in this document

rows: define vs declare, Block labels, % values vs labels, @ symbols, i1 / i32 and typed constants, ptr, align, "; preds" comments
PHI, alloca, load / store, void result, select
struct results (one entry: aggregates built field by field with `insertvalue`)
Terminator, br / conditional br, switch, ret, unreachable
call, CallBase / CallInst, tail / musttail, returns_twice, convergent, operand bundle, inline asm, naked, Function attribute vs call flag, Function declaration
Intrinsic, Coroutine intrinsic, Presplit coroutine, Personality function, EH pad, Address-taken basic block, Static entry alloca, Terminator whitelist
isa / cast / dyn_cast, LLVMContext, IRBuilder and insertion point, getInt32Ty / getInt32, DenseMap, PreservedAnalyses, eraseFromParent, isUsedOutsideOfBlock, DemotePHIToStack / DemoteRegToStack

blocks.text: Printed-IR vocabulary
How to read a printed module: what each mark — %, @, :, ;, align — denotes, and which symbols name values, which name blocks, and which name functions.
define vs declare

See the [Day 1 glossary](#lesson-26) entry "Declaration vs. definition (function)": a `declare` signature announces a function with no body; a `define` provides the body, and passes only run on definitions — `F.isDeclaration()` detects the former.
Lesson 17 rejects a declaration before the block traversal; a declared callee can still be called from supported functions.
See [functions in LangRef](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#functions).
Block labels

A label at the top of a basic block names it for jumps and for the printed listing; label %join inside a branch is an operand referring to that name. A label is not a value: it has no type, and it performs no operation when execution reaches it.
Lesson 15 separates the C++ variable, the block object, and the printed name: ms.dispatch is legal as an IR name even though it is not a legal C++ identifier.
See [functions in LangRef](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#functions).
% values vs labels

The % prefix names both local SSA values (%v = add …) and block labels (entry:). Context is the disambiguator: after = it names a value, before a colon it names a block, and after label it names a jump destination. Confusing the two is the most common reading error in the printed listings.

define i32 @merge(i1 %condition) {
entry:
  %v = add i32 1, 2
  br i1 %condition, label %a, label %b
a:
  ret i32 %v
b:
  ret i32 0
}
See [functions in LangRef](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#functions).
@ symbols

@ names a module-level symbol — a function or a global variable. The name has module scope, so @merge is unaffected by the block it appears in, and the same global can be referenced from any function in the module.
See [functions](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#functions) and [global variables](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#global-variables) in LangRef.
i1 / i32 and typed constants

iN is an integer type of N bits: i1 is a single bit used for conditions, i32 a 32-bit pattern. Constants are typed at the spelling — i32 0 is a 32-bit zero — and the type is what makes a literal usable in a given position. Signedness is not part of the type; it comes from operations such as icmp slt or sdiv.
Lesson 0 introduces i1 and i32; lesson 19 stores typed state constants (i32 0, i32 1, i32 2) into the state slot.
See [the type system](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#type-system) and [constant expressions](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#constant-expressions) in LangRef.
ptr

With opaque pointers every pointer is simply ptr; it no longer spells out the type it points to. That is why load i32, ptr %slot names the loaded value’s type first — the element type is not recoverable from the pointer itself.

define i32 @slot_example() {
entry:
  %slot = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 5, ptr %slot, align 4
  %v = load i32, ptr %slot, align 4
  ret i32 %v
}
See [opaque pointers](https://llvm.org/docs/OpaquePointers.html).
align

align N records that an address is guaranteed to be a multiple of N bytes. It is a placement promise, not a value to store: an aligned load or store lets the backend use aligned access, and an aligned alloca asks for suitably aligned storage. It is measured in bytes, never in elements or bits.

define i32 @aligned() {
entry:
  %slot = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 1, ptr %slot, align 4
  %v = load i32, ptr %slot, align 4
  ret i32 %v
}
Every Day 2 read-from-zero table flags the common misreading of align as a stored value.
See [the store instruction](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#store-instruction) in LangRef, where the align operand is documented.
“; preds” comments

; preds = %left, %right is a printer comment listing the block’s incoming edges. It is not an instruction and not an edge definition: the branch and switch operands create the edges, and the comment is a reading aid that updates whenever the graph changes.

define void @diamond(i1 %c) {
entry:
  br i1 %c, label %left, label %right
left:
  br label %join
right:
  br label %join
join:
  ret void
}
Every Day 2 read-from-zero table treats ; preds as comment only; the ms.dispatch block prints “No predecessors!” until the first hop is connected (lesson 16).
See [the syntax section](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#syntax) in LangRef.
Memory
The constructs that decide where a value lives: the PHI this pass demotes, the slots that hold demoted values, and the load/store pair that moves them.
PHI

See the [Day 1 glossary](#lesson-26) entry "PHI node / phi": at a block’s entry a PHI picks which value flows in from which predecessor — `%x = phi i32 [ 1, %left ], [ 2, %right ]` — because SSA forbids redefining a value’s name at a merge point.
Lessons 1–3 collect and demote PHIs. The gotcha: DemotePHIToStack erases the PHI, so the saved pointer must not be used after the call (lesson 3).
See [the PHI instruction](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#phi-instruction) in LangRef.
alloca

alloca reserves storage in the function’s stack frame and returns its address — a pointer, not the stored value. It does not initialize the storage, so a load before a store reads whatever bytes were there.

define i32 @make_slot() {
entry:
  %slot = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 9, ptr %slot, align 4
  %v = load i32, ptr %slot, align 4
  ret i32 %v
}
Lesson 6 recognizes the allocation itself; the guard accepts only static entry allocas (lesson 17).
See [the alloca instruction](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#alloca-instruction) in LangRef.
load / store

store writes a typed value to an address and produces no SSA result; load reads a typed value from an address and defines a new SSA value. The pair is how Day 2 carries values between blocks once PHIs and register-like results are demoted.

define i32 @move(i32 %x) {
entry:
  %slot = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 %x, ptr %slot, align 4
  %v = load i32, ptr %slot, align 4
  ret i32 %v
}
See [the load](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#load-instruction) and [store](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#store-instruction) instructions in LangRef.
void result

An instruction with a void result produces no value for another instruction to use: store, br, ret, and a void call all qualify. Value collection must skip void results because there is nothing to demote or reload.
Lesson 5 introduces the isVoidTy filter in the collection loop.
See [the void type](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#void-type) in LangRef.
select

select i1 C, T A, T B chooses a value: the result is A when C is true and B otherwise. It does not branch and does not conditionally execute the instructions that computed A and B — both operands are available when select runs. That is exactly what lets Day 2 encode the next state as a value.

define i32 @next_state(i32 %value) {
entry:
  %c0 = icmp eq i32 %value, 0
  %n1 = select i1 %c0, i32 0, i32 2
  %c1 = icmp eq i32 %value, 1
  %n = select i1 %c1, i32 1, i32 %n1
  ret i32 %n
}
Lesson 19 turns conditional branches into chains of comparisons and selects; lesson 20 lowers the original switch into the same shape.
See [the select instruction](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#select-instruction) in LangRef.
Aggregates (struct results)

An aggregate is a composite value such as { i32, i32 }, built field by field with insertvalue (starting from zeroinitializer, its all-zero value) and read with extractvalue. The guard rejects aggregate results: a struct result fails the only-scalar-results check even when every field is an integer.

define { i32, i32 } @pair(i32 %a, i32 %b) {
entry:
  %s = insertvalue { i32, i32 } zeroinitializer, i32 %a, 0
  %s2 = insertvalue { i32, i32 } %s, i32 %b, 1
  %first = extractvalue { i32, i32 } %s2, 0
  %second = extractvalue { i32, i32 } %s2, 1
  %r = add i32 %first, %second
  %out = insertvalue { i32, i32 } zeroinitializer, i32 %r, 0
  %out2 = insertvalue { i32, i32 } %out, i32 0, 1
  ret { i32, i32 } %out2
}
Lesson 17’s aggregate-result.ll fixture is rejected with “only scalar instruction results are supported”.
See [aggregate types](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#aggregate-types) in LangRef.
Control flow
The instructions that end a block and choose the next one: every edge in the graph is defined by a terminator, and the pass rewrites exactly these.
Terminator

See the [Day 1 glossary](#lesson-26) entry "Terminator": the last instruction of a basic block, which transfers control (`br`, `switch`, `ret`, `unreachable`, …); Day 1’s policy accepts `CondBr`, `UncondBr`, `Switch`, `Ret`, and `Unreachable` only.
The guard’s terminator whitelist names the endings the pass rewrites (lesson 17); lesson 21 rewrites every original terminator.
See [terminator instructions](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#terminator-instructions) in LangRef.
br / conditional br

br label %B transfers control unconditionally; br i1 %C, label %A, label %B goes to A when C is true and to B when it is false. A branch is the block’s final instruction and produces no result; it does not execute both destinations.
See [the br instruction](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#br-instruction) in LangRef.
switch

switch iN %V, label %DEFAULT [ iN C, label %D … ] chooses a destination from an integer value: the label after the condition is the default taken when no case matches, and each line inside the brackets pairs a typed case constant with a destination. The brackets are a case list, not an array.

define i32 @select_case(i32 %value) {
entry:
  switch i32 %value, label %other [
    i32 0, label %zero
    i32 1, label %one
  ]
zero:
  ret i32 10
one:
  ret i32 20
other:
  ret i32 -1
}
Day 2 carries two switches at once: the original program decision is lowered to comparisons and selects (lesson 20), while the dispatcher’s switch stays in place to decode state IDs (lesson 14).
See [the switch instruction](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#switch-instruction) in LangRef.
ret

ret ends this invocation and, when it carries a value, returns that value to the caller. It does not continue to the next printed block, and it does not go back to the dispatcher automatically — the rewritten program must route returns deliberately.
See [the ret instruction](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#ret-instruction) in LangRef.
unreachable
See the [Day 1 glossary](#lesson-26) entry "Unreachable": a terminator marking a point that cannot execute, transferring control nowhere.
Lesson 15 finishes the invalid block with it, and the dispatcher’s default case targets it (lesson 14).
See [the unreachable instruction](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#unreachable-instruction) in LangRef.
Calls and attributes
How one function may call another, and which flags on the call or the callee change what the compiler may assume — the guard rejects the calls it cannot preserve.
call

call transfers control to a callee with typed arguments and, unless the result is void, binds the result to an SSA value. A call is an ordinary instruction inside a block, but the callee’s properties — attributes, flags, bundles — constrain what a transformation may do around it.
See [the call instruction](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#call-instruction) in LangRef.
CallBase / CallInst

CallBase is the shared interface of the call-family instructions (call, invoke, callbr); CallInst is the ordinary call. Call-level markers that only the ordinary call carries, such as musttail, live on the derived class — which is why the guard first dyn_casts to CallBase for the shared checks and then to CallInst for musttail.
See the [CallBase doxygen](https://llvm.org/doxygen/classllvm_1_1CallBase.html).
tail / musttail

tail marks a call that may be turned into a tail-call transfer; musttail requires the transfer and constrains the instructions allowed between the call and the following return. An inserted spill reload or dispatcher hop can violate that structural promise silently, so the guard rejects musttail calls.
The Day 2 glossary’s tail-call entry carries the general concept; this entry is about the IR marker.
See [the call instruction](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#call-instruction) in LangRef, where musttail is documented.
returns_twice

A function attribute (the setjmp/longjmp family) saying the callee may return to its caller more than once. A model with one forward return path cannot represent that, so the guard reads the marker on the called function.
See [function attributes](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#function-attributes) in LangRef.
convergent

A marker, on a function or a call, describing a constraint on how control flow may be transformed around the operation: in grouped execution the set of participating threads can depend on the path taken. Routing through a shared dispatcher changes the graph, so the prototype excludes marked calls until it has a correctness argument for them.
See [convergent operation semantics](https://llvm.org/docs/ConvergentOperations.html).
operand bundle

Extra semantic information attached to a call in [ "tag"(payload) ] form — deoptimization state, funclet context, aliasing hints — not an ordinary argument. Counting arguments is a different question; the guard rejects any call carrying a bundle.
See [operand bundles](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#operand-bundles) in LangRef.
inline asm

A call whose callee is embedded assembly text rather than a symbol; register usage and clobber behavior are tied to that exact code, so moving the call or surrounding it with new operations is unsafe. The guard rejects isInlineAsm calls.
See [inline assembler expressions](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#inline-assembler-expressions) in LangRef.
naked

A function attribute suppressing the compiler’s prologue and epilogue: the body itself must satisfy the whole calling convention. Inserting a state slot or a dispatcher under that contract would change what the caller sees, so the guard checks hasFnAttribute(Naked) on the function, not on any call.
See [function attributes](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#function-attributes) in LangRef.
Function attribute vs call flag

Attributes such as naked or convergent belong to the function and are read with hasFnAttribute; flags such as tail or musttail belong to one particular call and are read through CallInst predicates. Each is checked where it lives, so a function-level check never sees a call-level marker and vice versa.
See [function attributes](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#function-attributes) and [call site attributes](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#call-site-attributes) in LangRef.
Function declaration

A declare signature with no body: the callee exists in the module but has no blocks to inspect or rewrite. Day 2’s guard rejects declarations before any other check because everything after it assumes a body.
See [functions](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#functions) in LangRef.
Function and block properties
The properties the guard queries before editing: which functions are intrinsics or coroutines, which blocks are address-taken or EH pads, and which terminators the pass rewrites.
Intrinsic

See the [Day 1 glossary](#lesson-26) entry "Intrinsic": an operation declared by LLVM itself under the reserved `llvm.` namespace, whose semantics LLVM knows and which is lowered directly to target code; in IR it appears as an ordinary `call`.
Lesson 17’s intrinsics.ll fixture is rejected with “intrinsic calls are outside this prototype’s scope”; the check runs through the callee’s isIntrinsic.
See [intrinsic functions](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#intrinsic-functions) in LangRef.
Coroutine intrinsic

See the [Day 1 glossary](#lesson-26) entry "Coroutine": a function that can be suspended and resumed, expressed in LLVM IR through the `llvm.coro.*` intrinsics (the `begin` / `end` / `suspend` / `resume` family that builds coroutine state machines). The guard does not handle coroutine IR, so the general intrinsic rule rejects these calls; the dedicated entry exists so a diagnostic can name the real cause.
See [the coroutines document](https://llvm.org/docs/Coroutines.html).
Presplit coroutine

See the [Day 1 glossary](#lesson-26) entry "Coroutine", which also names the presplit case: a coroutine the front end has already split into continuation blocks, detectable with `F.isPresplitCoroutine()`. Its CFG is not the shape this pass assumes, so the guard rejects it before any inspection.
See [the coroutines document](https://llvm.org/docs/Coroutines.html).
Personality function

See the [Day 1 glossary](#lesson-26) entry "Personality routine": the function a language runtime calls while an exception unwinds; a function that can receive exceptions carries one, and `F.hasPersonalityFn()` asks whether it does. The guard reads `hasPersonalityFn` and rejects, because the rewrite has no model for EH flow.
See [personality function](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#personality-function) in LangRef.
EH pad

See the [Day 1 glossary](#lesson-26) entry "EH pad": the first instruction of a block that receives exceptional control — `landingpad`, `catchpad`, `cleanuppad`, or `catchswitch` — asked by `BB.isEHPad()`.
Lesson 17 rejects the pad via isEHPad and the EH terminators via the whitelist.
See [exception handling](https://llvm.org/docs/ExceptionHandling.html).
Address-taken basic block

See the [Day 1 glossary](#lesson-26) entry "Address-taken block": a basic block whose address is used as a value in the IR (produced by `blockaddress`) — a value a program can compute with, not just a control-flow destination, so the CFG alone no longer describes control flow. `BasicBlock::hasAddressTaken` detects it, and the guard rejects.
See [addresses of basic blocks](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#addresses-of-basic-blocks) in LangRef.
Static entry alloca

An alloca with a compile-time constant count in the entry block — the only allocation the pass preserves. A non-static or non-entry alloca would change allocation frequency or lifetime if hoisted into the one-time setup, so AllocaInst::isStaticAlloca gates it.

define i32 @fixed_slot() {
entry:
  %slot = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 1, ptr %slot, align 4
  %v = load i32, ptr %slot, align 4
  ret i32 %v
}
Lesson 17 rejects the non-entry and variable-size cases; the nonentry-alloca.ll fixture is the focused test.
See [the alloca instruction](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#alloca-instruction) in LangRef.
Terminator whitelist

The set of block endings the pass rewrites: br, conditional br, switch, ret, unreachable. A switch over getTerminator()->getOpcode() rejects every other opcode, so an EH terminator or an indirect branch is named precisely rather than failing with a generic error.
See [terminator instructions](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#terminator-instructions) in LangRef; the whitelist itself is this pass’s design, introduced in lesson 17.
The C++ API side
The host-side C++ API the pass uses to read and build the IR, as opposed to the target program the IR describes: the context, the builders, the maps, and the free functions that perform the demotion.
isa / cast / dyn_cast

See the [Day 1 glossary](#lesson-26) entry "isa<T>(X) / dyn_cast<T>(X)": `isa` answers “is this value a T?” with a boolean; `dyn_cast` returns a `T*` on success and `nullptr` otherwise; `cast` asserts. Day 2 uses the if-initializer form so the pointer is typed and scoped to the check: the declaration, the check, and the use happen in one statement.
Lessons 1–2 teach the form, including why a bare isa test discards the typed pointer.
See [LLVM casting](https://llvm.org/docs/ProgrammersManual.html#the-isa-cast-and-dyn-cast-templates).
LLVMContext

The shared context for IR facilities: uniqued types and metadata live in it, so every query must go through the same context to find the same objects. A pass obtains it from the function it transforms with F.getContext().
See the [LLVMContext doxygen](https://llvm.org/doxygen/classllvm_1_1LLVMContext.html).
IRBuilder and insertion point

IRBuilder inserts instructions at a chosen position: the insertion point is where the next instruction goes, and a pointer-based constructor can insert before an existing instruction or at the end of a block. Lesson 14 builds new blocks and terminates them with the builder.

Mechanically, each `Create*` method constructs the instruction, links it into the block at the builder’s insertion point, and advances the point past it. Successive calls therefore write the instruction stream in order, and each call returns the new value as a `Value *` that a later call can use as an operand — in lesson 14, `CreateLoad` produces `ms.current` and the following `CreateSwitch` takes it as its condition. Operations with no SSA result (`CreateStore`, `CreateUnreachable`) return nothing, matching the void-result entry above.

The constructors choose the point in two ways. The pointer form `IRBuilder<>(invalidBlock)` targets the end of the block, which is the only legal position on a freshly created empty block — the `invalidBuilder` and `dispatchBuilder` of lesson 14. The iterator form `IRBuilder<>(&*entry->getFirstInsertionPt())` targets an existing block instead: `getFirstInsertionPt()` is an iterator to the first legal insertion position, `*` obtains that instruction, `&` hands it to the constructor, and every `Create*` on that builder (`setup`) inserts before it. `SetInsertionPoint` moves an existing builder to a new position. Each builder object holds its own point, so the three builders in the dispatcher step — `setup`, `dispatchBuilder`, `invalidBuilder` — write into three different blocks without stepping on each other.

Two behaviors the book leans on. First, a `Create*` call does not always create: when its operands are constants the method may fold the result and return a `Constant` without inserting any instruction at all — that is the constant-input `CreateSelect` lesson 14’s checkpoint names, and it is why “every Create... call adds exactly one instruction” is an unsafe assumption. Second, `IRBuilder<>` is the default instantiation of the template `IRBuilder<Derived>`: the empty angle brackets give the plain builder that constructs the ordinary instruction classes. Operand types and constants come from the builder’s context through `getInt32Ty()` / `getInt32(n)` (the next entry), not from raw constructor calls.
See the [IRBuilder doxygen](https://llvm.org/doxygen/classllvm_1_1IRBuilder.html).
getInt32Ty / getInt32

getInt32Ty() returns the i32 Type*; getInt32(2) returns the ConstantInt holding a particular value. A builder step often needs both — a type to declare storage, a value to store — and confusing the two is a common type error.
See the [IRBuilder doxygen](https://llvm.org/doxygen/classllvm_1_1IRBuilder.html), where both methods live.
DenseMap

LLVM’s open-addressing key/value container, used here to map BasicBlock* to an unsigned state ID. It is faster than unordered_map in hot pass loops, but its iteration order is not a display order: the vector preserves order, and the map only supports lookup.
Lesson 13’s fix: lookup does not insert a missing key, while operator[] does.
See the [DenseMap doxygen](https://llvm.org/doxygen/classllvm_1_1DenseMap.html).
PreservedAnalyses

See the [Day 1 glossary](#lesson-26) entry "PreservedAnalyses": the value a transformation pass returns, describing which cached analyses remain valid after its changes — `::all()` promises nothing was touched, `::none()` says recompute everything; it reports cache validity only, not behavior.
A changed CFG returns `none()` here: `all()` is a cache-validity promise, not an undo operation.
See [the new pass manager document](https://llvm.org/docs/NewPassManager.html).
eraseFromParent
Removes an instruction from its block and deletes it; the pointer dangles after the call. That is exactly what DemotePHIToStack does to your PHI, and why the pass collects pointers before it mutates.
See the [Instruction doxygen](https://llvm.org/doxygen/classllvm_1_1Instruction.html).
isUsedOutsideOfBlock

A method on an instruction asking whether its result has a user outside a given block — the cross-block test the value preparation runs. It is called on the defining instruction, with the defining block as the argument.
See the [Instruction doxygen](https://llvm.org/doxygen/classllvm_1_1Instruction.html).
DemotePHIToStack / DemoteRegToStack

Free functions in llvm/Transforms/Utils/Local.h: DemotePHIToStack(phi) replaces a PHI’s value flow with stores and loads and erases the PHI; DemoteRegToStack(*I) keeps the original calculation but routes its result through stack memory. Neither is a class method, and the PHI pointer is unusable after the first call.
Lessons 3 and 9 make the calls; lesson 8 reads the installed Local.h signatures first.
See the [Local.cpp source](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/main/llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/Local.cpp).
Checkpoint: Name a construct from this document and the API that reads or writes it. Then state which lesson introduced it and which invariant the construct protects.

items: The `unreachable` terminator — the construct that ends a block by asserting no defined execution reaches that point (actually executing it is undefined behavior, not recovery or input validation). It is written with the builder's `CreateUnreachable` and read as a terminator: `BasicBlock::getTerminator()` returning the `Instruction::Unreachable` opcode, which the guard's terminator whitelist checks.

Lesson 14 points the dispatcher's default case at `ms.invalid`, and lesson 15 finishes that block with `unreachable`; the invariant the construct protects is that the stored state ID is always one we assigned — every stored ID decodes to a real state block, and execution never reaches `ms.invalid`.

quiz.q: Which pair denotes a type and a value, respectively?
choices: getInt32Ty() and getInt32(2)
getInt32(2) and getInt32Ty()
eraseFromParent() and continue
quiz.why: An instruction builder often needs both an LLVM Type* and particular constant values. They are different API inputs.

lessons.originalTitle: Glossary. C++ terms used in Day 2
lessons.summary: The C++ language concepts the Day 2 lessons rely on: pointers and references, casts, classes, and translation units.
lessons.takeaway: Say whether a value is borrowed, copied, or owned before you write the expression.

blocks.text: Pointers and references
How the pass holds and borrows IR objects: pointers for the worklists that must point at instructions, references for the parameters that must not copy them, and the spelling choices between the two.
Pointer vs reference

See the [Day 1 glossary](#lesson-26) entry "Reference vs. pointer": a reference is another name for an existing object; a pointer stores an object’s address. Day 2’s worklists store pointers because they must point at the instruction; pass parameters take references because they borrow it.
See [references on cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/reference.html).
Borrowed reference parameter (Function &)

static bool build(llvm::Function &F) borrows the caller’s function: the body may read and modify it but never owns or copies it. That is why the pass mutates the IR in place instead of returning a new function.
Lesson 18 introduces the declaration; the pass’s own run() takes llvm::Function &F for the same reason.
See [references on cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/reference.html).
Address-of vs reference declaration

The & in a declaration can do two different jobs: next to a name it declares a reference (llvm::Function &F), and as an operator on an expression it takes the address (&BB). Lesson 13’s DenseMap fix is exactly this distinction: BB is a reference alias, and &BB produces the BasicBlock* key.
See [references on cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/reference.html).
Pointer-to-const vs const pointer

const T *p means the pointee is const: you may not write through p, but p may be reseated. T *const p means p itself is const: it may not be reseated, but the pointee is writable. Reading a function’s name as read-only data maps to the first half: the pass never rewrites the symbol, only its uses.
See [cv-qualifiers on cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/cv).
Iterator invalidation

A saved traversal position can stop being valid the moment the underlying collection changes: erasing an instruction mid-loop can leave the iterator past the end, and rehashing a DenseMap invalidates references into its storage. Day 2’s rule is collect all the pointers first, then mutate.
Lessons 1 and 3 make the collect-then-mutate order explicit; the lesson 12 note about DenseMap rehashing is the same rule on the map side.
See [vector::erase on cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/vector/erase.html) for how erasure invalidates positions.
Types and conversion
How C++ chooses and moves types without being told: deduction, the element type a range-for hands you, implicit conversions, and the short-circuit and if-initializer forms the pass relies on.
auto deduction

auto lets the compiler deduce the declared type from the initializer: auto *entry = &F.getEntryBlock() is a BasicBlock* without spelling it out. The deduction is fixed at the declaration; the type does not change with later uses.
See [auto on cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/auto.html).
Range-for element type

The element type of a range-for is set by the declaration: for (auto &BB : F) binds each BB to a reference to the block, while for (auto *BB : phis) iterates pointer values. Lesson 13’s pointer-key bug came from exactly this choice: the loop element is a reference, and the map wanted a pointer.
See [range-based for in expressions on cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/expressions.html).
Upcast / downcast

An upcast treats a derived object as its base type — always safe and automatic, as when &I is accepted where a Value* is expected. A downcast goes through the more specific type and is valid only after a check, which is what dyn_cast exists for.
See [casting on Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casting_(computer_programming)).
Short-circuit evaluation

a && b does not evaluate b when a is false; a || b does not evaluate b when a is true. That matters when the second operand performs a transformation: changed = changed || build(F) skips build whenever demotion already changed the function. Day 2’s fix evaluates build first and then combines, or uses |= on already-computed results.
Lesson 22 meets the bug directly: the orchestrator must not skip construction because demotion changed the function.
See [logical operators on cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/operator_other.html), where short-circuit evaluation is documented.
if-initializers

if (auto *phi = llvm::dyn_cast<llvm::PHINode>(&I)) declares a variable inside the condition and tests it: the pointer exists only inside the if, and the truth test is not null. It is Day 2’s standard checked-cast idiom: one declaration, one check, one scoped pointer.
Lessons 1–2 introduce the form, and lesson 17 uses it throughout the guard.
See [if on cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/if.html).
Classes and translation units
How the pass is split into files: namespaces and headers, declaration versus definition, and the class layout that keeps each pipeline stage in its own translation unit.
namespace

A namespace gives declarations a scoped name — minishield::StateMachineBuilder instead of a bare StateMachineBuilder that could collide with anything else in the translation unit. Day 2’s pass, guard, and builder all live in namespace minishield.
See [namespaces on cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/namespace.html).
#pragma once

See the [Day 1 glossary](#lesson-26) entry "#pragma once": a compiler directive meaning “include this header at most once per translation unit”. Day 2’s builder header (lesson 18) starts with it so the class is declared exactly once even when several files include it.
Lesson 18 introduces the header: the pragma prevents repeated inclusion, the include makes llvm::Function known, and the namespace gives the class its minishield:: name.
Introduced in lesson 18; see also [declarations on cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/declarations.html) for how headers declare what a translation unit may use.
Class vs struct

In C++ the two differ mostly in default access: a class defaults to private, a struct to public. Day 2 declares class StateMachineBuilder with an explicit public: section — the class default is private, so the public specifier is what lets callers use StateMachineBuilder::build(F).
See [classes on cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/class.html).
Static member function

A static member function has no object to call it on: it is invoked as StateMachineBuilder::build(F) and has no implicit this. That is why build() takes the function as an explicit parameter — there is no stored member state for it to reach.
See [static on cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/static.html).
Declaration vs definition

A declaration says what exists (bool build(llvm::Function &F);); a definition gives the body. Lesson 18 teaches the declaration first — a syntax-only step with no CMake change — and the definition comes later, when the body is ready. A translation unit compiles from declarations; linking resolves them to definitions.
See [declarations on cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/declarations.html).
Default arguments

A default argument supplies a value when the caller omits one, so the same call can stay minimal or be explicit: DemotePHIToStack(phi) uses its optional insertion-point argument at the default. Reading the installed declaration is what tells you which arguments are optional.
Lesson 8 reads the Local.h signatures and keeps the optional arguments at their defaults.
See [default arguments on cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/default_arguments.html).
Ownership and lifetime

Whoever owns an object decides when it dies. LLVM owns the IR objects: the function owns its blocks, and a block owns its instructions. A pass holding raw pointers borrows them — it must not outlive the object, and it must not use a pointer after the owner deletes it. A worklist of pointers is safe only while the underlying instructions still exist.
See [lifetime on cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/lifetime.html).
Checkpoint: Pick one expression from the Day 2 lessons and say whether each value in it is borrowed, copied, or owned. Then name the lesson that introduced the construct.

items: Pick `for (auto &BB : F)` (the state-assignment loop over the function's blocks): `F` is borrowed — a reference parameter the pass reads and mutates in place, never owning or copying it; each `BB` is borrowed too — `auto &` binds a reference to the actual block, not a copy, and a copy could not exist anyway because `BasicBlock` is noncopyable (so `for (auto BB : F)` fails to compile); the address-of expression `&BB` produces a `BasicBlock*` key for the state-ID map, where the pointer is a copy of the address but the block it names remains owned by the function.

The construct — a range-for over a function's blocks binding each block by reference — was introduced in lesson 1's PHI collection (the outer `for (auto &BB : F` around the inner `for (auto &I : BB`), and lesson 13's pointer-key fix (`&BB` as the `DenseMap` key rather than the reference itself) is what made the reference-versus-pointer distinction in this exact expression explicit.

quiz.q: In the declaration static bool build(llvm::Function &F), what does the & do to F?
choices: Borrows the caller's Function: the body may read and modify it but never owns or copies it
Copies the Function onto build's own stack
Declares a pointer that must be dereferenced before use
quiz.why: A reference parameter is an alias for the caller’s object. build() changes the caller’s Function in place, which is why the pass mutates the IR instead of returning a new one.
